Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

It took two attempts and more than a week of troubleshooting, but Google is once again declaring victory over YouTube‘s frustrating Server Error 400 bug on Android. This time, the manufacturer has confirmed that the issue is fixed and has simpler instructions for anyone still struggling to access the app.

In an patch to its official support thread, Google marked the issue as FIXED, saying Android people should now be able to open YouTube and load videos without the dreaded error message.

The announcement brings another chapter to a problem that Google previously thought it had solved.

It has been revealed that on November 1, YouTube announced that the error had been fixed, only to acknowledge its persistence two days later. The November 3 update confirmed that some Android customers were still encountering the error, prompting Google’s teams to continue investigating.

The problem prevented affected people from accessing YouTube or loading videos normally, often displaying a “Server Error 400” or “There was a problem with the server [400]” message. However, it wasn’t widespread enough to affect everyone.

Google’s latest announcement also changes the troubleshooting advice. Previously, affected owners were instructed to reinstall YouTube or clear the app’s storage, both of which remove downloaded videos. This time, Google simply recommends updating YouTube to the latest version and reopening the app if the error persists.

Google hasn’t explained what caused the problem or what changed behind the scenes to resolve it.

It has been revealed that given that the first all-clear proved premature, it’ll be interesting to see whether this latest fix holds. For now, though, Google considers the problem resolved and is asking anyone still experiencing trouble to report it in the official support thread.

This doesn’t yet appear to be a widespread issue, but it doesn’t seem to be an isolated one either. The complaints stem from a recent Google Support post, where a Pixel 10 Pro XL user reports that their device lost its wireless charging capabilities after installing Google’s November 5 revision, which rolled out with the new Pixel Drop.

According to the user, when they throw their phone onto a certified Qi2 wireless charger, the phone indicates that it is charging, but the battery percentage actually goes down. They added that they’ve tried out several Qi2 chargers that worked perfectly before the Pixel revision, but none really work now. Their battery diagnostics are normal, and the usual troubleshooting steps, including a hard reboot, don’t offer any relief.

In a recent development, others in the thread corroborated the claim. One user pointed out similar inconsistencies:.

A different user doubled down on the claim and said that Google Support hasn’t been very helpful:.

Recent findings suggest that although not exactly the same, a different user reported experiencing similar wireless charging problems after a recent software upgrade. The user reports seeing a “Connected but not charging” status and claims that the same wireless charger worked previously without issues using the same phone.

Recent findings suggest that repositioning the phone or restarting it “sometimes” corrects the challenges. The user didn’t explicitly link the problem to the November upgrade, but they did say that “recent updates seem to have broken wireless charging.” Note that there is no concrete evidence linking the bug to the November update, beyond timing and user claims.

In a recent development, interestingly, Google’s changelog for the November revision lists a battery and charging fix. The tech giant wrote that it fixed an issue that was causing the charging indicator to appear when no charger was connected. The fix is unlikely to be connected to the potential newly introduced bug.

Sources indicate that we’ve reached out to Google to ask whether it is aware of the complaints and if the November revision might be responsible. We’ll update this article if and when we hear back.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the decision was announced by NVIDIA’s board of directors who appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

In a move that has seemed inevitable for the past few days, Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, according to a statement from the firm.

In a recent development, the decision was announced by NVIDIA’s board of directors who appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Kress will serve in both roles until NVIDIA appoints a permanent replacement CEO. The board said it is considering both internal and external candidates.

It has been revealed that huang co-founded NVIDIA and has been its only CEO. He led the company through its transformation from a comfortably successful graphics chip maker into a $4 trillion global powerhouse that is the central player of the AI boom. He has also been the public face of it.

In a recent development, huang’s stunning downfall began two weeks ago when The New York Times published a story that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman from China who worked for a Singapore-based NVIDIA customer called Megaspeed. Reportedly, she had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Huang as Megaspeed funneled AI chips to China.

Recent findings suggest that on November 8, Huang issued a statement admitting to the affair and apologizing to his family, as well as NVIDIA employees and shareholders. That same day, the NVIDIA board put out its own statement that it was assigning outside counsel to look into the espionage but had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”.

Speculation about the future of NVIDIA and Huang’s role in it has run rampant, and was accelerated last night when The Latest York Times published a story that Huang had also had an affair with an NVIDIA executive who was a direct report. NVIDIA’s 10-member board met overnight following the news and put out its statement about Huang’s resignation and Kress’ appointment this morning.

Sources indicate that “Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey Jones, chair of NVIDIA’s board of directors, said in NVIDIA’s statement today. “The [b]oard has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”.

Following the news this morning, President Donald Trump, who has stood by Huang through the scandal, posted on Truth Social that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be his replacement. Trump wrote: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”.

Huang’s departure has affected NVIDIA’s stock price, but beyond that, it threatens to shake up the AI industry as a whole.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The crescent Moon is now more visible in the evening sky, with enough of its surface illuminated to start picking out some lunar features.
  • It has been revealed that as of Friday, Nov.
  • After nights of darkness and limited visibility, Moon gazing is back tonight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The crescent Moon is now more visible in the evening sky, with enough of its surface illuminated to start picking out some lunar features. Keep reading to find out what you might be able to see.

It has been revealed that as of Friday, Nov. 13, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Crescent phase, with 14% of its surface visible.

After nights of darkness and limited visibility, Moon gazing is back tonight. If you don't have any visual aids, you'll be able to see the Mare Crisium and the Mare Fecunditatis. With binoculars or a telescope, you'll also see the Endymion Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

The Moon takes approximately 29.5 days to complete one full cycle. As it orbits Earth, the amount of sunlight reflecting off its surface that we can see changes, creating the different phases. This takes us from the Newly introduced Moon to the Full Moon and back again, before the cycle begins once more, according to NASA.

Latest Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

According to recent reports, first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.
  • It has been revealed that gemini’s task automation is one of the more ambitious and impressive things Google has shipped on Android this year.
  • According to recent reports, beyond a handful of examples, Google hasn’t really shared which apps actually work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

It has been revealed that gemini’s task automation is one of the more ambitious and impressive things Google has shipped on Android this year. Instead of handing you a link, Gemini opens the app on a virtual screen, taps through it on your behalf, and stops just before checkout so you can confirm. It began rolling out in March with just six apps: Lyft, Uber, Grubhub, DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Starbucks, on the Galaxy S26 series and later the Pixel 10 series. In July, Google said support was expanding “to more than 40 popular apps,” and this week, it announced that task automation is expanding to the UK, India, and Japan.

According to recent reports, beyond a handful of examples, Google hasn’t really shared which apps actually work. Its blog posts and help pages only mention “select apps.” Google instead has tried to focus on the task category, mentioning support for “everyday tasks” like:.

However, I’ve now found the list of supported apps itself, and it’s far longer than Google has let on.

An Android Authority exclusive you won’t find anywhere else.

Gemini’s task automation runs on an Android framework called Computer Control, which we first spotted in October 2025. Google’s developer documentation claims the framework only works with “a limited set of target apps,” with plans to “expand this support over time.”.

Turns out, Google delivers this list of target apps from its servers to Android phones. Each entry pairs an app’s package name with its signing certificate, so only the official Play Store version of an app qualifies for task automation through Gemini.

Recent findings suggest that as of November 12, the target app list on stable Android 17 QPR2 holds 114 apps. That’s up from 106 just two days earlier, on November 10 on Android 17 QPR1.

The eight latest additions lean heavily on Australia and Canada: regional apps for McDonald’s, KFC, and Starbucks in Australia, plus Best Buy Canada, McDonald’s Canada, Burger King Canada, and KFC Canada, along with 7-Eleven’s 7NOW delivery app in the US. Neither Australia nor Canada are officially supported for Gemini task automation yet, so these additions could hint at where Google is headed next, though it hasn’t stated so.

Phones on Android Canary get a longer 134-app target app list: the same 114 apps plus 20 test additions, covered further below.

The target app list for Gemini task automation goes well beyond the categories Google has talked about. Alongside the expected food delivery, ride-hailing, travel, and shopping apps, it also includes work and productivity apps such as Microsoft Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams, and OneNote, as well as Slack and Evernote.

Industry observers note that curiously, the presence of this target app list isn’t limited to phones that officially support the Gemini task automation feature. I found the identical list on my Galaxy S26 Ultra, which supports task automation, and on my Pixel 7a and Pixel 9 Pro XL, which don’t. Phones still on Android 16 don’t get it at all, though.

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

Industry observers note that when Google mentioned the expansion in India this week, it didn’t specify which regional apps work with task automation. The target app list I found mentions these nine regional apps for India: Zomato, Blinkit, Rapido, BookMyShow, ixigo, McDelivery, KFC India, Burger King India, and Starbucks India.

To put this list to the test, I asked Gemini on my Galaxy S26 Ultra to order food from a nearby restaurant on Zomato.

Gemini opened Zomato, navigated out of a dark mode toggle screen, searched for the restaurant, found the dish, picked the right portion size, and added it to my cart (along with a free dessert, nice). It then stopped and asked me to finish the payment myself.

A request to add a liter of milk on Blinkit worked the same way: Gemini searched, picked a 1-liter pack of milk, and took me to the cart. Starbucks India worked up until checkout too.

Sources indicate that then I ran the same requests on competitor apps, Swiggy and Zepto, which aren’t on the list. Gemini refused both outright: “Swiggy is not available for automation” and “Zepto is not available for automation.”.

Both Swiggy (food delivery) and Zepto (grocery ordering) are covered under the app categories Google mentions, but since the apps aren’t explicitly allowlisted in the target app list, Gemini does not support task automation for them.

Recent findings suggest that confusingly, not every app present in the target app list works today. The clearest examples I ran into are Microsoft Word and Outlook.

When I asked Gemini to edit a document in Word, it replied, “I can’t directly edit files inside the Microsoft Word app on your device.” Asking it to share a Word file got “I don’t have access to Microsoft Word,” and asking it to open a recent document only either debuted the app (but not the document) or brought up a button to launch the app.

In a recent development, when my colleague C. Scott Brown tried creating a document on his Pixel 11 Pro in the US, Gemini simply generated a DOCX file itself and handed it to Word, without operating the app at all.

Outlook went the same way, with Gemini producing a compose-email link rather than automating anything.

If you pay closer attention to the wording of Gemini’s refusals, you can spot a pattern. Swiggy and Zepto are “not available for automation,” which suggests these apps are being blocked outright. Word shows “I can’t directly edit files” and “I don’t have access,” suggesting Gemini has a second layer of restrictions on top of Android’s target app list.

Recent findings suggest that this could mean that apps not only need to be on Google’s target app list to work, but Gemini also needs to support the kind of task you’re asking for — which is where Google’s task category could come in. Right now, the supported tasks include food, groceries, rides, and reservations, but not document work.

So why are Word, Excel, Teams, and Slack on the list at all? There’s a fair chance Google is laying the groundwork for productivity tasks down the line, and these entries are there for testing, so I wouldn’t count on Gemini filling out your spreadsheets just yet.

These are the apps on the stable Android 17 QPR2 target app list as of November 12, grouped by the market each app mainly serves:.

The list also includes a “com.sampleapp” placeholder, which I haven’t counted.

In a recent development, google hasn’t published this target app list or mentioned which apps work in the UK, India, or Japan. Since the list is delivered from Google’s servers, it could change at any time.

Sources indicate that as mentioned, being on the target app list doesn’t guarantee Gemini will automate all tasks within that app right now. Read this list alongside Google’s targeted “everyday tasks” list to see which tasks in which apps have the best chance of running through Gemini on your Gemini Intelligence-supporting Android 17 phone.

As of today, Gemini Intelligence is supported on these phones and tablets:.

It has been revealed that on Android Canary, the target app list is even longer still. My Pixel 9 Pro XL running the latest Android Canary 2611 presently carries 134 apps in the target app list! This includes the 114 apps in the stable list, plus another 20, namely Flipkart, Reddit, X, Strava, KakaoTalk, LINE, Costco, Domino’s, iFood, Rappi, Mercado Libre, Wolt, Shopee, Postmates, Safeway, MyFitnessPal, Peloton, Picsart, FaceApp, and AllTrails. Flipkart’s presence is interesting, given that Google is separately testing Flipkart checkout inside Gemini in India.

The Canary target app list also includes Google’s own mock versions of DoorDash, Uber, Lyft, Grubhub, Uber Eats, and Instacart, which look like internal test apps.

According to recent reports, during my testing, I learned that the Canary list includes the extra apps that sit on top of whatever the stable target app list holds at the time. For instance, the Canary list on November 10 showed 126 apps (106 apps from the then-stable list plus 20 Canary apps). When I jumped to the newest Android 17 QPR2 release, it showed the newer 114-app list, and jumping back to Canary got the newer 134-app list within minutes of boot.

We’ve reached out to Google for a statement on the target app list for Gemini task automation, and we’ll update this article when we learn more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shortly after bans on certain pornographic content took effect in the UK, some lawmakers are calling for further restrictions.

On Nov. 6, possessing and publishing explicit content depicting strangulation/suffocation, incest (including fake incest), and people under 16, or pretending to be, became criminal offenses.

Recent findings suggest that days later, on Nov. 10, a cross-party group called the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Commercial Sexual Exploitation published a report called "Only Exploitation," which calls for a step further: criminalizing online platforms profiting from commercial live streaming of pornography and other sex work. (A government spokesperson told The Mirror that it's reviewing the law on prostitution.).

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

The report claims that "visitors to webcamming platforms are no longer just pornography viewers; they become, in effect, pornography directors." It also contends that camming/livestreaming harms women and girls through sexual coercion and exploitation, security and privacy risks, perpetuates violent attitudes, and normalizes sexual exploitation. The report includes quotes from interviews with APPG and research such as one paper on webcam sex platform competition and another on Romanian women's experiences camming.

"The webcamming trade acts as a magnet for exploiters," Tonia Antoniazzi MP and Tracy Gilbert MP stated in the report's foreword.

However, Dr Carolina Are, digital criminologist at the London School of Economics and Political Science, told Mashable that the report doesn't consider that people can do sex work voluntarily. "It effectively likens sex work to exploitation, which is a known trope in anti-sex work campaigning," she remarked.

According to recent reports, the experiences narrated by participants are horrific and show how these platforms can be used for exploitation, Are continued, adding however that the report as a whole seems to blame the job for exploitation, when exploitation is done by perpetrators. It's enabled by stigmatisation against sex workers that doesn't encourage reporting, and by a tech infrastructure and governance that's for profit, and not for people.

The report also calls on the UK to outlaw "e-pimping," or individuals who facilitate and profit from another person performing on livestream, and that the country recognize e-pimping as human trafficking. It refers to "OnlyFans managers" as "e-pimps" and cites the BBC's recent investigation into how such managers and "agents" take advantage of models by controlling their earnings, as well as other journalistic reports.

Are said the investigations are reputable, but are used sensationally. Meanwhile, she pointed out that research reveals that many people choose to do digital sex work for reasons ranging from personal preference to the fact that much of sex work, including camming, can be done from home (which suits immunocompromised people, people with disabilities, caretakers, or those otherwise not suited for a 9-5).

Digital sex work has also been found to reduce violence against sex workers — "an opportunity this report seems to ignore," Are stated.

In a recent development, porn filmmaker and performer Vex Ashley told Mashable, "We're seeing an unprecedented rollback of our sexual freedoms and lives online. This isn't just about criminalising the imaginations and exploration of consenting adults but also sweeping the rug from under so many sex workers whose livelihoods and safety depend on these sites.".

Additionally, the group's report recommends enabling the withdrawal of consent with the distribution of pre-recorded porn, as well as allowing law enforcement to access all content hosted and streamed by porn sites.

"The withdrawal of consent part of the recommendations is important, and so is the recognition of exploitation for those who extort and abuse cammers," Are said. "But giving platforms and the police more surveillance power against an over-policed, over-censored and over-surveilled user base is concerning.".

According to recent reports, removing a source of income from marginalized people doesn't protect them, she said, also pointing out that the report doesn't touch on poverty, which is one of the main drivers of sex work. "So this report is removing a source of income for the same women that it claims to protect," she said, "potentially pushing them into more underground work where they may be more exposed to physical violence.".

Google’s Intelligent Eyewear is great at translation, but I wouldn’t use it to have a conversation

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.
  • According to recent reports, google is finally getting serious about smart glasses, and this week the first Intelligent Eyewear collections go up for pre-order thanks to a collaboration involving Gentle Monster, Warby Parker, and Samsung.
  • Recent findings suggest that A few days ago, I had the opportunity to get some early hands-on time with the smart glasses at Gentle Monster’s New York pop-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

According to recent reports, google is finally getting serious about smart glasses, and this week the first Intelligent Eyewear collections go up for pre-order thanks to a collaboration involving Gentle Monster, Warby Parker, and Samsung. That means that Google has to make a strong case for why shoppers will want to drop $400 or more this holiday season on these frames. One of the big features being promoted is the ability to act as a translation tool, helping to break down language barriers, but some aspects of that support end up working a lot better than others.

Recent findings suggest that A few days ago, I had the opportunity to get some early hands-on time with the smart glasses at Gentle Monster’s New York pop-up. The brand put together a visually stunning event space, packed with demos highlighting many of the different workflows owners might experience when using Android XR smart glasses: preparing recipe shopping lists, creating music playlists, and even getting workout tips.

If you saw Gentle Monster’s teaser video last week for its Joaquin Phoenix short film, you might have noticed that it felt a bit light on concrete details about what these glasses actually do. But amidst all the surreal imagery, we do get one call-out: “Translate for me,” Phoenix requests.

And indeed, smart glasses can be a very convenient way to easily access Google’s powerful translation services. One aspect that worked great for me was tapping into Gemini to have the glasses translate text on objects I was looking at. That can be anything from signs on a wall, to text on products at a market.

Industry observers note that here, Gemini’s able to use contextual clues to help sort out exactly what you’re interested in — pick something up, or point at it, and Gemini can infer that this is the text you need translated. And then, of course, you can ask follow-up questions to your heart’s content, or use that information to get Gemini started on other tasks.

Recent findings suggest that these glasses offer two distinct translation modes: There’s Gemini, which sort of operates with a jack-of-all-trades approach, or you can explicitly call up Translate with a dedicated two-finger tap on one arm of the frames. This latter mode is especially suitable for speech, and in some cases, it really shines.

Recent findings suggest that one such demo involved watching foreign-language TV programming. Even with audio coming through a small TV speaker, the glasses have no problem following along, piping out a translated copy through speakers in the frame’s arms which sound perfectly clear to the wearer, but are truly difficult for others to perceive, even just a couple feet away.

Recent findings suggest that I expected this to work nicely when I was facing the audio source, with beam-forming tech focusing the microphones’ attention. But I was also pleasantly surprised to learn that this works just as well for indirect speech — think: PA announcements, like maybe departures at a train station. Even when not looking straight at the speaker, translation works just fine. The glasses also keep up just fine when those announcements switch to a new language every few seconds, with no additional user input needed.

Industry observers note that so far, I’ve been looking at rather impersonal translation opportunities. What about when you need to interact one-on-one with someone whose language you don’t understand? Intelligent Eyewear is up to the task and does get the job done here. But the experience is also a whole lot more awkward than I think I’d be comfortable with, especially dealing with strangers.

Give your glasses that double-finger tap and they’ll be ready to start translating speech, no need to deliver a vocal command to Gemini, or specify the language — it just starts working. And if I’m judging Google on the actual quality of the translation provided, I’d have to give to these glasses high marks. No surprise there — Google’s had tons of experience with both speech-to-text and automatic translation.

The problem, at least as far as I’m concerned, lies in the experience side of this, and how you receive that translation. After the subject starts speaking, you’ll hear your glasses follow along with their translation just a beat later — it’s no interminable, multi-second pause, but there is a noticeable delay.

Sources indicate that that’s also just long enough to interfere with some of the subtle ways we communicate. For instance, I found myself instinctively nodding along and reacting to parts of the conversation, but swiftly realized how my actions now no longer align with the speaker’s words — and I’m responding to what they stated a sentence ago.

In a recent development, this being fully audio-based further complicates the temporal challenges here. You have to listen along to the translated words coming out of your glasses at a regular speaking pace. If you were just using Google Translate on your phone, you might be able to quickly glance over the fully translated message all at once, and zero-in on the part you need to respond to. With the glasses, it can feel like you’re waiting for the translation to catch up.

Sources indicate that there’s also the not-minor concern of this being one-way; your glasses don’t have a loudspeaker that can translate your own voice into someone else’s language. So, unless you’re speaking to someone who already has at least a limited grasp on your own tongue (or vice-versa), there’s still going to be a huge impediment in the way of this interaction feeling like a natural, flowing conversation.

According to recent reports, I don’t want to sound overly negative here, as this is still a very impressive translation solution for what it does. The important thing is to just not go into this with the wrong expectations. In certain circumstances, even this one-way, slightly delayed translation can be extremely useful. But maybe don’t give up on that language-learning app just yet.

Both Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear frames are available for pre-order now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of us don’t have hours to devote to working out, so when there’s an exercise that can strengthen multiple muscle groups at the same time, I’m quick to use with my personal training clients.

Quadruped rainbows are one such exercise. This no-equipment move targets the glutes, hamstrings, hips, deep core, and even the shoulder stabilizing muscles, making it a great option when time is limited. The standard version is appropriate for beginners, but there are plenty of ways to up the challenge level if you’re more advanced.

Roll out your yoga mat and give quadruped rainbows a try during your next workout.

Before trying any latest exercise, be sure to check in with your doctor first. They may recommend avoiding certain movements based on your health background.

Industry observers note that beginners should consider working with a certified personal trainer to learn how to do quadruped rainbows properly. A trainer can also provide modifications if needed and progression options when you’re ready. Doing any exercise with poor form can lead to pain or injury.

Aside from a yoga mat, those with sore knees may want to use a pillow or a rolled-up towel for additional cushioning.

It has been revealed that start with one set of 10 reps on each side. Gradually increase your reps to 12 on each side and add an additional set. Eventually, you’ll aim for 3 sets of 15 reps on each side.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Do quadruped rainbows 2-3 times a week at first, then work your way up to 3-4 times per week. The exercise can be done on its own, as a part of another workout, or as a warm-up for more intense exercise.

According to recent reports, you should feel muscle fatigue but never sharp pain when doing this exercise. Stop the exercise and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

Here’s how to do quadruped rainbows:.

This exercise works the glutes, hip abductors, hip adductors, hamstrings, deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques, and rotator cuff muscles.

Industry observers note that the arc-like movement of the leg promotes optimal hip mobility and range of motion. In the quadruped position, your deep core works to stabilize your entire body as the active leg moves into each position.

Additionally, quadruped rainbows don’t require any equipment and are accessible for a wide range of fitness levels and abilities.

It has been revealed that if you’ve just started to work out regularly, you may find it difficult to keep proper form during this exercise. The biggest form compensations I see are rotating the hips side to side as you move the leg back and forth, excessive arching in the lower back, and sinking the chest towards the floor.

It has been revealed that if you notice any of these compensations, it may indicate some deep core weakness. In addition to including exercises like diaphragmatic breathing, planks, and hollow holds in your routine, you may also want to modify the quadruped rainbow.

Instead of sweeping your leg to the side in a semi-circular motion, try simply lifting the active leg. Aim to bring the knee and ankle in line with the hips. Hold briefly, and then lower the toe back towards the floor.

You can also practice donkey kicks in preparation for the standard quadruped rainbow. Keep the active leg bent at a 90-degree angle, then kick the heel towards the ceiling. Pause briefly, then lower the active leg back to the starting position.

As you get stronger and more conditioned, quadruped rainbows may not challenge you like it did at first. The easiest way to increase the challenge is to add reps and sets.

That being noted, sometimes doing more than 15 reps of an exercise can get rather monotonous. Wearing ankle weights is another easy way to up the ante, as is performing the exercise on an unstable surface like a balance pad or Bosu ball. Just be sure your form stays solid throughout the exercise.

#516. I found a free AI trick that could make your old smart TV feel fresh again

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1314 w)
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomsguide

I found a free AI trick that could make your old smart TV feel fresh again

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's nothing more frustrating than a smart TV that takes forever to load an app, gets bogged down by menus or constantly recommends shows you have no interest in watching.
  • But what if you could give your existing TV a refresh without spending anything?
  • A free AI setup could help you clean up unnecessary apps, simplify your home screen and adjust settings that might be slowing things down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's nothing more frustrating than a smart TV that takes forever to load an app, gets bogged down by menus or constantly recommends shows you have no interest in watching. And if your TV still has a perfectly good picture, replacing it just because the software feels outdated seems like a waste of money.

But what if you could give your existing TV a refresh without spending anything?

A free AI setup could help you clean up unnecessary apps, simplify your home screen and adjust settings that might be slowing things down. Better yet, it runs locally on your computer, so you don't need another subscription or a cloud-based AI assistant.

By using a local AI agent, you can manage a smart TV over your home network. It isn't quite as simple as installing an app, and the results will depend on your television. But if you're comfortable following a few technical steps, it could be an interesting way to get more life out of a TV you already own.

The setup uses three free tools: Ollama, Hermes Agent and an AI model from the Qwen3 family.

In a recent development, ollama runs the AI model directly on your computer, while Hermes Agent acts as the assistant that carries out your instructions. Think of it this way, instead of asking a chatbot for advice and manually following its recommendations, you're asking an AI agent to inspect your TV and potentially make approved changes for you.

Sources indicate that for example, you could ask it to identify apps you no longer use, turn off unnecessary animations that randomly come on, or help simplify your home screen. The goal is to reduce clutter and potentially improve responsiveness, although there's no guarantee that these changes will make every TV noticeably faster.

Industry observers note that the biggest advantage is that the AI itself can operate without sending requests to a cloud service. Once the software and model have been downloaded, you can run the setup on your own hardware without paying per prompt.

Before jumping in, you'll need a computer capable of running a local AI model and a compatible smart TV connected to the same home network.

Android TV and Google TV are the most straightforward candidates for the original workflow because they support Android Debug Bridge, or ADB, which lets a computer communicate with the television.

Industry observers note that LG TVs running webOS also have developer tools, but they use a different connection process. Samsung's mainstream smart TVs generally run Tizen, so you shouldn't follow Android TV instructions on a Samsung set.

Here's the basic process for a compatible Android TV or Google TV.

Open your TV's Settings menu and look for the device information section, usually under System or About.

Find the Android TV OS build number and select it repeatedly, typically seven times, until developer options become available.

Next, look for debugging settings. Depending on your TV's software version, you may be able to enable wireless debugging and pair your computer over Wi-Fi.

Some older televisions require a different ADB connection method, so check the instructions for your specific model before proceeding.

According to recent reports, open your television's network settings and locate its IP address. You'll need this so your computer knows which device to connect to.

Make sure your computer and TV are connected to the same trusted home network.

Visit Ollama's website and install the version for your computer. The original tutorial uses a model from the Qwen3 family.

For example, you can download and run Qwen3 8B by entering the following command in your computer's terminal: ollama run qwen3:8b.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that running AI locally requires processing power and memory. If you're using an older computer, a smaller compatible model may be more practical, although its ability to follow complex instructions could be limited.

Next, install Hermes Agent and configure it to use your locally running model.

Industry observers note that hermes is the software that translates your requests into actions. The model decides what to do, while the agent uses the tools available on your computer to perform those tasks.

You'll also need to establish and authorize the connection between your computer and television. Simply entering the TV's IP address isn't enough on devices that require ADB pairing or other authentication.

This is where the fun begins. AI engineer and YouTube creator Fahd Mirza, who demonstrated how to use a free, locally running AI agent to manage an older smart TV, has shared a free prompt on GitHub designed to help the agent inspect and clean up an Android TV.

The prompt instructs the agent to check available memory, identify installed apps and separate them into categories based on whether they're needed.

It also asks the AI to get your permission before changing anything, disable apps rather than uninstall them and keep a record of changes so they can be reversed.

One of the more ambitious instructions asks the agent to build a simplified home screen without ads or unwanted recommendations. That's an interesting possibility, but it should be treated as an experimental request rather than a guaranteed feature. Full transparency, I wasn't able to pull that one off, but if you have tried and it worked for you, please let me know in the comments. Just start with something simple and reversible, such as asking the agent to report available memory without making any changes.

The most appealing thing about this approach is that it gives you another option before replacing a television that's otherwise working fine. There's also a privacy benefit. Since the AI model runs locally, your prompts don't have to be processed by a cloud AI provider. That doesn't mean your smart TV stops collecting data through its own apps and services, however.

Sources indicate that there are some important downsides. Developer settings can give software powerful access to your television, and an AI agent can make mistakes even when you've instructed it to ask permission first. Disabling the wrong system app could cause problems, while a factory reset may erase your settings and require you to sign in to your streaming services again. Not a big deal, but as someone who can never remember passwords, it's a frustration I felt was worth mentioning.

In a recent development, it's also worth remembering that removing apps or changing animations won't fix every performance problem. A TV with an aging processor or limited memory will still have those hardware limitations.

For most people, this isn't going to be easier than using the settings menu or connecting an inexpensive streaming stick. But if you enjoy experimenting with AI and want more control over a television you already own, it could help you get a little more mileage out of your current setup.

Breaking: 5 things iPhone 20 should steal from iPhone Duo (and 3 things it shouldn't)

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone Duo is easily the most impressive device Apple has made thus far, at least since the early years of the iPhone.
  • According to recent reports, but as big a deal as the first foldable iPhone is, 2027 will mark the 20th anniversary of the very first iPhone.
  • Recent findings suggest that but there's guaranteed to be a lot more to the next iPhone than just a fancy design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone Duo is easily the most impressive device Apple has made thus far, at least since the early years of the iPhone. Not only is it a whole new form factor, it includes things that you straight-up won't find on traditional iPhones. Certainly not the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

According to recent reports, but as big a deal as the first foldable iPhone is, 2027 will mark the 20th anniversary of the very first iPhone. Rumor has it that, like the iPhone X in 2017, Apple will celebrate the milestone with an all-upcoming iPhone design. Word has it that this so-called iPhone 20 will feature a curved glass body that makes the phone look like it's made of 100% glass.

Recent findings suggest that but there's guaranteed to be a lot more to the next iPhone than just a fancy design. And if Apple has any sense it should take some of the better parts of the iPhone Duo for the iPhone 20, while also making sure to ignore other aspects of the foldable's design.

Recent findings suggest that you may be thinking, "isn't the iPhone 20 supposed to have an all-glass design? How does titanium fit into it?", and you make a valid point. The titanium used on other iPhones is only present at the surface of the frame, and the internal body is made from much cheaper aluminum.

If the iPhone 20 replaces that metal frame with glass, then there's no space for titanium, right? Yes, but that hinges on the curved all-glass design rumor actually coming true. Glass is not the easiest material to work with, especially when you're trying to do latest things. So there's a chance that design may not happen, and if it doesn't Apple needs to bring back that premium material to get that mix of strength and low weight.

Because, let's be honest, the anodized aluminum shell isn't really cutting it right now.

In a recent development, steve Jobs may have hated the idea of using a stylus with an iPhone, but the iPhone Duo proved that their usefulness isn't just limited to iPads. Sure, the iPhone 20 won't have as much screen space as the iPhone Duo's 7.6-inch inner display, but that doesn't mean we have to be limited to finger-based control.

Offering Apple Pencil support on iPhones means you get a lot more precision control. Whether you want to draw, write, take notes, and so on. It offers a bunch more versatility to the way you control your iPhone, and in a way that's totally optional. This clearly isn't one of those early smartphones that only worked if you kept hold of a little plastic tip.

Recent findings suggest that in a similar situation, Apple may have insisted that Touch ID is wholly inferior to Face ID, from a security standpoint, but it's nice to have options. The iPhone Duo shows that Apple can add the power button Touch ID to an iPhone, offering a discreet fingerprint scanner away from the front of the phone.

Sources indicate that this shouldn't necessarily mean the loss of Face ID, as was the case with iPhone Duo. It would be nice if Apple offered both, and gave people the option of which biometric security option they prefer. Personally, I much prefer Touch ID over Face ID, but some of my colleagues would disagree.

Plus, where security is concerned, no amount of biometric security will make up for a weak passcode.

According to recent reports, split-screen multitasking is not an uncommon feature on modern phones, but it's been totally absent from iPhones until the launch of iPhone Duo — and that needs to change. Admittedly, split-screen multitasking is more troublesome on a phone screen, since there's less space to fit multiple windows. However, that doesn't mean it can't be useful on slab phones.

We've all experienced times when we're using our phone for something, and keep having to move back and forth between different apps. Having the option to multitask means that you could just load those two apps up side by side instead. Saving you the hassle of switching, and avoiding any awkward reloading that the apps might want to do when you return.

Another feature that's so common people don't even think about anymore is the hole punch camera. It's also something Apple seems to have deliberately avoided offering until the release of the iPhone Duo — and it's about time it came to more iPhones.

The obvious problem has always been Face ID hardware. This is why Apple had such large notches for so long, and why it later adopted the Dynamic Island. But we're getting to the stage where most of that hardware has been hidden away, and the iPhone 20 is the perfect time for Apple to push the rest of it under the screen where we can't see it.

If Apple can hide a camera under the Duo's screen, I'm sure it can hide the remainder of Face ID — even if the camera itself isn't ready to be out of sight.

One of the early iPhone 20 rumors was that it would have an uninterrupted display, thanks to the adoption of under-display tech. However, at least one recent rumor has contradicted those claims, and I hope it turns out to be correct. Apple markets the Duo's under-display camera as a "FaceTime camera," meant to be used for video calls rather than selfies. All because the camera quality is not very good compared to traditional selfie cameras.

The camera is hidden under the display by pixels that can effectively be switched off. Combined with a localized area of low pixel density, it allows light through to reach the camera. Sadly there are still obstacles in the way that interfere with that process, even if they're not as easy to see, and that affects the camera's quality. It's why under-display cameras fell out of favor in the first place.

According to recent reports, that's fine on a foldable that already has a traditional selfie camera, and the option to shoot selfies with the main cameras. But the iPhone 20 won't have either of those things, and opting for an under-display camera is just going to mean customers won't be able to take nice selfies.

We have seen an explosion of wide-shaped foldables this year, seemingly in anticipation of iPhone Fold and for the most part that design change has gone down pretty well. The shorter and wider screens are fairly comfortable to use, and there tends to be less unused space when you're watching a show or move on the foldable screen.

According to recent reports, but we've also started seeing some phone companies produce non-foldable devices with wider screens. I've never used one, and I can't comment on how they compare to normal phone dimensions, but this trend is not something Apple should copy.

In a recent development, apple isn't one for chasing trends, so this isn't likely to happen, but considering wider non-folding phones is still an unproven design, no phone firm should be rushing to switch up its entire design language. Least of all a company that only releases six models each year.

Industry observers note that the nanotexture display coating has a bunch of benefits for the iPhone Duo, ensuring a glare-free display and minimizing the look of the central crease. However, it also has the added hindrance of reducing the vividness of colors and making the screen look more washed out.

This is not something we want from the iPhone 20. There's no crease to hide, for starters, and the current anti-glare technology employed on iPhone 18 Pro Max seems to be doing a pretty good job and ensuring the screen stays readable in bright light. Which means the negatives of the nano-texture coating probably outweigh the positives. Unless Apple can solve the color problem and ensure the screen is still as durable as Ceramic Shield 2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that the HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

It has been revealed that the contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

The Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:.

This function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

It has been revealed that CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

Recent findings suggest that but APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently notes the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium problem in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

Industry observers note that none of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely new, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:.

Industry observers note that the browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most upcoming CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

The raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never update. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:.

Older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

Industry observers note that one thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”.

Industry observers note that mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

According to recent reports, take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.).

In a recent development, furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:.

Recent findings suggest that the background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

According to recent reports, and here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

It has been revealed that if the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

In a recent development, the function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

Industry observers note that if a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

According to recent reports, pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:.

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

According to recent reports, also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:.

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:.

One custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

In a recent development, this pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:.

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:.

Industry observers note that when the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

According to recent reports, the practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:.

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

In a recent development, there’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

For context on what this replaces:.

According to recent reports, sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

It has been revealed that the variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.).

Sources indicate that contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

That 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, once two distinct deal-shopping days, Black Friday and Cyber Monday have basically merged into one massive shopping extravaganza. The lines really began to blur when the world shut down in 2020, and brick-and-mortar stores hosted online sales in lieu of in-person Black Friday events. In 2026, lines outside stores are practically nonexistent. We certainly can't see them.

While major retailers will be running holiday sales throughout all of November, savvy shoppers know that Black Friday and Cyber Monday (and the few days surrounding them) still remain the absolute biggest shopping days of the year for their ability to reliably trigger record-low prices on major-ticket items (like TVs, Apple devices, smartwatches, headphones, and of course, Amazon's own devices). That includes discounts that beat Amazon's massively hyped October Prime Day deals.

Industry observers note that if you're debating when you should start adding big-ticket items to your cart and whether it's better to shop on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, you've come to the right place. After years of covering both sales extensively, here's our expert analysis.

Way back in the age of MySpace and AIM — aka 2005 — the National Retail Federation debuted the term "Cyber Monday" after realizing that the Monday after Thanksgiving saw a flood of online sales. This was likely due to shoppers using their faster internet connections at work on Monday morning to snag deals, or at least that's what they credited it to. That, of course, and the fact that online retailers wanted some of that holiday shopping bread, too. Thus, two distinct deal-shopping days were born: Black Friday, for those who wanted to shop in stores the day after Thanksgiving, and Cyber Monday, for those who preferred shopping from the comfort of their desks.

According to recent reports, over 20 years later, there's little — if any — real difference between the two due to the alleged "death of retail." Everyone and everything is online, so why wouldn't Black Friday be? Based on our years of experience covering both, we can truly say neither is a "better" day to shop. It really comes down to what you're looking for and how much demand there is for it. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that if you see a solid deal, grab it, no matter which sale title it falls under. There's not a tremendous amount of distinction anymore in terms of discounts on particular products, as there was in previous years. However, there are still rules to follow in some product categories: TV deals tend to be more dramatic and widespread for Black Friday, with a higher likelihood of selling out before the clock even turns to Cyber Monday, while waiting for Cyber Monday to double-check that there's not a newly introduced, better laptop deal is often wise.

But with the blurred lines of Cyber Week, many of these deals will cross over. As noted at BlackFriday.com, "Some TV deals will feature flashy discounts during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, but they might not have the specs you're after.".

TL;DR: The deals will be great for both shopping days, but it all depends on what you're looking for. If you see specs you like listed under a product at a price you like, grab it to be safe.

Black Friday proper falls on Nov. 27 in 2026, but it's honestly silly to even call it Black Friday at this point. It's no longer just on Friday — it's a month-long affair. You can shop deals at practically every retailer starting right after Halloween (before, even), with most labeling something an "early Black Friday deal" as early as November. Best Buy's official early Black Friday sale kicked off Nov. 6, while Target's began on Nov. 5. Amazon's actual Black Friday sale starts Nov. 19, but you can already find the "early Black Friday deal" tag on plenty of listings. In other words, if you want to get some early shopping done, have at it.

It has been revealed that once the clock strikes midnight on Friday, it's basically Cyber Monday (yes, even though it's actually Saturday). We don't make the rules. The deals won't change too much, but the search terms and official site banners will.

In a recent development, officially, Cyber Monday is on Monday, Nov. 30 in 2026. Unofficially, it basically starts the second Black Friday ends, with retailers calling sales "Cyber Monday" deals as early as Saturday, Nov. 28. So basically, semantics — and it's easier to just think of the Cyber Week language as interchangeable.

Topics Black Friday Cyber Monday.

In a recent development, black Friday will last most of November, but come Saturday, Nov. 28, it's Cyber Monday time. As we mentioned above, since Black Friday and Cyber Monday are basically one massive shopping holiday, you likely won't see that many changes in deals, just changes in the banners and advertising of them.

Cyber Monday sales will last from Saturday, Nov. 28 to midnight on Monday, Nov. 30. There's not a hard stop, as there's always deals that stay live for at least the day or two following, but the large bulk of the sale is over once Monday ends.

As store policy, Target stores are closed on Thanksgiving Day, but are open for Black Friday beginning at 6 a.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27.

Walmart will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27. Walmart has confirmed that physical stores will be closed on Thanksgiving Day "so associates can spend the day with their families.".

According to recent reports, all physical Best Buy locations will be closed on Thanksgiving. Doors will open at 6 a.m. local time on Friday, Nov. 27 for shoppers and close at 10 p.m.

Recent findings suggest that all Kohl's stores are closed on Thanksgiving but are open for in-store shopping beginning at 5 a.m. local time on Nov. 27, per a press release.

  • It has been revealed that I know a lot about that PC-like experience, having tested some of the best Android phones and their desktop interfaces — namely Samsung DeX on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Android 17 desktop mode with Pixel phones, and Lenovo’s Smart Connect on the Motorola Razr Fold.
  • Sources indicate that after spending over three weeks with the Acer Googlebook 14, I learned a lot about the platform, including its advantages and disadvantages over using my Android phone with a desktop mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After my colleague Tony Polanco wrapped up his Acer Googlebook 14 review, he handed over the 2-in-1 convertible to me to put it through its paces and see what an Android phone power user thinks of Google’s fresh computing platform. One of the reasons a Googlebook appeals to me is how seamlessly it supposedly works with your Android phone, while offering you a rich desktop experience.

It has been revealed that I know a lot about that PC-like experience, having tested some of the best Android phones and their desktop interfaces — namely Samsung DeX on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Android 17 desktop mode with Pixel phones, and Lenovo’s Smart Connect on the Motorola Razr Fold. These are features that I like to refer to as an extension of my phone, mainly because of how they deliver that desktop experience when connected to external devices like a monitor or AR glasses.

Sources indicate that after spending over three weeks with the Acer Googlebook 14, I learned a lot about the platform, including its advantages and disadvantages over using my Android phone with a desktop mode. Here’s what I found.

Industry observers note that the Acer Googlebook 14 is a 2-in-1 convertible laptop that bridges the gap between mobile and desktop productivity, packing a crisp 14-inch display, Intel Core Ultra 5 (Series 3) processor, and full Chrome extension support. With multi-user profiles, virtual workspaces, and seamless access to Android apps right out of the box, it’s an ideal everyday workhorse.

Sources indicate that as much as I love falling back on DeX when I accidentally leave my laptop at home, I get annoyed that Samsung still refuses to bring back support for multiple consumers. This isn’t an concern with the Acer Googlebook 14, as it lets me set up separate user accounts — each with its own unique lock code and personalized desktop.

Industry observers note that this is perfect because I would rather keep my work and personal accounts separate, and it’s also useful if you intend on letting your kids or other people access the laptop. That isn’t an option with Samsung DeX, which is one of its biggest limitations, though the Pixel’s desktop mode does let me switch profiles.

While the Acer Googlebook 14 handles basic multitasking well enough, its proper side-by-side window snapping is restricted to just two apps at a time — effectively making it no different from any phone desktop mode.

It has been revealed that I appreciate how smoothly both windows resize in tandem when dragging the center border slider, which makes it easy to prioritize a browser window next to Slack while I’m working. However, as someone who regularly juggles multiple apps at once, I would much rather be able to pin up to four apps simultaneously in a grid.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I use Chrome all the time, especially for doing work-related tasks. While I can lean on a phone desktop mode for most things related to Chrome, there’s simply one thing I cannot do: access the handful of Chrome extensions that are crucial for working with a content management system (CMS).

Industry observers note that with the Acer Googlebook 14, I can run the exact same desktop Chrome extensions I rely on for work, including price-checking tools, grammar checkers, link generators, and more. Having those tools built directly into the browser makes it feel more like a true laptop replacement.

It has been revealed that I’m more productive on a Googlebook than with my phone’s desktop mode thanks to how it supports multiple virtual desktops and virtually limitless apps. The beauty of having up to four desktops is that I can organize them based on my workflow — like keeping one dedicated to spreadsheets, another to social media, and the rest to all of my work-related apps.

In a recent development, even though phone desktop modes also offer several desktops for me to organize, their main limitation is that they’re normally capped at five apps. This isn’t a major disadvantage per se, but having access to far more on a Googlebook is helpful when I need it.

Despite Googlebook OS running on an Android foundation, I was surprised to discover that not every Android app from the Google Play Store is available for me to install. Several staples I rely on daily — including Amazon, Twitter/X, and CyberLink’s PowerDirector — simply aren’t available just yet.

I suspect it’s simply a matter of these developers optimizing their apps for this new laptop form factor. While I can easily fall back on the web versions for shopping on Amazon or scrolling through X, losing native access to a full-featured video editor like PowerDirector is a real setback. In contrast, when I use Samsung DeX or Pixel’s desktop mode, every app already installed on my phone is immediately accessible.

After putting in serious time with the Acer Googlebook 14, it’s clear that Googlebook OS has distinct advantages over phone desktop modes like Samsung DeX and Android 17’s native desktop experience.

Recent findings suggest that with full Chrome extension support, multiple virtual workspaces, and multi-user profile switching, I’m noticeably more productive on it than when working off a docked phone. However, there’s still room for improvement — particularly around app availability gaps and window-snapping limitations — before it can permanently replace my Windows laptop.

If you liked: "Super 8," "Jumanji," "The Mist,".

Set in a quiet 1982 suburb, "The End of Oak Street" follows the Platt family, led by Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor).

They're propelled by the narrative into a "Jurassic Park" style nightmare when their entire neighborhood gets warped into a prehistoric world. Now stranded and surrounded by apex predators, the family and their neighbors must put aside their differences and work together if they hope to survive. For a fun 99-minute shot in the arm of nostalgia this weekend, you could do far worse than this Spielbergian fever dream.

If you liked: "Chinatown," any of Taylor Sheridan's shows.

According to recent reports, the ever-prickly Misty speedruns one girl failure after another, all spit and vinegar as the slow drip of clues takes her to an old ex (Ross Lynch) and a seedy manager in Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund). If you liked: "Coraline," "Host," "The Babadook".

Industry observers note that chastain also looks like she's having a blast pulling double duty as both the loving, picture-perfect mom and her demonic lookalike. A sinister shape-shifter known as Other Mommy emerges from her closet, taking on the appearance of Bela's mother (Chastain) and pleading to be let into her heart. As the creature's threats become increasingly terrifying, Bela's parents (Jay Duplass and Chastain) do everything they can to keep their daughter safe.

Buy or rent "The Other Mommy" on Amazon or Apple.
