The Fenix 9 Pro is Garmin's flagship watch and offers a more attractive design than the Enduro 4, along with extra features and more choice in the size and display you get.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is cheaper and lighter than the Fenix 9 Pro, and offers better battery life too.

Buying one of the best Garmin watches brings with it some guarantees with regard to the features you can expect, especially at the higher end of the brand’s line-up, where the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Garmin Enduro 4 both sit.

These watches offer stellar sports tracking and training analysis, along with the best navigation tools you’ll find on a smartwatch thanks to their offline routable maps. They are also equally accurate with GPS and heart rate, in my experience, and run the same software.

However, after testing the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Enduro 4 extensively, there are certainly some key differences between the two in other areas, most notably design and battery life.

If you want more details on either watch, check out my Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review or Garmin Enduro 4 review, but read on for a summary of the differences between them I noticed when testing them individually and at the same time.

The biggest difference between the two watches is price, since the Garmin Enduro 4 costs much less than the Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll pay $899 for the Enduro 4 right now, while the cheapest Fenix 9 Pro model is $1,099, whether you choose the AMOLED version or the Fenix 9 Pro Solar with a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display like the Enduro.

The key thing that the Fenix 9 Pro offers with its design is choice. It comes in three sizes — 43mm, 47mm and 51mm — and you can pick between an AMOLED or MIP display, and even choose between colors for the bezel and sensor guard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In contrast, the Enduro 4 comes in one style and size. It’s a 51mm watch with a MIP display, and it only uses titanium for its bezel, with a mostly plastic case, whereas the Fenix 9 Pro has a full titanium case.

According to recent reports, this gives the Fenix 9 Pro a more elegant look, but it also makes it considerably heavier than the Enduro 4. I tested a 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED, and both it and the Enduro 4 are large watches, but the Enduro 4 counters that a little by being so light.

When it comes to the display, picking between AMOLED and MIP will come down to personal preferences.

I find AMOLED brighter and clearer in almost all conditions, and just as good as MIP in bright sunlight these days, and I prefer using an AMOLED watch in general, but MIP uses less power and is less obvious on the wrist, and the Enduro 4’s display was still clear enough to see at all times.

Both watches have sapphire crystal screens and built-in flashlights, but you get an extra green mode on the Fenix 9 Pro’s flashlight.

You also get a diveproof watch with the Fenix 9 Pro, which can be used to depths of 40m. The Enduro 4 has a high waterproof rating of 10ATM and is fine for swimming, but isn’t a diving watch.

Another addition on the Fenix line is a mic and speaker, which can be used to take voice notes and give voice commands to the watch.

One advantage of the Enduro 4 is that it ships with Garmin's fabric ComfortFit band as standard, which I much prefer to the silicone band on the Fenix 9 Pro. You can buy the ComfortFit band separately, but it will cost $59.

According to recent reports, the design differences speak to the approach behind the two watches. The Enduro 4 is built to be simpler and lighter, which helps it to be more affordable, but the Fenix 9 Pro is the all-singing, all-dancing option with a variety of models to pick between.

The two watches share very similar sports tracking and training analysis features, and both have proved to be similarly accurate throughout my testing.

There’s only one difference worth flagging in this area, which is that the Fenix 9 Pro is a diveproof watch and has Garmin’s scuba, apnea and snorkel sports modes.

One of the biggest features you get on the Fenix 9 Pro (InReach model) that isn’t available on the Enduro 4 is LTE and satellite connectivity.

This feature requires a subscription but allows you to stay in contact with the world when you’re off the grid or phone-free, through messaging and the ability to send SOS alerts.

Sources indicate that otherwise, both watches share the usual Garmin smart features. They can store music and link to streaming services, make NFC payments through Garmin Pay, and have access to the Connect IQ app store.

Along with being cheaper and lighter, the main advantage of the Enduro 4 is its incredible battery life.

Whatever Fenix 9 Pro you opt for, including the Solar MIP watch, the Enduro 4 will outlast it in both watch and GPS modes, partly because it has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

Sources indicate that I've compared the 51mm models of the Fenix 9 Pro to the Enduro 4 below. Note that to get the full solar battery life listed, you need to be out and about in sunny conditions for three hours a day on average.

In my use, the Enduro 4 lasted me 16 days on its first charge and is tracking for 17-18 on its second charge, whereas the 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED lasts me 10-11 days with the screen set to always-on.

This was during the British winter too, when I gave the Enduro 4 almost nothing in terms of a solar charging boost, so you can expect the gap to be wider in sunnier climates.

The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro line-up offers more features and choice than the Enduro 4, and I prefer the all-titanium design of the Fenix and its brighter AMOLED display.

However, the Enduro 4’s relative simplicity will appeal to many people, as will its lower price, longer battery life, and lighter design.

If you’ve been eyeing the Fenix 9 Pro Solar in particular and don’t really need the connectivity features on the watch, then I think the Enduro 4 is a better value buy. Or even the Garmin Enduro 3, for that matter, since it has a similar design and feature set to the latest model.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fall is in full swing, and if your yard looks anything like mine, you’re probably busy clearing scattered leaves while tending to a tired lawn.

What makes it look so worn down are probably the sparse, empty spots across the yard — which leaves me asking: is it too late to plant grass seed in November?

Luckily, I called on some lawn experts to shed some light on this and offer their advice on achieving a lush, resilient lawn even in this colder season.

So before you get ready to sow, here is what you need to consider before grabbing your seed packet and getting started.

While November is typically not the right month to sow grass seed, this can also depend on your regional climate, local soil temperatures, and grass seed type.

For instance, with cool-season grasses (such as Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass, tall fescue), you should only overseed once the temperatures drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not necessarily too late — but it is more of a riskier time to do so,” advises Chris Bonnett, founder of GardeningExpress. “If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like where you are.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“The soil temperature is the most crucial thing, as the seeds will need a mild environment to germinate, and you'll need the soil temperatures to be consistently around 46.4 °F to 50 °F or above for germination.”.

"If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like".

Sources indicate that on the other hand, warm-season varieties like Bermuda grass, zoysiagrass, centipedegrass, and Bahiagrass begin going dormant as the weather cools down. As a result, planting them during cold spells reduces their chances of growing. This is especially the case during colder snaps and the risk of frost.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost, so it has time to germinate and build some root growth before winter dormancy sets in," advises Matthew Koch, Ph.D., research and development at ScottsMiracle-Gro.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost.

"Regions that experience a milder fall, also known as the Transition Zone (roughly Kansas through the Mid-Atlantic, including areas extending toward the Carolinas), might be able to have one final feeding before winter, but it is entirely dependent on the local climate, growing conditions, and grass type.".

Sources indicate that however, if the soil is too cold, experts suggest waiting until warmer weather begins during springtime. “I’d recommend waiting until the spring, adds Bonnett.

"There’s no benefit in rushing to sow grass seed if it’s not going to have the right conditions to germinate and establish well.”.

It has been revealed that so if temperatures haven’t yet dropped, what is the best method for overseeding a lawn? To give your lawn an optimal head start in establishing healthy grass, experts suggest sowing a fast-germinating seed mix.

Recent findings suggest that “If the conditions are mild enough, choose a fast-germinating grass seed mix such as one containing perennial ryegrass,” adds Bonnett. “This will help give your lawn the best chance of establishing.”.

Of course, preparation is essential, so start by eliminating weeds, clearing leaves, and leveling the ground with a rake before you start seeding.

In a recent development, “Scatter the seed evenly and gently rake it into the top layer of the soil. Keep the area slightly moist but avoid overwatering, especially in November when rainfall is more frequent. If the ground is already wet or waterlogged, avoid planting.”.

Sources indicate that fair warning: I’ll be spoiling major events from seasons 1 and 2. So, without further ado, here are five things you should remember before “Percy Jackson” season 3.

Thalia Grace’s return at the end of season 2 comes with a major twist that changes everything heading into season 3. In the original books, Zeus turned his daughter into a pine tree to save her life after monsters mortally wounded her. However, the series reveals that he actually imprisoned her as punishment after she refused to obey him and become his weapon in the coming war.

Sources indicate that when Clarisse (Dior Goodjohn) uses the Golden Fleece to heal Camp Half-Blood’s protective borders, Thalia returns to human form. The revelation also raises questions about who the demigods can trust. Chiron (Glynn Turman) and the camp’s leaders had hidden the truth about Thalia from Percy, Annabeth and Grover for years. Her hatred of Zeus could also bring her closer to Luke Castellan (Charlie Bushnell) and Kronos, although where her loyalties ultimately lie remains unclear.

Most importantly, Thalia’s return complicates the Great Prophecy. As Zeus’s daughter, she’s another child of the Big Three who could fulfil the prediction, meaning Percy might not be the only demigod capable of deciding Olympus’s fate.

In a recent development, thalia’s return wasn’t just a side effect of healing Camp Half-Blood. It also gave Kronos another way to threaten Olympus. The Great Prophecy states that a child of one of the “Big Three” gods (Zeus, Poseidon or Hades) who reaches the age of 16 will decide whether Olympus survives or falls.

Industry observers note that before Thalia returned, Percy was the main demigod connected to the prophecy. Now, Zeus’s daughter could also fulfil it, making the situation much more complicated. The two immediately clash after Thalia wakes up, setting up a potential rivalry between them.

It has been revealed that her return also gives Kronos another opportunity to turn a powerful demigod against the gods. Thalia has plenty of reasons to hate Zeus, which could make her vulnerable to his influence. As season 3 approaches, both Percy and Thalia could play a major role in deciding the fate of Olympus.

Sources indicate that after the battle at Thalia’s tree, Percy briefly sees his father, Poseidon (Toby Stephens), in a vision while unconscious. Poseidon tells him that the war against Kronos has officially begun and asks Percy’s Cyclops half-brother, Tyson (Daniel Diemer), to help make weapons in the underwater forges.

Recent findings suggest that tyson happily accepts, finally feeling like he has a place alongside his father. However, his departure leaves Percy facing the growing threat on his own. According to recent reports, the moment also reveals that the conflict with Kronos is much bigger than the fight at camp. With Tyson helping build weapons beneath the sea, season 3 could explore more of the underwater world and Poseidon’s role in the coming war.

Luke Castellan has become an increasingly dangerous threat by the end of season 2. Industry observers note that the attack also exposes how poorly Camp Half-Blood is being run. After King Tantalus (Timothy Simons) is killed during the siege, Dionysus (Jason Mantzoukas) reluctantly takes charge again but does little to organize the campers. Instead, Percy steps up and gives an inspiring speech, encouraging everyone to defend their home.

This also helps explain why Luke has turned against the Olympian gods. He believes they mistreat their children and care more about their own power than the demigods’ lives. With Zeus’s treatment of Thalia only adding to that argument, Luke has plenty of ammunition to convince others to join Kronos. Heading into season 3, he’s still a major threat to Percy and everyone at Camp Half-Blood.

Season 3 adapts “The Titan’s Curse,” which sees Annabeth Chase captured by Kronos’ forces. Her disappearance sets Percy on another dangerous quest to rescue his friend, but it also puts his biggest weakness to the test: his loyalty to the people he loves.

It’s another example of how far he’s willing to go to protect the people closest to him. As the Great Prophecy draws closer, Percy will have to balance his feelings for Annabeth and his friends with the fate of Olympus.

It has been revealed that google Sheets is great for organizing information, but sharing it with others isn’t always convenient. Say you’re managing a project with multiple deadlines and tasks. You might have everything organized in a spreadsheet, but no one wants to scroll through dozens of rows just to see what’s happening next.

Recent findings suggest that google already has a feature called Canvas that uses Gemini to turn spreadsheet data into interactive dashboards, calendars, and task boards. Now, it’s making these creations easier to share by giving them their own links, without requiring access to the original spreadsheet.

For example, if you’re organizing an event, you could turn your planning spreadsheet into an interactive schedule and share it with attendees. They could check timings and find the information they need, while only the organizers would have access to edit the spreadsheet.

Recent findings suggest that what’s particularly nice is that you can control who sees the published Canvas separately from the spreadsheet itself. You can also choose whether it updates automatically when the spreadsheet changes or stays exactly as it was when you published it. That could come in handy when sharing a project dashboard where deadlines and progress are constantly changing.

To try it, you’ll need editing access to the spreadsheet. Simply open the Canvas sharing menu, select Publish Canvas, and choose who can access it. Once done, click Publish, and you can also copy the link, change the audience, or stop sharing it whenever you want.

#474. Advancing science and engineering with Antigravity's /teamwork

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2850 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Research

Advancing science and engineering with Antigravity's /teamwork

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Research

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vahab Mirrokni, Google Fellow and VP, Google Research.
  • We share recent results from Antigravity’s /teamwork multiagent systems, which enhance human-AI collaborations to solve open problems across mathematics, chemistry, systems software, and ML engineering.
  • In a recent development, over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vahab Mirrokni, Google Fellow and VP, Google Research.

We share recent results from Antigravity’s /teamwork multiagent systems, which enhance human-AI collaborations to solve open problems across mathematics, chemistry, systems software, and ML engineering. All of this work is done in collaboration with human experts, and we are making these tools available externally.

In a recent development, over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years. Using Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and multi-agent workflows such as Antigravity’s /teamwork (building on various Gemini models), these collaborations have produced new innovations across information theory, formal verifications, molecular structure discoveries, and kernel optimization, along with several production infrastructure gains at Google. We are making these agentic tools available in Antigravity’s /teamwork (alongside /boost and other agents) so that researchers and developers can apply them to their own work.

Frontier research and systems engineering require navigating vast literature, building custom computational pipelines, testing against physical measurements, and verifying every step. Progress comes from an interactive discovery loop where researchers frame questions and define the theoretical or physical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, explore large search spaces, test candidate designs, and check long chains of logic.

Two limits of current language models motivate /teamwork's design. First, model generation can be unpredictable, leaving a gap between a single attempt and finding the correct answer. The system bridges this gap by pairing parallel exploration with dedicated falsifiers (e.g., the Lean 4 proof checker, unmodified software test suites, execution simulators, web search, or hardware counters) to automatically verify which candidate solutions work.

It has been revealed that second, AI models often lose track of details over multi-day tasks because attention disperses across growing context windows. To prevent this, /teamwork partitions context by construction: each specialized agent receives only the exact files and tools it needs for a specific step. Coordinators hand off tasks to fresh successors, while critics and auditors challenge and verify results from clean contexts without the original producer's reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that teamwork expresses these workflows as declarative self-improving natural-language patterns and dynamically routes each user prompt to the pattern best suited to the task. These patterns range from distributed coding and iterative problem-solving (packaged standalone as /boost, a sequential solve-and-verify loop refined from prior trajectories) to specialized research workflows like long proof and document review, all of which are available in Antigravity today. This allows teams to design custom specifications from past run transcripts routing across different harness patterns and dynamically improving agentic harness. While many of these features are available in Antigravity, we will provide more updates in the coming weeks providing all the features to our external users on Antigravity. Following our previous posts on Antigravity /teamwork, we provide latest results to open challenges empowered by new variants of /teamwork and Gemini 4 models.

Industry observers note that across mathematics and theoretical computer science, researchers paired with Gemini 4 and /teamwork harnesses to collaborate on large-scale proofs and generate complete algorithms and proofs directly from open problem statements. We present several examples.

Researchers from Google, CUHK, USC, and CMU used /teamwork's Long Proof pattern (implementing Stellar Colosseum in Antigravity) to prove information theory's 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in full generality. The result confirms that when a random bit string passes through a noisy channel, no compression of the input to a single bit preserves more information than a "dictator function", which just copies a single input bit. Gemini first found counterexamples to a generalized conjecture from the CUHK team's earlier paper. The CUHK team then proposed a new candidate function that reduced the conjecture to a 14-variable optimization problem, along with a key analytical lower bound. Gemini 4 Argon and earlier Gemini models then partitioned the parameter space and developed most of the new analytical bounds and interval-arithmetic certificates. They also extended the proof from balanced to unbalanced functions without human input. The team formalized the entire proof in Lean 4, producing 50 million lines of code.

In a recent development, researchers also posed open problems directly to Gemini 4 and to multi-agent harnesses such as Stellar Colosseum and /teamwork, receiving end-to-end algorithms and proofs (often with Lean 4 formalizations) that the authors verified, simplified, and edited for publication. In adaptive data analysis, a multi-agent harness running on Gemini 4 Argon independently proved and Lean-verified near-optimal sample bounds for statistical queries chosen adaptively from earlier answers, closing a gap open since 2014. These bounds yield the first nearly space-optimal algorithm for data streams with both insertions and deletions that stays accurate against adaptive adversaries. In quantum computing, a new construction settled a 2014 open question by finding the first n-bit Boolean functions needing strictly more than n/2 quantum queries at constant error, while pinning down the exact query overhead across symmetric functions.

In a recent development, several results break long standing barriers in processing and compressing large matrices and graphs. For fifty years until STOC 2024, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication and triangle detection (avoiding the algebraic cancellations of fast matrix multiplication) saved only logarithmic factors over cubic time. A fresh deterministic algorithm resolves STOC 2024's main open question, achieving its target speedup over cubic time. In high-dimensional geometry, a new lower bound resolves an open problem on sparse networks, proving that approximating all pairwise distances among n points within any constant factor can require polynomially more than n edges, even with extra Steiner points and arbitrarily many hops. In randomized linear algebra, stacked sparse sketches resolve a 2025 open question by breaking the classical sparsity barrier for compressing a matrix to linear dimension without collapsing any direction of an r-dimensional subspace, needing only √log r nonzeros per row (quadratically fewer than the log r required to preserve all lengths) and nearly matching a new lower bound. For weighted graphs under dynamic edge-weight insertions and deletions, Stellar Colosseum resolved an open question left by FOCS 2022, developing the first single-pass streaming algorithm for cut sparsification that achieves near-optimal memory, update time, and reconstruction time simultaneously.

Industry observers note that our results also span optimization, arithmetic, data structures, and statistics. In optimization, resolving an open question on online inverse linear optimization (inferring an expert's hidden objective from decisions over time), the approach gave a deterministic algorithm achieving optimal regret while cutting runtime from exponential in the dimension to polynomial time. For n-bit integer multiplication, multi-agent campaigns simplified the theoretical Turing-machine bound below n log n, while a separate effort gave a fresh O(n log n) algorithm on a single two-dimensional grid whose C implementation matches the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) bit-for-bit up to a billion bits. In data structures, another result made significant progress on Tarjan's 1985 Deque Conjecture (whether self-adjusting splay trees handle insertions and deletions at both ends in constant amortized time), proving a new upper bound on the per-operation overhead that simultaneously beats every finitely iterated inverse-Ackermann function, verified in Lean 4. Finally, in high-dimensional statistics, the approach proved that approximate leave-one-out cross-validation, which avoids refitting the model from scratch, remains accurate for non-smooth sparse penalties like elastic net.

Checking a computer-assisted manuscript by hand places a heavy burden on peer reviewers, and subtle flaws can hide inside long calculations. Formalizing mathematics in Lean 4 turns a proof into code that a computer kernel checks line by line. Once human mathematicians confirm that the formal theorem statement matches the original problem, the proof only compiles if every logical step holds.

Many of the deepest open problems in mathematics govern how physical waves propagate, how dynamical systems evolve, and whether polynomial equations have integer solutions. Working directly from informal proofs, our multi-agent framework, LEAP, developed with colleagues in Google Cloud AI and paired with Argon, has made progress in these core areas.

Recent findings suggest that notably, /teamwork-LEAP fully autonomously produced an end-to-end, machine-checked formalization of the Weil conjectures, the landmark results on counting solutions of polynomial equations over finite fields that culminated in Pierre Deligne's 1974 proof. This formalization spans about 1.8 million lines of Lean, produced across 28,800 subagent invocations. The system also synthesized over 919,000 lines of Lean to produce the first formalization of a recent proof of Hilbert's tenth problem over general rings of integers. It also independently reproduces an end-to-end formalization of a recent proof of finite-time blowup for the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with smooth forcing, part of one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and open for about 90 years.

According to recent reports, beyond these, it also generated the first formalization of the Birkhoff conjecture, a dynamical-systems problem open since 1927. Moreover, it formalized for the first time the 3D Bochner–Riesz conjecture, a central problem in harmonic analysis open for more than 50 years, finding and fixing a gap in a recently released informal proof along the way. Additional machine-checked breakthroughs include resolving the C¹ regularity of infinity-harmonic functions in three and higher dimensions (an open question for about 20 years), formalizing Killip and Vişan's theorem that the KdV water-wave equation is well-posed in H⁻¹ and verifying a UCLA group's informal proofs of the 40-year-old Jamison Caterpillar Conjecture, the Ağırseven-Ollis conjecture, and an improved upper bound on Erdős Problem #1063.

Sources indicate that finally, we provided Deep Review for authors of another CS conference: ahead of STOC 2027, authors of 578 submissions (over a third of all submissions) opted in to receive Deep Review feedback on their drafts. In an ongoing author survey (N = 70), 90% of respondents rated the feedback mostly or almost all factual and 90% noted they would use the tool again. Over 30% said Deep Review caught substantive proof bugs or mathematically significant typos, and 14% said it found technical gaps that took more than an hour to fix. Surveyed authors shared that “Tools of this kind can help produce cleaner and more precise research, faster” and that DeepReview provides peace of mind on scientific discovery”. We provide owners two weekly calls to Deep Review for free. Deep Review is also implemented as /teamwork's document review pattern and available in Antigravity. Read more about DeepReview in our recent blog post.

Beyond formal proofs, pairing specialized generator agents with independent verifier agents enables discovery workflows in experimental laboratory science.

In a recent development, determining a molecule’s structure from experimental nuclear magnetic resonance data is one of chemistry’s hardest puzzles. For example, in HIV protease inhibitors, one misplaced bond separates an inactive look-alike from a drug. By organizing 30 specialized agents into a self-correcting loop with /teamwork and a physics-informed spectral simulator, we achieved 95% top-1 exact match and 100% top-3 accuracy on complex benchmark molecules, nearly doubling single-agent performance. Beyond teaching Gemini to reason over structure, this lays the groundwork for ongoing works on 3D protein and complex structures dynamics. Beyond this example, science problems including applications in nuclear fusion and quantum algorithms reported in the Gemini 4 blog post benefited from /teamwork and the Argon model.

Sources indicate that we also applied a similar multi-round auditing workflow to build empirical benchmarks. Starting from five human-specified acceptance criteria like data anonymization, 29 agents running on Argon over 11.5 hours turned 13 public tables into a 50-task causal inference benchmark. In these tasks, models must determine whether a causal effect can be identified and estimate it against a known answer. After initial checks, separate reviewer and auditor agents caught shortcuts, flagged wording hints, and vetoed hallucinated scripts, turning each into a permanent test. Automating this heavily manual task generation supplies the hard problems needed to help Gemini answer counterfactual "what-if" questions.

When paired with objective evaluators such as network benchmarks, game engines, unmodified test suites, and hardware timers, /teamwork campaigns can execute multi-day software and hardware engineering projects.

Sources indicate that using /teamwork and Argon, we built FarArray, a low-latency kernel-bypass Partitioned Global Address Space based on the SNAP microkernel. Applications built on FarArray include lock-free Connected Components, which scale to 1-trillion-edge graphs with 60x to 90x throughput gains and 40x to 180x speedups at 6x lower RAM over TCP key-value stores. Similarly, InstantEmbedding (Personalized PageRank) reduced peak DRAM by up to 14x and runtime by 11x to 27x over accelerated MapReduce implementations. The team also used /teamwork and Argon to create custom TPU kernels for Graph Neural Networks, delivering up to a 185x High Bandwidth Memory reduction and 8x to 15x speedups in forward and backward passes. Further details are available in our recent Antigravity blog post.

Recent findings suggest that to test autonomous optimization over long horizons, hill-climbing teams on Argon trained a 9x9 Go engine from scratch starting from a basic AlphaZero implementation. Human researchers set the chip allocation and evaluation setup, while the harness ran autonomous campaigns for faster self-play (achieving a 2,300x speedup) and faster Elo readings, promoting champions strictly via statistical tests on locked records. In under eight days, the engine gained roughly 2,600 Elo, reaching 1,885 Elo, placing it between KataGo at 16 and 32 visits per move.

According to recent reports, A game played for this post between our final champion (black) and the network the Elo hill-climb started from (white). The final champion won by 22.5 points (area scoring, komi 7.5). It was the only game played for the post.

Large code migrations fail when agents stub out dependencies or alter tests to make a broken port pass. A new /teamwork rewrite pattern, soon to be available in Antigravity, solved this by scheduling each module only after its dependencies compile, linking every leaf module against the original, unmodified test suite. Building on the initial 25% port of the Zircon microkernel, a two-week Argon campaign rewrote the remaining C++ code, adding about 800,000 lines of safe Rust that pass all kernel unit tests and boot on arm64 hardware. /teamwork also rewrote libgav1, Google's AV1 video decoder, from C++ into around 170k lines Rust, achieving 100% bit-exact parity across a broad conformance test suite. Initially, the port was around 4x slower than the original C++ code. However, after giving /teamwork access to profiling tools and a mandate to maximize speed on sample video clips, the Rust port became 20-30% faster than the original C++ and hand-optimized assembly code on both x86_64 and ARM.

For day-to-day coding tasks, the Antigravity /boost command packages /teamwork's iterative coding pattern. A long-running /teamwork campaign analyzed past run trajectories and found that tightly coupled code is best handled through sequential implementation and revision stages rather than parallel splits, improving /boost on coding tasks. This is an example of a harness optimizing another harness for token efficiency.

For machine learning systems, full hardware evaluations of custom JAX and Pallas TPU kernels take 7 to 32 minutes, limiting how many candidates prior optimization agents can explore. Using /teamwork's DuoDiscover pattern on Argon, four parallel agents identified performance bottlenecks and constructed fast, 23-second proxy evaluators called yardsticks. These yardsticks produce candidate orderings that are continuously validated against periodic full hardware runs using Kendall's rank correlation. DuoDiscover achieves a 4.09x geometric-mean speedup over reference implementations across 17 JAXBench kernels and a 2.99x geometric-mean speedup across 7 hand-optimized vLLM TPU-Inference Pallas kernels for frontier open-weight models.

#473. Industry News: Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2206 w)

Industry News: Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Recent findings suggest that we know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

Industry observers note that that gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

This is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

For years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

Recent findings suggest that but audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple upcoming features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

According to recent reports, the WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

In a recent development, models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

In a recent development, now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The problem wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

The same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

The fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

This is usually where someone notes, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility issue caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

Recent findings suggest that catching an accessibility issue as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

Teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

In a recent development, the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

According to recent reports, accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

Industry observers note that at that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

According to recent reports, instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

In a recent development, comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

In a recent development, focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

It has been revealed that none of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

In a recent development, engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

Legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the manufacturer is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

In a recent development, but compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

Recent findings suggest that in the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million consumers with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Industry observers note that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

According to recent reports, step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

In a recent development, for dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

If you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

An accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

None of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

But there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real people with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

Accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” ….

Industry observers note that “Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

It has been revealed that using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

Sources indicate that it’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very massive deal.

Verdict: This period drama is a well-executed adaptation of August Wilson's award-winning 1985 play of the same name. Unfortunately, it notably feels like you're watching a play; it struggles to make the case for why it's a dramatic work of cinema as opposed to a theatrical revival. But as Denzel Washington and Viola Davis start pitching a perfect game, you stop nitpicking and let the performances take over.

Where to watch: Stream "Fences" for free on Tubi or YouTube.

In a recent development, "Fences" was a movie I circled on my calendar as I made my way through this year-long Denzel Watchathon. This is considered a seminal work in the legendary actor's career. It's his third directorial effort in his filmography and by far the best. It also earned him his seventh Oscar nomination as an actor (his second of three he'd earn in the 2010s alone).

Once you watch it, it's no surprise why this performance makes the highlight reel. This movie is essentially crafted to serve his character, except for the few scenes where it's designed to highlight Viola Davis. She plays Denzel's on-screen wife in this period drama film, and I'd argue it's her performance that's the more impressive of the two.

Unfortunately, if I have to nitpick, this strength is also the movie's biggest weakness. "Fences" is adapted from August Wilson's 1985 play of the same name. That play was a roaring success, earning Wilson both a Pulitzer and a Tony Award in 1987. Watching this film adaptation, one wouldn't be shocked if Denzel and Wilson (who also wrote the screenplay for this movie) didn't change a thing from the Broadway version. The entire time, it feels unmistakably like you're watching a play.

This isn't inherently a bad thing; I often like movies adapted from plays, and to be clear, I thought this film was excellent. But unlike, say, "A Few Good Men," I failed to see what was added to the performances, to the story, etc., by turning Wilson's play into a cinematic experience. If you had simply had this same cast act out the play on a stage and filmed it on a Sony Handycam, it'd probably be just as good.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's right now streaming for free on Tubi, one of the best free streaming services we've tested. You can also stream it for free on YouTube (with ads).

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:.

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far.

The sixth installment in August Wilson's 10-part "Pittsburgh Cycle," "Fences," centers around Troy. Portrayed by Denzel Washington in this adaptation, he's a middle-aged man working as a sanitation worker. He appears to be an ordinary working-class Pittsburgher, albeit sans Yinzer accent. But as the story unfolds, it's swiftly apparent that Troy wasn't always destined for an ordinary life.

Troy, as revealed by his longtime friend, Bono (Stephen McKinley Henderson), was at one point one of the best baseball players in America. But he had the bad luck of being a Black player in the years before Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier in Major League Baseball. So while his Negro League career earned him plaudits and adulation, it didn't exactly bring in the cash. And you can only dine on praise for so long before reality sets in.

Industry observers note that complicating things is ... well, everything else. His marriage to Rose (Viola Davis) appears healthy, but early on in the movie there are hints this isn't the case. It's clear that money can be a pain point for Troy, who now has less of it than ever because he's no longer collecting part of his brother's (Mykelti Williamson) disability check from the Army. When Troy's 34-year-old son, Lyons (Russell Hornsby), comes asking for money, it's clear that Troy thinks he'll never see that money again, and that he doesn't have enough cash to waste. Even on family.

But it's not Lyons's relationship with his father at the core of "Fences." Instead, the film focuses on Troy's relationship with his other son, Cory. He's 17 years old and the only child produced by Troy and Rose's marriage. His relationship with his dad is somewhat rocky and complicated by the fact that colleges are recruiting Cory for football. Troy, a former pro athlete who now makes a living hauling trash, wants Cory to avoid sports entirely for fear that it will lead him down the same path Troy went down.

In a recent development, davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

Despite all this focus on Troy and his sons, it's Viola Davis who steals the movie as Rose. Denzel is supposed to be excellent in this movie. He's given incredible lines. He's the main character. Every character exists in this story to be a reflection of his impact on their lives or to highlight a trial and tribulation Troy has had to deal with. There's a scene early on where Cory asks why Troy doesn't like him, and Denzel just cooks, as the Gen Z youths would say. In fact, if you've seen a scene from this movie on TikTok, it's probably this scene of Denzel as Troy taking his son down a peg.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

Sources indicate that in that aforementioned scene, she's not openly weeping, sobbing, or screaming at the top of her lungs, all of which would be perfectly reasonable responses given the news she just received. However, she manages to do a feat of physical acting where snot just runs from her nostrils. It's the clear aftermath of a moment of grief, underlying the fact that she's not nearly as composed as she's forcing herself to appear on the outside.

Industry observers note that when I say that Davis steals this movie and doesn't let go, I mean it. She was the lone Oscar winner for "Fences," deservedly taking home the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress. It might be the first movie since "The Manchurian Candidate" where I felt that an actress took the spotlight from Denzel and there was simply nothing he could do about it.

Recent findings suggest that but again, Denzel is great in this movie. He earns an Oscar nomination; the movie itself earns a Best Picture nomination, in no small part due to his performance and direction. It's a tough watch at times. Because it feels like a play but lacks the intimate, almost physical connection between thespian and theatergoer, it can also lose your interest on occasion.

Recent findings suggest that that all is rapidly brushed aside, though, as the film reaches its climax. The performances at the center of this movie are the definition of must-watch. And now that it's currently available to stream at home for free, you really have no excuse not to check it out if you haven't already.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft's massive, productivity-destroying software outage appears to be receding as of Friday morning, but that's only the start of the process for businesses looking to get some of their Office 365 money back.
  • Several important enterprise software products, such as Outlook and Teams, were functionally offline for many users on Thursday and into Friday.
  • The answer to that question is nuanced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft's massive, productivity-destroying software outage appears to be receding as of Friday morning, but that's only the start of the process for businesses looking to get some of their Office 365 money back.

Several important enterprise software products, such as Outlook and Teams, were functionally offline for many users on Thursday and into Friday. Since Office 365 is a service businesses have to pay for, it raises the question: Can those businesses receive some form of compensation from Microsoft for the time lost?

The answer to that question is nuanced. Let's get into it.

Industry observers note that according to helpful resources like these explainers from Quartz and Office Watch, the short answer is no; Microsoft does not owe anyone money as a result of this outage. But that doesn't mean the company doesn't owe any compensation, as it offers credits (essentially a reduction on the next bill) in the event of an outage.

Recent findings suggest that one important thing to note: You have to request a credit. Microsoft doesn't offer them automatically.

Industry observers note that purchasing Microsoft's software suite involves a service-level agreement (SLA). This SLA includes provisions related to outages and compensation. In this case, Microsoft's SLA promises 99.9 percent uptime each month for each piece of software in the suite, such as OneDrive and Outlook. If any of those services fall below the 99.9 percent threshold, it's possible to claim a credit. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

"Possible" is the key word here, though, as both Quartz and Office Watch make it very clear that Microsoft is extremely strict about how it calculates downtime in these instances. The actual math is too complicated to fully get into here, but Microsoft counts downtime in terms of "user minutes," or the amount of time the services were down multiplied by the number of owners demonstrably affected.

Industry observers note that credits are also prorated depending on how much uptime was lost, so a small amount of downtime might only be worth a 25 or 50 percent credit. Where this gets even more complicated is that Microsoft calculates credits according to each individual service, not the entire software bundle. If you only lost service time in Outlook, but other parts of the Office 365 suite worked, you'd only get a small credit for Outlook.

All of this is to say that, depending on the size of the affected business and the amount of downtime it experienced, one of these credits could be worth only a few measly dollars.

Industry observers note that to be very clear, individual workers who lost service time due to the significant outage cannot file a claim or receive compensation. Businesses who license this software from Microsoft can do it, but even that is more complicated than you'd think.

In a recent development, businesses only have until the end of December to file these claims, for starters. If a business purchased Microsoft software directly from Microsoft, it can go to the Office admin center to file a claim. They will need to provide a lot of information, such as incident IDs and specific descriptions of how long service was unavailable to people. From there, Microsoft will perform its own calculations to determine whether the business receives a credit.

In a recent development, many businesses do not purchase these Microsoft products directly from the organization, instead obtaining them through Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partners or other indirect resellers. In that case, the business will have to bug the provider to submit a claim on their behalf. Depending on the provider, that may or may not happen in a timely or productive manner.

Given the number of hoops that businesses have to jump through to get one of these credits, one could argue it's not worth the hassle, depending on the size of a business and how much time it lost.

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just unveiled a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video ….

According to recent reports, amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

In a recent development, AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

It has been revealed that when a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving consumers more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the organization unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets owners** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:.

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two fresh AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” states the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a fresh color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”.

Recent findings suggest that another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:.

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe declared that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps owners find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more rapidly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

It has been revealed that as for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more swiftly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”.

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add latest files to a Google Drive folder, patch the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:.

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping consumers organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Initiative Mode, which lets owners review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when people step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

In a recent development, these assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the tech giant’s blog.
