Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that the design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how customers provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

To pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

In a recent development, picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our customers to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

Recent findings suggest that the allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on customers. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

According to recent reports, when an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

According to recent reports, A blank chat box creates a major problem for owners who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

It has been revealed that when an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status upgrade. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

The cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most notable.

According to recent reports, before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

Designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for people with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

According to recent reports, table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

The following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

With this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

It has been revealed that to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

Here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

In a recent development, this is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because people often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

In a recent development, the Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

Industry observers note that the Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-people and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Industry observers note that workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

Industry observers note that the Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

Once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

In a recent development, when you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your consumers.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

With Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

According to recent reports, choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Consumers might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status upgrade only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

In a recent development, table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve owners whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Sources indicate that field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

According to recent reports, to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

High-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

In a recent development, second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

The resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

Sources indicate that the AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Sources indicate that once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

In a recent development, an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

In a recent development, the future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

According to recent reports, to get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

According to recent reports, I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

Sources indicate that we focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Future OnePlus software updates will be based on ColorOS, the skin that pilots OPPO devices.

Given that the two brands belong to the same parent manufacturer, it seemed only a matter of time. The two skins share many commonalities, but as my colleague Dhruv experienced recently running ColorOS 17 on his OnePlus 15, they couldn’t look or feel more different.

Of course, we wanted to know what you, our readers, thought. We ran a poll asking for your views on ColorOS taking over OnePlus devices, and the verdict is rather surprising.

What do you think of ColorOS on OnePlus phones?

Sources indicate that while the “Prefer OxygenOS” camp racked up the most votes, a surprising number of readers aren’t lamenting the loss. Just under 40% of respondents prefer the original OnePlus skin, while 30.7% “don’t mind” the new ColorOS experience. Given the backlash OnePlus faced after pulling out of the US in particular, these results are far closer than I would’ve expected.

In fact, if you include the 18.1% of respondents who “Like the new design but don’t need the AI additions” and the 11.1% who “Like the features, but could do without the Liquid Glass look,” the majority of respondents are largely in favor of the move to ColorOS on OnePlus phones, despite minor reservations.

It’s worth noting that Dhruv’s hands-on ColorOS 17 experience was mostly positive, too. This may have skewed respondents’ opinions, but the results still suggest that more readers are coming to terms with, and in some cases embracing, the change.

The underlying changes especially to notifications and background is not a subtle change but hit with a hammer change.

On Thursday, a Microsoft outage affected Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft 365 services, starting around 12:30 p.m. ET.

Recent findings suggest that by 1 p.m. ET, nearly 130,000 user error reports were submitted to Downdetector, and owners reported trouble loading their inboxes and sending or receiving emails. Copilot users also reported problems.

Microsoft initially flagged trouble accessing Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas. Exchange Online is the service that stores and delivers email for many Outlook owners.

The company later warned that the glitch "may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for owners in any region.".

Industry observers note that the outage dragged out into the evening, and eventually Friday morning, before Microsoft's mitigations began to take effect. By 7:09 a.m. ET, the manufacturer revealed on X that it was finally seeing gradual recovery.

"We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Some users may still experience intermittent problems as recovery actions continue.".

In response to Mashable's questions about the outage, Charles Lamanna, EVP, Copilot, Agents and Platform at Microsoft, provided the following statement:.

"We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. We know our customers rely on our services to get key work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.".

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Innocn E49M1R isn’t your standard super ultrawide monitor. Instead of a curved panel like on other popular massive displays, it’s completely flat and gives you the screen real estate of two 27-inch, 1440p monitors running across your desk.

According to recent reports, when connected to your PC or Mac, you can have two full-sized browser windows or apps running side by side. This makes the E49M1R an excellent choice for productivity, though with a 165Hz panel, Mini-LED backlighting, and AMD FreeSync Premium, it also provides a very immersive gaming experience — granted you have a PC powerful enough to run games at this monitor’s native resolution.

I’ve been using the E49M1R as my daily driver for a month now, and it’s definitely changed how I work. While I’ve used a standard 21:9 ultrawide display for almost a decade, jumping to 32:9 and all that extra screen space has made a real difference while multitasking. Still, it has its trade-offs. While this monitor offers dual HDMI and DisplayPort connections, it’s missing a USB-C port for a one-cable connection to your laptop. Likewise, due to its VA panel and sheer width, colors can appear washed out at the edges if you’re sitting too close.

My Innocn E49M1R review will help you decide if this is the best monitor for your workflow and your desk, or if it’s worth going with something smaller or slightly curved instead.

2 x HDMI 2.1, 2 x DisplayPort 1.4, 1 x audio out, 2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-B.

47.82 × 1.99 × 14.43 inches (without stand), 47.82 × 9.31 × 21.44 inches (with stand).

29.32 pounds with stand (13.3kg).

It has been revealed that the Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, as there’s no other flat super ultrawide display this large. It takes up the full width of most desks, but in return, you get an impressively bright picture, plenty of screen real estate, enough input ports to connect four devices at once, and built-in speakers for the complete package.

Sources indicate that at 47.82 x 1.99 x 14.43 inches, the E49M1R is the largest monitor I’ve ever unboxed. Just like with a large TV, I’d recommend having someone help you unpack it and install the included metal stand. In addition, you also get a power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a DisplayPort cable in the box. Unfortunately, there isn’t a USB-B cable included, which you’ll need if you want to take advantage of the E49M1R’s built-in USB hub — more on that later.

Just like with the other Innocn monitors I’ve tested, installing the metal stand is a breeze. It simply snaps into the back of the monitor, and a single thumb screw attaches the arm to its sturdy metal base. If you’d rather use one of the best monitor arms instead of the included stand, there are 100 x 100 VESA mounting holes on the back of the display.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that one thing I really appreciate about the E49M1R is that instead of tucking all the ports on the underside like you often see on other monitors, they’re all positioned on the back. Along with being height-adjustable, the stand features a cutout near the bottom to make routing cables up to the display easier.

Port-wise, you get dual HDMI 2.1 inputs and dual DisplayPort 1.4 connections, alongside an audio jack. There’s also a USB-B upstream port that, when connected to your computer, lets you use the two USB-A ports next to it for wireless dongles or a webcam. This isn’t a KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) switch, though, as you can’t share those peripherals across two separate computers. At the same time, there’s no USB-C port with Power Delivery, which feels like an odd omission on a premium, super ultrawide monitor like the E49M1R.

According to recent reports, with the E49M1R unboxed and the stand installed, it was time to get it set up on my desk. Now a word of warning here — if you have a desk that’s 48 inches wide, you likely won’t have room for a full desktop PC, though you could tuck one of the best mini PCs underneath this massive display.

I set the E49M1R up on a desk shelf attached to the back of the Secretlab Magnus Evo, and even though that desk is 60 inches wide, things still felt a bit cramped. Fortunately, I’m in the process of reviewing the GMKtec Evo-X3, which is quite thin and designed to be used vertically.

So what’s it like sitting in front of a massive, 49-inch flat super ultrawide? It was definitely daunting at first, but after a few hours, my eyes and neck adjusted to the larger display. By default, you can position one app or browser window on either side, and this felt a lot like the dual-monitor setup I put together last year — just without a gap between the two screens.

Recent findings suggest that while using the E49M1R with two Chrome windows side by side worked well enough, it wasn’t until I installed Microsoft’s PowerToys utility that I could take full advantage of this monitor. Using PowerToys’ built-in FancyZones window manager, I was able to split this 49-inch display into thirds, keeping a smaller window for video calls in the middle with two larger browser windows on either side for multitasking. This worked great, as I could look straight at the center of the screen while presenting and glance off to the side when I needed to check notes or respond to a quick message.

In a recent development, as someone who’s been using an ultrawide monitor for years, making the jump from 21:9 to 32:9 felt natural. If you’ve been using a standard 16:9 display on its own, though, you might be better off switching to a 21:9 ultrawide first before going all the way up to a super ultrawide — especially with a completely flat one like the E49M1R.

One thing you’ll likely have to deal with when switching to an ultrawide — or even a super ultrawide — monitor is black bars on the sides of most video content. However, when you find a video with the right aspect ratio for your screen, it’s a sight to behold.

Industry observers note that to put the E49M1R’s video capabilities to the test, I scoured YouTube for 32:9 trailers until I found one for Godzilla vs. Kong. Seeing King Kong leaping across the landscape and fighting in Hollow Earth was downright awesome, and even though this was a compressed YouTube stream, the picture still looked fantastic on the E49M1R.

Based on our lab tests, you can see that while the E49M1R isn’t as bright as some other premium monitors when displaying content in SDR, it absolutely shines with HDR enabled — hitting a blistering 1,474 nits. It did fairly well with color accuracy, though this is a productivity monitor, and I wouldn’t recommend it for color grading or other heavy graphical work.

Recent findings suggest that while 32:9 videos may be hard to find online, the same can’t be said for games. With a powerful gaming PC, you can fully immerse yourself in the action across the E49M1R’s entire 49-inch display.

In a recent development, even though it was a tight fit, I managed to get the GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro set up on the side of the E49M1R and play some Red Dead Redemption 2. Riding on my horse across the Wild West as Arthur Morgan felt almost like a dream come true, as I could take in all the scenery thanks to the E49M1R’s wider field of view. I’m sure playing a racing game like Forza Horizon 6 would have been even better, though.

It’s worth noting that while the E49M1R has a 165Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, the display definitely lags behind the best gaming monitors when it comes to response time. At 8ms, it’s better suited for slower-paced games, which is why I tested it out with Red Dead Redemption 2 as opposed to a fast-paced, competitive shooter.

All in all, though, you can certainly play games on the E49M1R — even if it’s ultimately better suited for multi-window productivity tasks.

There’s truly no super ultrawide monitor quite like the Innocn E49M1R, thanks to its massive, completely flat display. However, that sheer width can cause colors on either side to look washed out depending on how close you’re sitting, and a USB-C port would have been a welcome addition.

Although this is the first super ultrawide monitor I’ve tested, I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time using two of Innocn’s ultrawide displays: the 40C1U and the 40C1R. While the former is a premium display with a 5K2K resolution and the latter is a more budget-friendly gaming monitor, both feature USB-C with Power Delivery.

Unfortunately, the E49M1R doesn’t. Now, I know some budget laptops would struggle to drive a massive display like this one, but most modern machines can handle it just fine. With Power Delivery built in, you also wouldn’t need to reach for your laptop charger — instead, you could just plug in your Windows laptop or MacBook and get right to work on the E49M1R’s 49-inch screen.

For a monitor with a list price of $999, the lack of a USB-C port is really puzzling, especially since I’ve tested much cheaper displays from Innocn that have one.

Now, whether you prefer a flat or curved ultrawide is something you’ll have to figure out on your own. Personally, I like flat ultrawides since they take up less space on my desk and can easily be wall-mounted or attached to a monitor arm.

With the E49M1R and its VA panel, however, its massive width creates a sort of optical illusion. Even though the picture on either side is just as bright as it is at the center, it doesn’t always appear that way — particularly when you’re sitting very close to the display. For instance, with three Chrome windows side by side, content on the outer two would appear washed out when I turned my head to look at it. However, if I pulled my office chair back a bit, it looked completely normal.

Recent findings suggest that now, if you’re dead set on having the largest, flattest super ultrawide monitor out there, I’d recommend pairing the E49M1R with a very deep desk. That way, you can position the monitor at the very back edge to mitigate this optical illusion. If you’re short on space, though, and aren’t using one of the best standing desks, you could always wall-mount this display just like you would a TV.

Sources indicate that the Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, and it’s a great fit for those who want as much screen real estate as possible without a multi-monitor setup or having to give up desk space for a curved display. That alone would be enough, but its Mini-LED backlighting really makes colors pop and blacks appear deeper, too. You also get plenty of ports alongside a built-in USB hub.

It has been revealed that while I would have liked a built-in KVM switch as well, that isn’t necessarily a dealbreaker. Missing a USB-C port with Power Delivery could be a problem if you’re mainly a laptop user — though if you primarily use a desktop computer, this won’t be an concern, even if it still would have been a nice addition.

Sources indicate that the Innocn E49M1R delivers and then some for anyone who wants the widest, flattest super ultrawide monitor you can get. At full price, you’re getting plenty of screen space for your buck — just make sure this display isn’t too wide for your setup and that you have a desk major enough to house it first.

#454. Users Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

📅 2026-07-03 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (643 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

Users Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

📅 2026-07-03 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • We often hear about shiny newly introduced tools that change everything (yet again).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We often hear about shiny newly introduced tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Consumers don’t get excited about shiny newly introduced “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

According to recent reports, I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and significant design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

So no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, customers can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

Industry observers note that it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where users want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

Recent findings suggest that user’s value doesn’t emerge from consumers having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping users do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that turbo-browser-mcp is a Playwright-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) server built to cut LLM token waste and multi-turn latency in browser automation. It consolidates 25-33 fine-grained browser primitives into 10 batched tools featuring delta DOM snapshots, single-turn React/Shadow DOM/iframe form prefill, direct disk file uploads (no Base64 in context), parallel tab sessions, network blocking presets, and a default human-in-the-loop Submit guard.

All figures below come from benchmarks/benchmark.mjs (npm run benchmark) running headless Chromium locally with exact OpenAI o200k_base tokenization (tiktoken 0.14.0):.

Note on latency vs LLM inference turns: Eliminating 10 round-trips on a 10-field form saves both 7x in browser execution (574 ms -> 82 ms) and 10 separate LLM inference round-trips (2-5s per turn in agent loops) plus ~71,800 replayed history tokens.

Industry observers note that standard MCP servers charge an LLM round-trip for every snapshot, field fill, choice, upload, and verification check. Each turn re-sends the growing conversation history back into the model.

Prefills an entire form in one MCP call while flushing microtasks and macrotasks between controlled inputs:.

Run the benchmark suite yourself with Chromium and Playwright installed:.

Environment & methodology: Headless Chromium via playwright-core, counting exact OpenAI o200k_base tokens via Python tiktoken (approx-bpe fallback if tiktoken is unavailable). Cumulative workflow tokens model standard chat-history replay across $N$ sequential turns: $\sum_{i=1}^{N} (N - i + 1) \cdot T_i$, plus a one-shot baseline where the first turn captures context before acting.

Sources indicate that iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a fresh iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

Sources indicate that for example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a newly introduced optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a latest option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’.

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this fresh setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

According to recent reports, when the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

Industry observers note that I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The upcoming setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Industry observers note that would you trust an AI agent to make purchases online on your behalf? AI companies are hoping you will.

However, many e-commerce and financial service companies are skeptical of the technology and have blocked AI agents from using their platforms.

On Friday, OpenAI launched a latest product called ChatGPT Wallet that appears to be an attempt to address that skepticism.

Industry observers note that according to OpenAI, ChatGPT Wallet will let AI agents make purchases for customers without sharing their credit card information each time. In addition, "security checks" are required for every purchase an AI agent makes. This entails a human user manually reviewing and approving every purchase.

"People add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details," according to ChatGPT. "Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan.".

Instead of revealing credit card information to vendors, ChatGPT remarked it will purchase items using a payment token that serves as a substitute for the actual card's details. Recent findings suggest that E-commerce giant Amazon notably blocked AI agents, such as Meta's Muse, from accessing its platform in September due to security concerns. Banks like JPMorgan Chase followed suit and also blocked Muse and other AI agents. And, just this week, United Airlines blocked AI agents from booking flights due to similar security concerns.

In addition to launching ChatGPT Wallet with major credit card company partnerships, OpenAI is releasing "tools and guidance" for businesses to encourage support for shopping AI agents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Microsoft continues to try to fix a huge service outage that has disrupted software services globally, a new report dropped, possibly confirming something most of us could have guessed.

In a recent development, ookla and DownDetector published a report on Friday afternoon claiming that the Microsoft outage was, by a significant margin, the largest such outage of 2026, based on the number of customers who reported problems on DownDetector. Going by that metric, Microsoft's outage was reported 7.4 million times, compared to just 2.8 million reports for a YouTube outage in February that ranked second among all outages in 2026.

During the Microsoft outage, DownDetector mentioned that it received a peak of 19,650 user error reports for Microsoft's services per minute, which is more than 1,500 times the normal level. Nearly 24 hours later, consumers are still reporting errors for Microsoft.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Aside from the sheer number of reports, the length of the outage was also noteworthy. Outlook and other Microsoft enterprise software services were out for more than 24 hours, compared to a recent 11-hour outage in August, as Mashable reported at the time.

Recent findings suggest that there is one major caveat to all of this: DownDetector relies on user reports rather than anything more verifiable. This has caused companies to sometimes dispute the site's data, which is exactly what Amazon Web Services did (rather passively aggressively) after DownDetector incorrectly showed that AWS was experiencing problems at the same time that Outlook was on Thursday. Mashable reached out to Microsoft, but the company declined to comment on the Ookla report.

As of late Friday afternoon, Microsoft's outage appears to be subsiding, though the company has yet to publish an ETA for full recovery.

Designing For Distressed Users: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

According to recent reports, mental health applications keep facing a continuing, measurable crisis: many people stop using them rapidly. The data is stark: almost 95% of people who open the app on day 1 abandon the app by day 30, with a median 30-day retention of only 3.3%. Even the recognised mental health giants lose around 50% of their users within the first ten days. This severe engagement loss and retention collapse are why effective interface design must be a clinical and operational priority. Good design is not merely aesthetic; it is a fundamental tool for user retention.

Industry observers note that while many factors drive this abandonment, research suggests that mental health apps have tended to prioritise visual appeal at the expense of what actually sustains users. In a space defined by vulnerability and cognitive strain, chasing visual fashion risks adding effort when users have the least to spare — quietly trading away the utility and trust the app depends on. Users don’t open mental health apps out of curiosity, but from need — often while stressed, anxious, overwhelmed, or exhausted. In these states, an unconventional icon, a confusing gesture, or a flashy animation instead of a delightful surprise becomes an extra cognitive overload. Moreover, it becomes a reason to disengage.

Industry observers note that in those moments, visual experimentation from a mild distraction can turn into a friction that undermines the very help the app is meant to deliver. A solution must be a visual interface that is simple in usage and understanding from the first moment.

Crucially, improving engagement depends less on which UI trends you follow than on a single test applied to each one of them: does a trend lower the cost of using the app when the user can least afford it?

Before we look into the specific problems, we must recognise a core tension: many UI trends are optimised for goals that mental health apps don’t share.

Pursuing the former directly overrides the latter. It’s not a surface-level error of colour or font; it’s a foundational conflict of purpose. This tension surfaces across five fronts, each a place where adopting a trend on novelty alone can cost more engagement than it seeks to create.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed principles are not based on a single A/B test or one isolated study. They are built from published research on mental health app engagement, cognitive load, accessibility, and emotional response in mHealth, set against competitive product audits and app-store evidence, and pressure-tested against my own quantitative and qualitative product work. That last source I treat as an illustration, understanding the limits of personal experience. In this context, validation is less about proving that one interface pattern universally works and more about asking whether a design reduces effort, preserves agency, avoids emotional mismatch, and remains usable when the user is already under strain.

Sources indicate that A note on the examples: This isn’t a ranking of apps. Every app has its own positioning, target audience, constraints, and business pressures that may not be visible from outside, and a pattern that strains a user in distress may be exactly right for that product’s actual goal. I’m reading individual, visible design decisions for one question only: how they might affect someone arriving in a low-capacity state.

According to recent reports, the primary goal of any mental health tool is to reduce, not increase, cognitive load. Yet, many trendy interfaces achieve the opposite. Neo-brutalist layouts with stark contrasts demand visual parsing. Hidden navigation menus that rely on non-standard swipes turn simple tasks into puzzles. Abstract, unlabeled icons force customers to guess rather than recognise. Each of these patterns adds friction — seconds of hesitation, a moment of confusion — and for a user whose mental energy is already low, those costs start to accumulate.

This friction is most damaging during acute need. Research suggests that when a user is in a state of high anxiety or depression, even typing or making simple choices can feel overwhelming. When an interface demands high cognitive effort at the moment support is needed, it doesn’t just make that session harder — it gives an overwhelmed user a reason to close the app, and a reason not to reopen it. Each point of confusion can become a place where a user may quit for good.

Other findings show that apps with simple interfaces reduce the time and effort required to engage, directly improving retention. Conversely, a complex, trend-driven UI increases that time, creating an obstacle course that undermines the very healthy habit formation the app is meant to support.

This does not mean that every mental health product must be visually plain or minimal. The issue is whether the interface meets the user’s current capacity.

A panic-support tool, for example, works best when it offers a small number of obvious actions, rather than asking the user to browse. However, if a calming action meant for a moment of panic instead surfaces an upgrade screen, the product fails the user at precisely the point where failing matters most. Monetization is not the issue by itself; the issue is whether it appears at a point where the user expects immediate support.

Industry observers note that nonori shows the same principle in a more reflective context. The app does not present the user with a large content library or a complex dashboard at the start. Instead, it leads them through a simple, linear sequence of small actions. The value of this pattern is that it reduces the effort needed to begin. When a user is tired, anxious, or mentally overloaded, knowing exactly what to do next can lower the barrier to returning.

At the other end of the spectrum, comprehensive tracking apps show a different trade-off. Bearable, for example, is genuinely powerful: it consolidates almost everything a person tracks — mood, symptoms, sleep, medication, habits, reports, correlations — into one place. For consumers managing chronic conditions or preparing for medical appointments, this can be genuinely useful. But the same comprehensiveness can become a burden for an exhausted user. Dense dashboards and multi-step check-ins require executive capacity — the very resource that anxiety, depression, burnout, or brain fog often reduce.

A similar tension appears in anxiety apps with strong support content but busy entry points. A product may contain useful features yet still make the first screen feel noisy with too many cards, locked items, playful characters, or upgrade prompts. This is not evidence that the product is bad. It demonstrates how the same interface can feel very different depending on the user’s state: clear enough during exploration, but too demanding during distress.

This insight shaped a guiding principle for our work: every interaction point must meet owners at their current level of capacity, removing mechanical and cognitive barriers rather than adding to them. This principle guided our integration of low-friction, state-aware interactions in apps like Bear Room, a stress and anxiety reduction app, and Teeni, an emotional-wellbeing app for parents of teens.

According to recent reports, in Bear Room, we already had a fast mood-based flow built around four emotion cards. At the same time, our product research supported a second need: customers also wanted more personalised support. We avoided making this a long selection flow or a typing-only route because both can still create friction for people under stress or anxiety. Instead, we made voice a primary, prominent path, always alongside a text alternative. A central microphone button allows users to share what’s on their mind. The app then uses AI to analyse the input and provide a tailored set of coping practices.

Sources indicate that rather than picking a single entry model, we kept two paths because they served different states. That matched what we saw in later analytics and user conversations: quick emotional selection worked better when consumers wanted speed, while open voice or text input worked better when they wanted personalisation and to feel more heard. This was more a pattern we noticed, without having the exact measured results.

Similarly, in Teeni, we directly addressed the cognitive friction of parenting stress by introducing a “Quick Relief” button. This creates an empathy-friendly flow for parents experiencing anger or frustration. The button initiates a dedicated “Hot Flow,” allowing them to first vent and relieve their immediate negative emotions through voice input. Only after this emotional release does the app gently guide them into the more reflective “Cold Flow” for the rest of the app’s resources. This sequential, state-sensitive design acknowledges that a user in peak distress cannot navigate a complex app; they need a direct, simple, and validating first step.

These solutions directly tackle cognitive friction by meeting users at their level of capacity, resisting trends that add visual or interaction complexity. Voice input and single-action buttons remove the mechanical and cognitive burden of navigation and typing. The result is an interface that feels reliably non-judgmental and genuinely helpful when users are least equipped to navigate complexity.

It has been revealed that A user’s emotional state is the context in which a mental health app operates. This is why its visual language must be empathetic and considerate. Research investigating how colour and aesthetics influence mood in mHealth apps suggests a critical insight: people in distress show a strong preference for subtlety. They long for dark palettes, sleek and sophisticated looks, and clean, uncluttered aesthetics, explicitly noting that cheerful, bright colours, while seemingly appropriate, can create a jarring, even physically uncomfortable conflict with their current mood.

This does not mean that every mental health or wellbeing app should look dark, quiet, or clinically restrained. The category is broad: it includes self-care, anxiety support, habit change, addiction recovery, trauma tools, therapy-adjacent products, and apps for more severe mental health contexts. A playful visual style may be appropriate for one product and a poor fit for another. What matters is not whether the interface is bright or muted, but whether its emotional tone fits the product’s purpose and the likely state in which users arrive.

According to recent reports, emotional mismatch can also appear in mechanics, not only in aesthetics. In Calmer, an anxiety and panic relief app, the interface itself appeared relatively clean and relaxed. Yet some of its engagement and monetisation mechanics sit in a different register from that relaxed: a discount wheel, or confetti celebrating a logged low mood. For a user who just recorded a hard moment, that shift — from quiet support to upsell or celebration — can land as a mismatch, whatever its intent.

It has been revealed that for Bear Room, we prototyped a “cosy room” design informed by direct feedback from our users, which echoed the study’s conclusions. Several users in our research described the apps they had tried for similar needs as “too bright, too happy, and too overwhelming”. Users longed for a digital safe space. This was part of what pointed us toward a quieter palette in the final design: muted, earthy tones — neutral hues like soft greens and taupes — set against darker, calming backgrounds. For this product — a refuge for users arriving overwhelmed — that meant a middle ground: a space that feels safe without being gloomy. The interface avoided any bright alerts or sudden animations, making calmness the core feature.

In a recent development, this case underscores a critical principle: an overly cheerful, bold, or trend-forward interface can feel dismissive to someone in distress, creating a conflict that erodes trust. As Bear Room shows, trust is built when the interface respectfully aligns with the user’s emotional reality, offering solace through subtlety (which creates an overall feeling of a “welcoming and safe atmosphere”), not a solution through saturation.

It has been revealed that mental health often relies on routine and predictability. Yet many contemporary UI trends thrive on novelty and disruption, intentionally reimagining fundamental navigation. When an app introduces a novel interaction pattern, such as a unique swipe or a non-standard button behavior, it asks the user to learn something before they can act, forcing them into cognitive effort they can’t afford.

This does not mean that mental health apps must be plain, rigid, or generic. A product can have its own character, playfulness, and sense of identity. The question is whether that identity remains understandable and predictable when the user returns in a low-capacity state. A gamified self-care app like Finch may work well when the user arrives ready to explore, play, and build a routine. But open it after a hard day just to mark one task done, and the can’t-skip celebration screens that delight an engaged user become one more layer to get through before they reach what they came for.

A similar tension appears in large meditation and wellbeing platforms. Apps such as Headspace and Calm offer extensive libraries of different content. This breadth can be valuable during exploration. But in moments of stress, the product question becomes sharper: can the user return and immediately find the exact support they need, or do they have to search, filter, and relearn the structure?

Someone experiencing anxiety or executive dysfunction needs to use the tool in a straightforward navigation manner, not an interface they have to learn each time anew.

According to recent reports, PTSD Coach, a public-health-oriented trauma-support app designed to help people learn about and manage symptoms after trauma, offers a useful positive example. Its interface is not trying to be fashion-forward. Its strength lies in a stable information architecture: users can learn, track symptoms, manage symptoms, and get support through clearly separated areas. For a user returning during distress, this predictability matters more than novelty.

Recent findings suggest that CALMzone offers another useful example. Some of its breathing animations differ from standard visual patterns, but they remain tied to the exercise itself: the animation reveals what to do, when to inhale, and when to hold. The guided audio screen also explicitly invites the user to put the phone down and listen. This is a rare and valuable form of interaction design: the product’s success is not more screen time, but reduced effort and regulation.

These insights guided our approach in applications like Bear Room, where navigation reliability was treated as a therapeutic feature. We intentionally crafted an experience of an empathetic guided flow.

Recognising that users would likely approach in states of overwhelm, we structured the interface as a clear, unwavering path, with a visible “Start” sign. Key emotional support tools here are represented as the room’s objects — symbols of daily life, unmistakably recognised by all. They are visually highlighted by design so that the user won’t get lost in the elements, can easily access the needed tool, and can remember their way around the digital space upon the next return to the app.

Trend-driven interfaces sacrifice this navigational certainty for novelty. Each unconventional choice in mHealth apps, when core functions are buried behind experimental interactions or placed in unexpected locations, leads to a cumulative effect of fatigue instead of innovation. Users are not in a place to explore. They abandon the entire practice of seeking digital support when every interaction feels like solving a fresh puzzle. This does not restrict experimentation; it simply means that animations, micro-interactions, AI, or playful mechanics must serve the user’s state rather than interrupt it.

Recent findings suggest that many popular UI trends can be exclusionary when applied without adaptation. The minimalist trend of low-contrast text fails users with visual impairments. Gesture-only navigation marginalises those with motor difficulties. Visually dense, animated interfaces can overwhelm users with cognitive or attentional conditions. In mental health, the population needing support disproportionately includes individuals with these accessibility needs.

Sources indicate that choosing a trending aesthetic over an accessible one is therefore an active decision to limit the app’s reach and efficacy. It ensures that those who might benefit most cannot use the tool effectively. Accessibility isn’t a layer you add at the end; it’s a constraint you design within, with most of it codified in Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2. Body text needs 4.5:1 contrast against its background, large text and interface elements 3:1 — exactly what low-contrast minimalism fails. Interactive targets need a floor of 24×24 px (more for unsteady hands). Every gesture needs a visible button fallback, or you risk excluding anyone who can’t perform the swipe.

A final, and often overlooked, consequence of trend-following is the adoption of engagement mechanics designed for entertainment, educational, or productivity apps. Features like streaks, aggressive notifications, and gamified reward systems are engineered to maximise screen time and create dependency. Although they have long been considered effective tools for increasing retention, in a mental health context, this approach can easily be misguided. What presents as “motivation” can quickly transform into a source of performance pressure and guilt. For a user managing depression, a broken streak or a missed daily goal can exacerbate the very feelings the app aims to alleviate.

These mechanics are not inherently unethical. In routine-building products, they can help some customers. The risk appears when they are transferred into mental health contexts without adapting for shame, low energy, relapse, and non-linear recovery. A streak, for example, is not just a retention mechanic when the user is emotionally vulnerable. It can become a visible record of whether they have “kept up” with their well-being.

In the apps I reviewed, this tension appeared through familiar persuasion patterns: streaks, streak freezes, commitment copy, urgency-based notifications, “don’t miss this offer” prompts, and success-framed buttons such as “Yes, I want to succeed.” In self-care or wellbeing products, these details can make the app feel less like a supportive tool and more like another system the user has to satisfy.

Designers still need return triggers. A mental health app has little value if owners install it once and forget it exists. But return mechanics must be adapted to the emotional context. In Bear Room, for example, this philosophy is embodied in short, forgiving three-day streaks: the streak does not reset when a user misses a day, and every third day brings a small benefit. The goal is not to punish absence, but to gently support return.

The same principle applies to lighter interactions. Bear Room includes a simple, optional bubble-popping game. Its purpose, however, is not to hook the user but to offer a brief, calming interlude. It is deliberately finite, providing a small mood lift and gently signposting other resources within the app. The value is in the momentary relief, not the extended session.

This commitment to supportive, non-coercive design extends to foundational app architecture:.

In mental health technology, sustainable retention is earned not by capturing attention, but by becoming a consistently respectful and helpful presence in a user’s life.

The mHealth apps design invites finding a challenging balance between boosting their use without being too demanding.

In a recent development, this is not a niche concern affecting a fringe audience. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that about one billion people globally live with a mental disorder, with depression alone affecting nearly 5% of adults. Critically, the overall number is rising — in the last decade, depression and anxiety cases have increased by 25%. This vast and vulnerable population cannot afford for its tools to fail due to poor design. While UI trends aren’t inherently problematic, their application within wellbeing products demands a radically contextual approach.

Even a five-minute decompression tool between meetings has an emotional context, and a style chosen for its look — glassmorphism, a certain flavour of ultra-minimalism — can miss it, however sophisticated the audience. The point isn’t that these styles are wrong; it’s that the look has to answer to the moment. Soft biomorphic shapes or fluid transitions can genuinely help when they directly serve the goal of calm — and the same elements become noise when they’re there to impress.

The five fronts outlined above are not just a diagnostic lens; they are the foundation of an evaluation framework for anyone designing in the mental health space. Before incorporating any trendy visual or interaction pattern, it is worth running it through each of them in sequence:.

A design that passes all five holds together as something more than usable: it becomes a tool that users can trust enough to return to in moments of genuine need.

It has been revealed that trends can be inspiring. They can win awards and generate buzz. But in mental health, sometimes the best design is the one that helps owners feel understood — a quiet helper they trust enough to return to in moments of stress and vulnerability. It doesn’t steal the spotlight, but focuses on the user’s emotions. In the end, the ultimate goal is not for the interface to be seen — but for the support to be felt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the newly introduced Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the upcoming Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

Industry observers note that the most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

According to recent reports, you can use the upcoming Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the fresh speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the upcoming Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update: The ground stop has been lifted, and domestic flights resumed late Friday.

Recent findings suggest that in an extraordinarily rare move, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) unveiled that all flights in the U.S. are grounded on Friday afternoon.

The FAA said this nationwide ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.".

According to recent reports, U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy posted a confirmation of the outage on his X account, attributing the ground stop order to "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy added, “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.".

The FAA has only ordered the grounding of all flights nationwide on two prior occasions. The first was on 9/11, and the second was on Jan. 11, 2023, when all flights were grounded for 90 minutes due to problems with the Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system. In 2024, the CrowdStrike IT outage led some major airlines to issue a global stoppage.

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication concerns impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the FAA said in a statement. "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice," read an air traffic control advisory reported by Axios. For those preparing to board a flight, this will obviously cause delays.

Travelers who need to monitor the status of their air travel should make sure to turn on notifications with their airline in order to receive up-to-the-minute updates regarding their specific flights.

To check the status of flights online, you can use the following resources:.

Flighty: An iOS app that uses FAA air traffic control data to track flights.

FlightAware: A website and app (Android and iOS) that provides live tracking for flights.

Misery Map: A FlightAware map showing cancellations and delays around the country.

Flightradar24: Another live radar map available through a website and app (Android and iOS).

As of this writing, the Misery Map shows 2,438 delays and counting.

The FAA also provides broad status updates regarding active airport events on its National Airspace System Status website located at https://nasstatus.faa.gov/.

Flyers can also check the social media profiles and websites of specific airports for local updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a â90 + 30â vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days âsoak timeâ for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put customers at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. âPatch gapâ is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant enhancement. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

Recent findings suggest that LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a latest vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:.

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Industry observers note that starting today, our policy is âFull 90â, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a âFull 60â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a âFull 30â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

It has been revealed that we are also removing most âspecial casesâ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:.

Recent findings suggest that project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this fresh policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm owners by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the newly introduced policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors arenât equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and donât attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.

While our analysis isnât always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That mentioned, we donât feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerabilityâs severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

Recent findings suggest that when vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesnât change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

Sources indicate that itâs also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies, as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

Sources indicate that the question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.

We still proposal to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.

They say that a lot of times, while locking the screen on their Pixel 9 Pro Fold, the notification drawer drops and remains on the screen. The issue occurs only within the first few seconds after locking the screen, which is also confirmed by another user, MerkurMan. They add that the screen continues to respond for almost 4 seconds after it is locked when Tap to Wake is turned off. This behavior is obviously unintended.
