  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that when a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anastasia Sycheva is the founder and art director of Feely Studio, a branding agency for technology startups. Since 2016, she has helped SaaS, fintech, … More about Anastasia ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that when a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined. The result is a gap between what the brand is supposed to communicate and what the designer is expected to create. This is the space I like to call the “pre-concept” phase.

It has been revealed that at the beginning of a project, designers usually receive many inputs: a brief, a few stakeholder conversations, competitor references, maybe a moodboard or a list of adjectives. From there, they are expected to create visual concepts that feel right. But “right” is difficult to judge when the team has not agreed on what the brand is supposed to communicate in the first place.

Sources indicate that as an example, a health tech organization we worked with mentioned they wanted to look modern, trustworthy, and disruptive. At first, “disruptive” sounded like a push toward something bold and unconventional. But as we talked, it became clear that disruption, for them, still had to feel credible inside a conservative healthcare environment. Their clients were large government medical institutions. A brand that felt too rebellious, experimental, or visually loud would not create the right kind of trust.

In other words, their version of “disruptive” looked more traditional than the word suggested.

The problem was not that the client used the wrong language. The problem was that the language was too broad to guide design decisions. Before a designer can turn strategy into a visual concept, those words need to become more specific. What kind of modern? Trustworthy in what way? Disruptive compared to whom? And how far can the brand move away from category expectations before it starts to feel wrong for its audience?

Sources indicate that this article is about that pre-concept phase: the work that happens after the kickoff but before the first visual direction. While the broader brand identity process for digital products includes strategy, concepts, implementation, and the assets a product team needs to build consistently, this article focuses on the earlier work that makes the first concept possible: researching the brand context, uncovering hidden assumptions with stakeholders, and turning shared direction into a visual foundation. Rather, a practical bridge between what the brand needs to mean and how it might begin to look.

The first place to build that bridge is the brand workshop, where broad discovery needs to become a clearer understanding of the brand context.

A brand workshop will naturally cover the standard discovery topics: the business, its goals, the product or service, the competitive landscape, and the target audience. This article will not try to list every question a designer should ask in that workshop. For readers who want a broader starting point, we prepared a Brand Workshop Toolkit: Questions and Exercises, a FigJam framework we use in our studio to structure discovery conversations.

Recent findings suggest that here, I want to focus on a smaller set of questions that are easy to skip but extremely useful before visual work begins. These questions are less about collecting facts and more about clarifying perception. They help the team understand what the brand needs to make people believe, where it needs to feel credible, and which category assumptions it should follow or challenge.

Perception sits at the center of brand discovery because the brand is shaped in someone else’s mind.

If the brand ultimately lives in someone else’s perception, the workshop has to clarify what perception the team is trying to create.

The perception questions I focus on are:.

These questions help reveal the assumptions behind people’s opinions, instead of simply adding more opinions to the room. The questions matter because brand attributes often sound aligned before they are actually understood. A stakeholder may say the brand should feel “premium,” and everyone may nod. But one person may mean refined and editorial. Another may mean expensive and exclusive. Another may mean clean, quiet, and minimal. The word sounds shared, but it can lead to three completely different visual systems.

For instance, in the health tech project mentioned earlier, the client described the desired brand as “disruptive.” In many categories, that might suggest something bold, loud, or unconventional. But their audience was large government medical institutions, so disruption had to be expressed through clarity, efficiency, and confidence rather than rebellion. If we had taken the word at face value, the visual direction could easily have moved too far from what their audience would trust.

Sources indicate that in another project, a fintech team wanted the brand to feel “bold” without losing credibility. That word created useful tension. The word bold could mean bright colors, oversized typography, and a highly expressive system. But in a financial category, it also had to carry signals of security, control, and competence. The question was not whether the brand should be bold, but what kind of boldness would still feel trustworthy.

When the team can define what these attributes mean in context, the designer is no longer working from broad adjectives. They are working from a clearer design problem.

Sources indicate that strategically selected questions can uncover part of the verbal layer, but words alone are rarely enough. To move from language into visual direction, it helps to incorporate exercises that make stakeholders think through images, associations, and relative perception.

Jake Knapp makes a similar point in GV’s Three-Hour Brand Sprint:.

The following two exercises help translate what stakeholders say about the brand into material that can later inform look and feel, design principles, and concept development.

This is also where stakeholder participation becomes notable. When clients only receive a strategy presentation, they can stay passive. They may agree in the meeting without noticing the assumptions they are bringing into the process. But when they have to place a competitor on a map, choose an image, or explain why a certain reference feels credible, they become active participants. Their attitudes, beliefs, and disagreements become visible before they have a chance to derail the first concept review.

I usually start by looking outward at the category, then inward at the brand itself.

Before the workshop, collect screenshots of competitor brands, websites, product interfaces, social visuals, or other visible brand touchpoints. During the workshop, ask the client team to place those competitors on a simple two-axis map.

This exercise is not about deciding which competitors have “good” or “bad” design. It is about understanding how the client reads the category: what feels credible, what feels generic, what feels too conservative, what feels too experimental, and where there may be an open visual territory for the brand.

In a recent development, the axes should be chosen based on the tension the brand needs to solve. For example:.

For a health tech tech giant that wants to feel innovative but works with conservative medical institutions, the map might use traditional to progressive and corporate to human. For a fintech brand that wants to stand out without losing trust, it might use understated to bold and accessible to exclusive.

In a recent development, the most useful part of this exercise is often not the final map, but the disagreement it creates. One stakeholder may read a competitor as progressive, while another sees it as generic. One may see a brand as premium, while another reads it as cold. These disagreements reveal how different people define trust, innovation, credibility, and differentiation. That is exactly the kind of ambiguity that needs to be resolved before design begins.

According to recent reports, after the team has discussed the category, I like to turn the conversation inward. One exercise we use for this is called Visual Brand Driver. Each stakeholder is asked to choose images for a set of unrelated categories: transport, typeface, activity, furniture, mood, object, animal, architecture, and drink.

It has been revealed that the instruction is key: the images should not represent the person’s personal taste. They should represent the company.

In a recent development, for example, if the company were a type of transport, what would it be? A quiet electric car, a high-speed train, a private jet, a bicycle, a delivery van? If it were a piece of furniture, would it be a soft lounge chair, a precise modular desk, or a heavy boardroom table?

In a recent development, after choosing the images, each person adds four or five adjectives to explain why they selected them. This part matters more than the image itself. The same object can mean different things to different people. A train might suggest speed, structure, reliability, mass accessibility, or a fixed route. A lounge chair might suggest comfort, calm, informality, or lack of urgency.

In a recent development, the exercise helps create a deeper layer of brand perception. Instead of asking people to describe the tech giant directly, it asks them to think through metaphor and association. Patterns and contradictions become visible. One stakeholder may see the brand as refined and calm, another as energetic and experimental. One may describe the company as precise and structured, another as warm and flexible.

Sources indicate that those differences are not a problem. They are useful materials. They show what needs to be clarified before the visual concept phase begins.

This exercise is also helpful because it separates brand perception from aesthetic preference. A stakeholder may personally like a certain image, but if it does not describe the tech giant, it should not be part of the exercise. That distinction is important throughout the branding process. The question is not “Do we like this?” but “Does this express the right thing about the brand?”.

Industry observers note that once the workshop has revealed the main assumptions, the next client meeting can turn that shared understanding into a visual foundation. This is still not the first identity concept. It is a working layer between strategy and design, where the client can react to perception, visual principles, and early asset directions before the designer invests time in full concepts.

We usually structure this meeting around three connected layers:.

Together, these layers move the conversation from perception to practical design boundaries.

Look and feel boards are not collections of visuals the team likes. They are perception boards. The designer collects references based on the workshop: desired perception, category tension, competitor codes, stakeholder disagreements, and brand character.

Recent findings suggest that if the brand needs to feel trustworthy, modern, and human, the board should help the team discuss what kind of trust, modernity, and humanity are appropriate. Is the brand calm and institutional, or warm and accessible? Is it progressive through precision, or through a more expressive editorial tone?

The point is to let the client respond to perception before reacting to a logo, color palette, or finished visual system.

Design code makes the direction more specific by translating key brand ideas into visual principles.

For a parenting app in Germany, personalized support for your unique journey might become organic shapes, handwritten lines, and softer compositions. Parenting is messy and magical might become soft gradients, layered imagery, and playful irregularity. Research-backed support for real life might introduce doctor calls, data snapshots, infographics, and editorial layouts that make the brand feel credible.

Sources indicate that for a PR agency working with prop tech companies, momentum in motion might become lines, arrows, ripple effects, or motion blur. Springboard might become a lift-off moment and elastic visual energy. Building blocks might become modular shapes or stacked compositions.

Sources indicate that the team is not choosing the final graphic expression here. It is testing whether the visual metaphors make sense before concept design begins.

The final layer brings the conversation down to the building blocks of identity: typography, color, logo style, photography, illustration, and graphic language.

At this stage, the team can discuss questions such as:.

Recent findings suggest that this gives the designer boundaries without making the final identity predictable. The next step is still concept design, but the team is no longer starting from vague adjectives or private expectations.

Before moving into the first concept, it helps to pause and check whether the team has enough shared direction. The checklist is not meant to make every decision in advance. It is meant to make sure the designer is not starting from vague words, hidden assumptions, or unresolved disagreements.

Before creating the first concept, check whether the team has:.

According to recent reports, this last point is especially useful. A strong pre-concept phase not only tells the designer what to explore. It also clarifies what to avoid: directions that would be too expected, too cold, too playful, too conservative, too loud, too generic, or too far from what the audience can trust.

Industry observers note that when the team can name those boundaries, the first concept becomes easier to evaluate. The conversation shifts from “I like it” or “I do not like it” to “Does this express the brand we agreed on?”.

Recent findings suggest that the first concept should not feel like a guess or a surprise reveal. It should feel like the next step in a direction the team already understands.

That does not mean removing intuition, experimentation, or creative risk from the branding process. It means giving those things a sharper problem to solve. When the team has clarified the brand character, tested visual perception, translated ideas into design principles, and discussed the early building blocks of the identity, the designer can explore with more confidence.

Pre-concept work does not need to make the final identity predictable. It needs to make the conversation around it more meaningful. Instead of asking whether the work matches someone’s private expectation, the team can ask a better question: Does this visual direction express what the brand needs to become?

  • According to recent reports, several sources told CBS News Friday evening that the ground stop was caused by a communication system reboot.
  • Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage was caused by an outdated air traffic control system coming up against the processing power of newly implemented modern technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trump administration officials and Air Traffic Control (ATC) insiders are shedding light on Friday's nationwide ground stop, which resulted in massive delays for thousands of flights and nearly all domestic travelers.

According to recent reports, several sources told CBS News Friday evening that the ground stop was caused by a communication system reboot. According to multiple insiders with knowledge of the incident, an patch to a private communications network used by air traffic controllers forced the system to reboot and impede communications at the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers, CBS News reported.

Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage was caused by an outdated air traffic control system coming up against the processing power of newly implemented modern technology.

It has been revealed that "Our routers got overloaded by the data," remarked Duffy. The secretary said the overloaded routers, which he described as "'80s copper lines", caused instability in communications at Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) and Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Out of an "abundance of caution," the FAA issued the ground stop.

It has been revealed that duffy asserted that only older lines were affected, not newly installed ATC tech. Duffy then called on Congress to provide $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the system completely. The ground stop has now been lifted.

As recently as 6 p.m. ET, insiders reported the FAA was still investigating the circumstances behind the communication blackout.

Industry observers note that following confirmation of a telecommunications outage, social media users theorized the blackout may have been a consequence of the FAA's upcoming AI-powered air traffic control system, known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART. Others suggested the recent Microsoft outage could have been a factor.

Industry observers note that when asked if AI played a role in the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the press that officials couldn't "rule anything out." In comments to the press later that evening, Mullin once again affirmed officials haven't found any indication of a cybersecurity attack but couldn't rule out interference entirely. "There’s nothing completely certain right now. It does not appear that way," Mullin noted. "The public was never at danger. There was never any lives at risk. There were no flights at risk.".

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the organization behind SMART, denied speculation that the new AI tool was involved in the ground stop. Microsoft also issued a statement, writing: "We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.".

The FAA has undertaken an administration-wide modernization project, including phasing out the use of floppy disks for storing weather conditions, airport status updates, equipment concerns, and other critical information.

6 reasons I’d still buy the Galaxy S26 Ultra instead of the Motorola Signature 27

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.
  • Industry observers note that on paper, the Motorola Signature 27 looks like an almost unbeatable flagship.
  • Yet, numbers in a vacuum do not make a flagship a must-buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Industry observers note that on paper, the Motorola Signature 27 looks like an almost unbeatable flagship. With a massive 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, an eye-catching 200MP telephoto camera, and a newer 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, Motorola has built an uncompromising spec-sheet juggernaut.

Yet, numbers in a vacuum do not make a flagship a must-buy. Despite Motorola’s aggressive leap into the ultra-premium tier, there are good reasons to continue leaning towards the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra as a potentially smarter, more cohesive purchase. Here are six reasons you should pick Samsung’s flagship over Motorola’s latest challenger.

According to recent reports, one of the Signature 27’s claims to fame is its incredibly bright display, which reportedly peaks at an eye-melting 12,000 nits. However, as we know, these figures are usually only achievable in very specific scenarios, typically when viewing HDR content under particular lighting conditions. Potentially useful, but unlikely to actually change the way you use your phone.

It has been revealed that samsung’s Privacy Display, on the other hand, marks a dramatic change in the way you can use your new handset. Granted, the technology actually makes the screen look a little dimmer and flatter when it’s active. But that’s a small price to pay for being able to block out all or just part of your display when specific apps are active, keeping your banking details and messages away from prying eyes.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone who regularly uses their phone on public transport or in crowded places, Privacy Display is the sort of feature you appreciate every single day. Much more so than a slightly brighter display.

Sources indicate that I’m not going to pretend I don’t want a bigger battery in my phone; I’m quite the convert to silicon-carbon cells like the 7,000mAh behemoth packed into the Signature 27. It certainly dwarfs the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 5,000mAh capacity, and Motorola claims it will charge almost as promptly: 52 minutes versus Samsung’s 45 minutes.

However, that extra longevity comes with some notable trade-offs. The Signature 27 weighs 227g (8.01 oz), making it a fraction heavier than Samsung’s 214g (7.55 oz) flagship. The new Motorola flagship is also 8mm thick, compared with 7.9mm for the Ultra, before considering the camera bumps.

Sources indicate that that’s unlikely to be a deal-breaker, but Samsung also includes the S Pen in its slightly slimmer, lighter frame; a handy tool for jotting down notes, editing photos, and annotating screenshots. Unfortunately, Samsung dropped S Pen Bluetooth support with the S25 Ultra, meaning features like Air Actions are no longer available. This may feel like a backward step for series fans, though I never found much use for remotely triggering the camera or controlling media with the little accessory.

Motorola might have the edge on longevity, but the S Pen is still an undeniably useful power-user tool that can help you get more done throughout the day.

According to recent reports, speaking of power users, Samsung Dex remains the best-in-class experience for turning your smartphone into a pocket PC. Simply hook your phone up to a compatible display via a USB-C-to-HDMI cable or wirelessly, and you’re up and running with a powerful desktop-style environment.

Industry observers note that deX lets you use a larger screen to work on documents, spreadsheets, and presentations while keeping access to the same document storage you already have on your phone. The setup supports desktop UX essentials, including multi-window, copy and paste, and multi-desktop support. We’ve even had success turning an Ultra flagship into a lightweight gaming PC setup via a combination of Dex and GameNative.

The Signature 27’s closest tool is Smart Connect, which works with supported Motorola and Lenovo laptops to share content and continue some activities across form factors. That’s handy, no doubt, but it requires you to be more deeply invested in a single ecosystem and certainly doesn’t help if you just want to get work done with only a phone in your pocket.

Motorola builds some pretty great software too, and the Signature 27 has a few neat tricks of its own, but nothing quite in the same league as the advanced customization available through Samsung’s Good Lock app. If you want to make your phone truly your own, the Galaxy S26 Ultra has this ace firmly up its sleeve.

Industry observers note that whether you want to completely rethink your screen layout, tweak navigation gestures, or change how notifications appear, Good Lock has a module for it. For instance, LockStar gives you much more control over the layout and features of your lock screen. One Hand Operation+ adds powerful gesture controls, while Sound Assistant and Camera Assistant let you fine-tune parts of the audio and camera experiences that Samsung’s standard settings don’t expose.

Moto Gestures and a suite of customization options help make Hello UI feel like your own, but Samsung’s Good Lock provides even more tools to tinker with One UI and change how your Ultra behaves.

According to recent reports, both the Signature 27 and Galaxy S26 Ultra promise seven years of OS upgrades and security patches; exactly what you should expect when spending top dollar on a modern flagship. However, only one of these brands has a solid reputation for consistently delivering, and that’s Samsung.

Outside of Google’s Pixel updates, Samsung’s global rollout speed and monthly patch cadence under One UI remain pretty much the gold standard in the Android space. Motorola, meanwhile, is still establishing a proven track record for rapid, multi-year maintenance on this scale. Owners regularly complain about delays and seemingly out-of-order enhancement priorities on Motorola phones. And while Samsung has missed the occasional deadline, it has been very reliable when it comes to delivering updates to flagships and mid-rangers, new and old.

According to recent reports, time will tell if Motorola addresses this bugbear with the Signature 27. But if you want a proven track record, Samsung is hands down the safer pick.

When it comes to cameras, battery capacity, performance, and, dare I say it, even design, the Signature 27 probably has the hardware edge over the Galaxy S26 Ultra. However, all those extra goodies don’t come cheap; the Signature 27 costs a whopping $1,599 in the US.

Recent findings suggest that the S26 Ultra has a lower starting price of $1,299, saving you $300 that could be put towards additional storage or accessories, if you want. Not to mention that Samsung’s flagships can often benefit from carrier deals, trade-in values, and frequent retail promotions, especially this many months after launch.

Of course, price isn’t everything at this end of the market, and Motorola has clearly invested heavily in its hardware. But when the slightly more affordable phone also brings a more mature software experience and several genuinely useful extras, the Signature 27 has a harder time justifying its premium.

Sources indicate that none of these reasons alone makes the Galaxy S26 Ultra categorically better than the Motorola Signature 27. In many respects, the two are either evenly matched, or you can point to several specifications that lean in Motorola’s favor.

Sources indicate that however, Samsung knows how to build power-user phones like few others. Having the S Pen tucked into the phone, turning it into a desktop PC, tweaking One UI with Good Lock, and hiding my screen from prying eyes are all compelling experiences that are hard to emulate elsewhere. None is essential, but together they make the S26 Ultra feel more versatile — and for me, that’s what makes it the more compelling flagship.

U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy also confirmed the flight stoppage on X.

It has been revealed that "The [FAA] issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication problem impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.".

Sources indicate that the FAA rarely halts traffic coast to coast, leaving many travelers with questions about their flight status and the cause of the grounding. Here's what we know so far.

According to recent reports, the FAA's original explanation was that the ground stoppage was necessary "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." That was a vague and somewhat anxiety-inducing communication, as many Americans associate nationwide ground stoppages with the tragedy of Sept. 11, when flights were also stopped in dramatic fashion.

However, the FAA soon clarified in a statement that the order was issued due to a telecommunications issue.

"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage — out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.".

However, CNN reported this extraordinary quote, citing an unnamed airline source: "Ten minutes ago, they were on a crisis call and there was still no clear answer as to a cause." More recently, CNN reported that the FAA told airlines that the problem originated with "network routers.".

Sources indicate that in a White House press briefing late Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin explained the ground stop was the result of outdated air traffic control systems. Duffy mentioned the analogue systems were "overloaded" by a patchwork of newly-installed modern technology, which caused inconsistencies in radar and communications. The FAA ordered the ground stop out of an "abundance of caution," officials explained.

In a recent development, according to the Misery Map, a visualization of cancellations and delays produced by the flight-tracking service FlightAware, there have been 2,406 delays and 763 cancellations so far today. At the same time yesterday, FlightAware recorded 410 delays and six cancellations.

Industry observers note that because of the chaotic nature of a sudden ground stoppage, many travelers may be stuck sitting in planes on the tarmac. One Mashable reporter is currently in exactly that situation.

In the hours after the FAA grounded all domestic flights, major airports are warning travelers to check their flight status before heading to the airport. The X account of Fresh York City's John F. Kennedy Airport wrote, "Travelers should confirm their flight status with their airline before heading to the airport." Dulles International Airport in Washington, DC issued the following advisory to travelers: "Prior to coming to the airport, check with your airline regarding the status of your flight." The FAA has only grounded all planes nationwide on two prior occasions. It happened for the first time on 9/11, and then again on Jan. 11, 2023. In 2024, the infamous CrowdStrike IT outage led major airlines to glitch a global stoppage.

As with yesterday's global Microsoft outage, online commentators rapidly speculated that a cyberattack may have been the cause of the ground stoppage, but there is currently no reason to believe that is the case. The FAA has clearly stated that it's the result of "a temporary telecommunications outage." Mullin reiterated in the Friday briefing that there were "no indications" of foreign interference as of now.

The FAA's IT infrastructure is notoriously out of date. Just last week, Mashable reported on the administration's prepares to finally phase out floppy disks — two years from now.

CBS News reported that multiple sources told them "[a]n patch to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage." A Florida-based company, L3Harris, operates that system, according to CBS News.

Speaking at a news conference, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin remarked, "This is not another 9/11," according to KOMO News.

Sources indicate that "There is no fear to the public. I want to make sure we say this again — there is no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," the secretary stated.

In recent days, the FAA revealed it was expanding the use of an AI tool to help air traffic controllers manage traffic, according to Ars Technica. However, there is no evidence that the current stoppage and the AI rollout are related. That hasn't stopped frustrated travelers from speculating on a connection, however.

On Friday evening, the manufacturer behind the newly introduced AI tool stated that there was absolutely no connection between the ground stoppage and its work.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, it's impossible to answer that question. As we already noted, the last nationwide ground stoppage in 2023 lasted approximately 90 minutes, according to the FAA's communications at the time.

If CNN's source who claimed the FAA at the moment has no idea what caused the problem is correct, it could drag on much longer than travelers would like.

We should also note that it's at the moment Friday the 13th.

#423. I thought Breath of the Wild ruined classic Zelda for me, then I played Ocarina of Time on Nintendo Switch 2 — and I was very wrong

I thought Breath of the Wild ruined classic Zelda for me, then I played Ocarina of Time on Nintendo Switch 2 — and I was very wrong

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In February 2021, I wrote an op-ed titled “Breath of the Wild ruined traditional Zelda for me.” Back then, I mused that Breath of the Wild being my first-ever Zelda game had made going back to the older titles in the beloved Nintendo franchise difficult.
  • I’ll cut my past self a little slack.
  • Nevertheless, I definitely wrote off classic Zelda games too hastily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In February 2021, I wrote an op-ed titled “Breath of the Wild ruined traditional Zelda for me.” Back then, I mused that Breath of the Wild being my first-ever Zelda game had made going back to the older titles in the beloved Nintendo franchise difficult. Flash-forward to now, and I’m roughly halfway through the new Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2, and I’m loving it.

I’ll cut my past self a little slack. February 2021 was more than five years ago, and a person’s tastes can change a lot in that amount of time. Heck, in those days, I also thought Souls games weren’t for me. Now in 2026, I’ve beaten every modern title FromSoftware has released (bar Dark Souls 2; it’s in my overflowing backlog) and am basically obsessed with the Soulslike genre.

Nevertheless, I definitely wrote off classic Zelda games too hastily. Turns out all it took was pretty much the most acclaimed video game of all time getting a stunning remake for me to see just how foolish I had been. Consider this follow-up article my formal apology to Link.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2, and in a word, it's stunning. This complete remake of the classic Nintendo 64 offers overhauled visuals, improved controls, and a few smart tweaks to make the timeless game even more modern. Ocarina of Time was considered a masterpiece back in 1998, and this new version on Switch 2 has earned the same plaudits.

Ocarina of Time starts a little slow. Lots of text boxes and simple tutorials. But once the adventure really begins, and Young Link is tasked with finding three Spiritual Stones (the first is obtained during the prologue chapter), I started to discover exactly why longtime fans bemoan Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom’s lack of “proper” Zelda dungeons.

But it was only once I had obtained all three stones and transformed into grown-up Link that I really understood what makes these dungeons so special, and why fans still beg for the series to bring them back. Nintendo’s penchant for creative and satisfying puzzles is on full display in the Forest, Fire and Water Temple, and I’m very excited to head to the remaining dungeons and discover what’s hiding within their twisting corridors.

The Fire Temple is a great example of phenomenal design, as the underground lava-laden cavern loops back on itself in surprising and creative ways. The infamous Water Temple might actually be my frontrunner favorite, probably because the remake has stripped away the friction of the original.

Best of all is the way each dungeon gives you a fresh tool to play with, which is then vital to unlocking the dungeon’s many secrets; it is a consistently brilliant way of asking players to make use of their entire arsenal of tools.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite aspect of Breath of the Wild (and sequel Tears of the Kingdom) has always been the puzzle shrines. While it’s not an original opinion, the dungeons in Ocarina of Time feel like a couple dozen BOTW puzzle shrines stitched together in an environmentally cohesive manner.

Delving into a dungeon feels appropriately epic, and each one (or at least, each one I’ve experienced so far) begs to be fully explored with treasure chests and secrets for those willing to look in every corner. They’re just a blast, and yes, I can finally admit, they flow better than Breath of the Wild’s pretty repetitive Divine Beast dungeons.

Industry observers note that while I’ve at long last come around to the strengths of the traditional Zelda formula, that doesn’t mean I’ve suddenly lost my intense love for Breath of the Wild and its own acclaimed formula. Sorry, Ocarina stans, but Link’s 2017 adventure remains my favorite game in the series (of the ones I’ve played).

In a recent development, if there is one element where Ocarina of Time can’t compete with Breath of the Wild, it’s in the latter's ability to let you solve puzzles in a multitude of ways. In Ocarina of Time, the tools at Link’s disposal are more rudimentary (understandable, it’s ultimately a remake of a game from 1998), typically giving players a singular way to progress. In Breath of the Wild (and especially Tears of the Kingdom), you can “break” puzzles in ingenious ways.

While playing modern Zelda, I’ve found myself looking up online guides, not even because I need help with a puzzle, but merely to see the different ways other players solved the various roadblocks in Link’s path. In Ocarina of Time, players will reach the exit in pretty much the same way.

But that's not necessarily to say there's no appeal to Ocarina of Time's more linear progression. As mentioned, the way tools like the hookshot are slowly dished out, giving you incentive to return to previous areas with a larger arsenal, is something that Breath of the Wild lacks. In that case, you get pretty much all your traversal and puzzle-solving abilities in the first area.

I think both classic and modern Zelda have huge strengths, and opting for one over the other in any future Zelda games would be disappointing. I hope the development team at Nintendo mashes the two design philosophies together. Imagine a Zelda game with an exploration-focused open Hyrule but also containing lengthy, tightly crafted dungeons? Best of both worlds.

Tears of the Kingdom was a step in this direction, but its dungeons still don’t compare to those in Ocarina of Time. So, I don’t know if what would now be my “dream” Zelda game will ever exist, and it’ll probably be a good few years now before Nintendo is ready to talk about the next mainline 3D game in the series. But I really hope Link’s next flagship adventure takes the best part of both traditional and modern Zelda games and satisfies fans of both camps.

A great example of blending the latest and old is FromSoftware's Elden Ring, which offers a refreshing sense of freedom in its expansive overworld but also contains several "Legacy Dungeons." These are designed more like the smaller-scale areas found in the Dark Souls series. I hope that the Zelda team takes a similar approach when crafting whatever is next for the franchise.

In the meantime, I should probably circle back and give other classic Zelda games a chance, or maybe I’ll just keep my fingers crossed that the rumored Majora’s Mask remake materializes. I hear some fans consider it even better.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

#420. No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1230 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives. That people are craving new AI features, new AI products, new AI workflows — that would all magically replace all existing outdated practices and broken ways of working.

According to recent reports, but in reality, it seems like people don’t want more AI at all — at least not in the way most AI leaders envision it. Unsurprisingly, many AI features have low adoption and retention — at a very high cost of delivery, and a high risk of reputation damage.

It’s remarkably difficult to make a strong argument with senior leadership, but AI is not a value proposition. New AI features don’t magically make for happy or excited customers. Because AI features are often bolt-ons and separate tools for employees to use, they typically take people out of their regular way of working.

It has been revealed that AI is pretty good at amplifying shortcuts and shortcomings in organizations — from data quality to decision making. It can’t magically fix years of accumulated quick patches, technical debt, broken culture and internal politics. If anything, they become more visible with AI as inconsistencies or conflicting priorities and get handed directly to users, who are then left to make sense of the mess themselves.

Recent findings suggest that because in most organizations, work typically requires hopping on and off between plenty of disconnected and fragmented systems, with a newly introduced AI tool, they now have yet another system that they also need to hop on and off. Often it produces more work, and typically it’s not particularly rewarding work either.

According to recent reports, on top of that, people are very much aware of the cost of finding and fixing AI hallucinations. Asking AI to generate a response might feel easier than writing from scratch, but it has a cost:.

Industry observers note that for many people, AI isn’t something they can proactively choose and explore on their own — it arrives uninvited, at someone else’s pace. On top of that, plenty of messages amplify fears and worries about AI replacing work — so it’s hardly surprising that the perception of AI isn’t excitement. It’s resistance to change and deep anxiety about one’s place in a world that seems to be changing without them.

Recent findings suggest that at best, AI features might be silently accepted or nodded away. At worst, AI raises concerns, doubts, caution — and calls for a healthy dose of skepticism. And sometimes it’s perceived as a threat or liability — because unlike other features, AI is neither predictable nor reliable.

Industry observers note that people don’t dream of AI art museums or AI fridges or AI hotel reception or AI-narrated children’s books. They don’t want their children to have romantic AI partners. Most people don’t want to actively manage (and clean up after) a swarm of AI agents roaming in their bank accounts and acting on their behalf in the real world. And most notably, people don’t really want a magical box to speak to or type into all the time.

Industry observers note that I’m always puzzled by the comparison of AI features with how unreliable humans are. But people don’t compare software with other people. They compare features with features — and if one feature in one product is unreliable, while a similar feature works flawlessly in another, they choose the latter. It’s not about AI or not AI, but rather what works consistently and reliably, and what doesn’t.

Recent findings suggest that many conversations about AI are conversations about the speed of delivery. But to many people, there is little value in increasing the speed of delivery. They want to do things well, with enough time to think and make good decisions. They also want to enjoy the time they spend working on things, rather than just ship faster. There is an enormous feeling of reward and achievement that slowly disappears, one vibe-coded change at a time.

People don’t change much. And after all these years, they (still) want features that are fast, accessible, reliable, predictable and useful — every single time. And ideally not the ones that replace their entire workflow, but that augment their way of working — and that take over the most mundane, annoying, and boring tasks that they find no pleasure in.

Many jobs are exposed to AI automation, but in many of them there is a rewarding, unique, creative part that requires taste, point of view, and perhaps even human intuition. And if AI automates boring parts of it, that’s an advantage for everyone. That’s also what enhances productivity and brings more joy in daily life.

Industry observers note that when AI automates tedious and mentally exhausting tasks, its value is much easier to grasp. But for that, AI shouldn’t feel like a bolt-on. It should be deeply integrated into people’s existing workflows. It must also match existing mental models that they have developed and fine-tuned for years or decades. AI should adapt to how people think and make decisions, not the other way around.

Industry observers note that and it doesn’t really matter if these features are branded as “AI”, “smart” or “automation”. However, they must work well for people using them. And that means that people must be aware of use cases where it actually helps them, and be inspired to find more use cases on their own.

Ironically, tools that work well there aren’t “AI-first” — they are “AI-second”. Subtle, humble, calm, ambient, taking a supportive role in the background for work that otherwise is remarkably dull and unnecessary.

Sources indicate that perhaps I’m missing a bigger picture, and perhaps I’m just old school — but I really do like people. Their stories, their thinking, their emotions, their enthusiasm, their laughing. AI can be remarkably helpful in many situations, but so are people. And between the two, I would favor spending time with a human — however imperfect they are — every single time.

No, people don’t need more AI in their lives — they need AI to automate all the boring stuff they have to deal with every day, so they have more time and headspace to do things that they actually love and enjoy doing. That doesn’t mean spending more time with AI — but spending more time with people they love.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

In a recent development, from testing these stand mixers, they both mean business and are sturdy, reliable appliances, but if you’re looking for an appliance to stay out permanently on your countertop, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus would be my choice — though my interior style is more modern cottage than modern urban. Strands, the Latest York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

#414. Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3403 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github

Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety concerns in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior.
  • Sources indicate that rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting.
  • Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly notable as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety concerns in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Sources indicate that rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly notable as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

In a recent development, unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In a recent development, in this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

Recent findings suggest that this post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:.

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

It has been revealed that we identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. Iterator::map_windows, a nightly API, yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:.

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the newly introduced buffer first and filled it afterward:.

Sources indicate that after line 197, buffer breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The clone() call on line 201 runs the user’s T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the latest buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

Industry observers note that the recently stabilized Allocator API highlights how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library’s unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait’s methods or from drop. The proposal notes that “unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness.”.

Sources indicate that unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:.

Sources indicate that the same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

Another of our bug reports indicates how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:.

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:.

The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:.

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

join reveals how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Industry observers note that others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

In a recent development, the first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:.

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:.

Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:.

It has been revealed that line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the upcoming mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other complications discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

It has been revealed that our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a latest program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:.

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:.

Sources indicate that line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the latest program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.

In a recent development, getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

In a recent development, every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:.

Sources indicate that the first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

Industry observers note that what we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

Industry observers note that the third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Sources indicate that rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

According to recent reports, for the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

According to recent reports, rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

It has been revealed that at Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our newly introduced multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful concerns, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.
