#412. When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

📅 2026-07-17 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2076 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

📅 2026-07-17 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I Code.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • We’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken. The rule of “Never block the main thread.”.

According to recent reports, you almost can’t miss it as a web developer; it’s in almost every performance guide, and to be fair, it is good advice. We all know the browser’s main thread is single-threaded, meaning it can only do one thing at a time.

Plus, as we know, the main thread isn’t ours alone; we share it with the browser’s rendering engine, input handlers, and other critical tasks. As a result, the less time we hold onto the main thread, the more responsive an app feels. That leads us to share tasks with background workers as we’ve convinced ourselves there should be a hard line between the UI and any computation, and that line shouldn’t be crossed.

And that is what a “recommended” architecture looks like.

But I dare say that *sometimes*, moving the data to a worker is slower than just letting the main thread do the work.

In a recent development, I found this out a few months ago while building a Chrome extension with screenshotting features called Fastary. I kept finding a latency of about 2 to 3 seconds in all my testing, even after using an Offscreen Document (a background process in Chrome extensions) to handle the canvas operations. A screenshot task should feel instant without lag, after all.

Industry observers note that it is quite ironic that by reflex, we move work away from the main thread to avoid freezing the UI, but sometimes the act of moving that work (e.g., serializing, copying, and deserializing) can also freeze the UI. And sometimes the recommended approach of letting the background do the work can be slower than just doing the work on the main thread.

To put things in perspective, let’s understand why we isolate browser contexts and how they communicate with each other, with emphasis on the communication part.

According to recent reports, A browser is more than a single environment. Different environments are running at the same time, each having its own memory space, what it can access, and rules:.

In a recent development, each one of these is isolated from the others. A web worker or background script lives in a different memory space from the main thread. They cannot just reach and read each other’s variables or logic, and this is known as the “shared-nothing” architecture.

How do these isolated environments communicate? They explicitly message each other back and forth using APIs, like postMessage().

Industry observers note that postMessage() tells the browser to take a piece of data and deliver it to the context that requested it. But to do this, the browser relies on the Structured Clone Algorithm (SCA).

You’re probably familiar with JSON.stringify(). SCA is similar, but much stronger and smarter. In its simplest form, SCA is a deep, recursive copy operation, i.e., cloning. It walks through the entire data structure it is given, clones every single value, serializes it into a transportable format, ships those bytes to the target contexts, and then reconstructs the original object on the receiving side.

SCA is fast, or maybe fast-ish… For a small regular config object like {theme: "dark"}, it is imperceptible; you don’t even notice it. The story changes, however, when dealing with heavy data because the SCA is a synchronous blocking O(n) operation, i.e., the cost increases linearly with the size of your data.

In a recent development, let’s put that into perspective. A user clicks a button, and internally, an 8MB image payload is sent to a background worker for processing. When you call postMessage(), the main thread must immediately stop what it is doing to run this serialization and copying process.

Recent findings suggest that I’m sure some of you are already thinking, “Why not just use Transferable objects?” And that is a valid point. Let’s talk about that.

It has been revealed that developers who really pursue ultra-high-performance web apps usually use Transferable objects (e.g., ArrayBuffer, ImageBitmap, or MessagePort) to bypass the Structured Clone Algorithm. This is because when you transfer an object, you’re not making a copy (like SCM). Instead, the browser switches ownership of the data from one context to another.

It has been revealed that the browser performs a hand-off whereby the sending context loses access to the data instantly, and the receiving context takes full control. It is actually insanely fast. According to Chrome Developers’ benchmark, transferring a massive 32MB ArrayBuffer can take under 7ms, compared to about 300ms when cloning with SCM. That’s a 43x speed boost.

Recent findings suggest that but like all good things, there are downsides. To name a few:.

So, as far as my screenshot extension went, Transferable objects were not an option.

Why do we even bother isolating contexts at all? Why not just leave it all to the main thread?

Offloading long-running CPU tasks to a background thread is absolutely the right thing to do. The browser needs to paint a new frame every 16.6ms to keep things fluid; that means any task that takes >50ms is generally considered “long”. Offloading to the background is absolutely the right thing to do.

The matter, however, is that we’ve turned this “never block the main thread” into an absolute rule, without asking is this task expensive to process or expensive to move?

I have come to realize now that the rule is less “never block the main thread” than “never block the main thread for too long.”.

My goal with the Fastary extension was to make it feel like a native app, running as smoothly and instantly as you would expect a native app to.

In a recent development, as you already know, I took the recommended approach to use the Offscreen Document to handle DOM work in the background. But to my surprise, that took a different turn.

In a recent development, the Offscreen Document API is a clear winner. You create a hidden, undisplayed document that runs entirely in the background. It has a DOM and supports Canvas. For example, if I want to crop a screenshot, stitch multiple screenshots together, perform heavy image manipulation, or add a watermark, Offscreen Document was made for that.

Turns out that was not the best approach. This was my architecture:.

But when I tested it, the screenshot didn’t feel instant. As I said earlier, there was a consistent 2–3 second lag.

According to recent reports, I figured out that when captureVisibleTab() takes a screenshot, it returns a Base64 URL string, and on a standard 1080p screen, that string could be approximately 1MB or more, depending on how detailed the image is. It gets even more interesting on modern Retina displays (e.g., MacBooks) as they tend to automatically double the image’s size by default.

Keep in mind that since the image payload could be doubled and extension messaging relies on JSON serialization (as of this writing), we potentially deal with massive synchronous communication that costs an entire round trip.

Recent findings suggest that the image string data is JSON-serialized at least twice: once when going into the Offscreen Document and once coming back out with the processed results to the background worker. The actual image processing (cropping) done inside the Offscreen Document was fast, no doubt, but I can’t say the same about the transfer overhead.

As if the latency itself wasn’t enough, I noticed a rather subtle bug — which, now that I think of it, was more of my ignorance. After a screenshot was taken, the crop result was completely off in a way that either weirdly scaled the image or resulted in incorrect coordinates.

Sources indicate that it turns out that when a user selects a region to crop, the content script gets the box coordinates using getBoundingClientRect(), which is measured in CSS pixels; this is what the DOM uses. But when the screenshot is captured natively in Chrome, the browser doesn’t crop it automatically; it instead uses the physical hardware pixels to get the full screen capture. And the browser uses devicePixelRatio (DPR) to know how many physical pixels should represent one CSS pixel. Basically, if a user on a Retinal display (DPR = 2) highlights an area of 400x300 CSS pixels, the actual captured image area is 800x600 physical pixels.

In a recent development, for an accurate crop, I needed to apply these two different measurement systems with the right DPR, i.e., scale the crop coordinates by the DPR. But remember, Offscreen Documents have no physical display. Processing any image would have a default DPR equal to 1. To fix this, I would have to capture the exact devicePixelRatio from the active tab, serialize it, pass it alongside the image payload, and manually do the scaling math inside the Offscreen Document. The complexity starts to compound.

What if I broke the golden rule and did the work on the main thread instead?

Sources indicate that some developers will argue that UI tasks are the only things that should run on the main thread, but I don’t fully agree with that. Personally, I believe that user explicitly-invoked actions that need immediate results can sometimes get a solid pass to run on the main thread, provided the work is incredibly fast (e.g., 1s).

According to recent reports, that’s what I did: scrap out the Offscreen Document and reengineer the logic. Instead of:.

…I decided to run the whole image processing in the active tab:.

Sources indicate that this approach completely clears out multiple context hops and round trips that JSON serialization requires. The only cross-context transfer involves sending the data URL from the background to the content script.

The Retina DPI concern essentially solved itself, as the content script runs directly inside the real, active browser tab because it knows the monitor’s real devicePixelRatio.

But there’s an elephant in the room that you may have noticed.

Sure, the image is now processed on the main thread, and the background manipulates the canvas in the active tab. I could technically be blocking the main thread. That’s where I amended the “no blocking the main thread” rule to “no blocking the main thread for too long.” In this specific case, at least, blocking the main thread for a task the user requests for approximately one second is justifiable. It works conversely as well: maybe don’t isolate processes if the data transfer cost is greater than the processing cost.

I’ve boiled it down to a mental model that depends on whether the task is:.

Sources indicate that these are tasks where the primary cost is computation and not the size of the data itself. These are tasks where most of the time is spent on doing calculations or heavy transformations, e.g., image compression, audio profiling, physics simulation, etc.

The transfer cost for these tasks is minuscule compared to the actual work.

In a recent development, these tasks are the exact opposite. These tasks are only expensive because of the size. The processing time is almost insignificant, but the data is expensive to transport, e.g., image cropping, filtering an array, shallow copy, etc.

Sources indicate that in my specific case, offloading the task to the background falls mostly into negative-sum efficiency. If we are talking about moving megabytes of data to perform a 50ms operation, there is no benefit to offloading it to the background.

Perhaps we can think of it like this:.

According to recent reports, looking at this, if the “background processing time” is the most dominant task in your operation, then isolation is the clear winner. But if serialization, plus deserialization, plus transit exceeds that cost, then there’s no need to isolate things.

And if you can’t figure out if the task is CPU-heavy or data-heavy, it certainly doesn’t hurt to measure it, for example, using performance.mark() and performance.measure() around postMessage calls to profile the transfer cost.

It has been revealed that while Google Messages is still ultimately Google Messages, these changes make the app feel so much more modern and polished than before. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

In a recent development, finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#404. Weaponizing And Defending The React Flight Protocol: Deserialization Sinks In RSCs

Weaponizing And Defending The React Flight Protocol: Deserialization Sinks In RSCs

📅 2026-07-21 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, react Server Components don’t send HTML to your browser.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, react Server Components don’t send HTML to your browser. They don’t send JSON either. When a server component renders, what actually travels over the wire is a custom streaming protocol called Flight. It’s a line-delimited format with its own type system, its own reference resolution, and its own rules for reconstructing executable behavior on the client.

It has been revealed that most React developers have never opened the Network tab and actually looked at a Flight payload. It looks like a mix of JSON fragments, dollar-sign-prefixed references, and module pointers that the React runtime silently reassembles into a live component tree. The framework handles it, so nobody questions it.

I’m not sure most teams have thought carefully about what that trust actually implies.

It has been revealed that I started pulling apart the Flight protocol after CVE-2025-55182 dropped in December 2025. The security community called it React2Shell, and for good reason. It was a CVSS 10.0, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability sitting in the Flight deserialization layer. One crafted HTTP request to a Server Function endpoint, and an attacker had shell access. No credentials needed.

The federal Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency (CISA) added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Sysdig tied in-the-wild exploitation to North Korean state-sponsored actors deploying file-less implants through the Ethereum blockchain. That’s the kind of CVE that gets your attention.

Industry observers note that after spending time in the source (mostly getOutlinedModel and getChunk, which is where the resolution logic that matters actually lives), I realized React2Shell wasn’t a one-off parsing bug. It was a symptom. Flight reconstructs executable references, lazy-loaded components, server RPC endpoints, and async state from a stream of text. That’s a deserialization system.

The attack surface extends well beyond a single missing hasOwnProperty check. This article covers how Flight works on the wire, where the deserialization sinks are, what attackers have already weaponized, and what’s still exposed.

This leads to a ranked, practical set of defenses for your own Server Components: schema validation on every Server Action, the server-only package, cross-site request forgery (CSRF) hardening beyond framework defaults, and an assessment of what the Taint API and Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) provide.

Open your browser’s Network tab on any Next.js App Router page and look for requests returning Content-Type: text/x-component. That’s Flight. It’s not a single JSON blob. It’s a streaming, line-delimited format where each line is a self-contained “row” that the client-side React runtime processes as it arrives over the connection.

Here’s what a simple Flight payload looks like in practice:.

Row 1 is an import directive. It tells the client to load ClientComponent.js from the bundler’s chunk map. Row 2 is a JSON tree that constructs an HTML element, and the "$1" inside children is a reference back to chunk 1 (the imported component). Row 0 defines the server execution context, marking this as a RootLayout running in the Server environment. Even in this tiny example, you can see the mix of structural data, module references, and cross-chunk pointers that makes Flight different from plain JSON.

It has been revealed that every row follows the same syntax: :\n. The row ID is a numeric identifier that other rows can reference. The tag is a single character (or short string) that tells the parser what kind of data follows. The payload is the actual content.

Here are the row tags I found while reading through the source:.

So far, this might look like a benign structured data format with some custom tags, but the real complexity and attack surface live in the prefix system.

This is where I started paying closer attention.

It has been revealed that when the client-side parser encounters a string value starting with $, it doesn’t treat it as literal text. It intercepts the string, checks the prefix, and routes it through a type-specific resolution path. The parseModelString function in ReactFlightClient.js is where this happens. It’s essentially a substantial switch statement on the character after $.

Every other prefix resolves a chunk and gives you the parsed result. $@ hands you the raw internal Chunk object instead, the wrapper React uses to track resolution state, pending callbacks, and internal metadata (which is why it’s used for Promises and why exploits use it to get a mutable handle). Exposing framework plumbing through the protocol looks like a design mistake to me, though I’d be interested to hear the rationale if there is one.

And $: (property access) is the other critical prefix. It lets the protocol specify a path like $1:user:name, which tells the parser to resolve chunk 1, then access .user, then access .name on the result. That’s arbitrary property traversal driven by data in the stream. If you’ve spent any time auditing JavaScript for prototype pollution, that pattern should feel familiar.

It has been revealed that flight is not JSON with extra steps. JSON gives you data. Flight gives you behavior. It reconstructs module references that trigger client-side code loading, creates server action endpoints the client can invoke as RPC calls, sets up Promise chains that the React runtime will await, and builds lazy-loaded component boundaries that execute on demand.

In a recent development, whether React developers think of it that way or not, the mechanics look very similar to deserialization systems that have historically caused problems. The stream doesn’t just describe what the UI looks like. It instructs the client runtime on what code to load, what functions to call, and what to trust.

If you want to read the implementation yourself, fair warning: the chunk resolution path is miserable to follow. State transitions bounce between helper functions, and the naming obscures what the code is actually doing. I gave up on static reading and just set breakpoints. The key files are react-client/src/ReactFlightClient.js for the client-side parser (look for parseModelString, getChunk, reviveModel, and getOutlinedModel) and react-server/src/ReactFlightServer.js for the serialization side. The reply handler for Server Actions lives in react-server/src/ReactFlightReplyServer.js.

The deserialization pattern is familiar: Java’s ObjectInputStream gave us ysoserial, Python’s pickle executes code on load(), PHP’s unserialize chains __wakeup and __destruct methods, and .NET’s BinaryFormatter was deprecated entirely.

It has been revealed that so JavaScript should be immune to this, right? JSON.parse() only produces plain data objects. No constructors fire. No magic methods run. You get back exactly what the JSON string describes, nothing more.

It has been revealed that that’s true for raw JSON.parse(). But it stops being true the moment a framework wraps custom deserialization logic around it. And that’s exactly what Flight does.

Recent findings suggest that javaScript uses prototype-based inheritance. Every object has a __proto__ link to its prototype, and property lookups walk up this chain. If an attacker injects __proto__ or constructor.prototype as a key during reconstruction, they modify the shared base prototypes that all objects inherit from. Downstream code reads attacker-controlled values without knowing.

Flight’s $: prefix performs property traversal on deserialized objects. The getOutlinedModel function walks colon-separated paths like $1:user:name by iterating through each segment and accessing it on the parent object. If those path segments include __proto__ or constructor, the traversal walks straight up the prototype chain. That’s not a theoretical risk. It’s exactly how React2Shell worked.

The V8 engine (and the JavaScript spec) treats any object with a .then property as a Thenable. When you await something, the runtime checks for .then and calls it if it exists. No class check. No internal slot verification. If .then is callable, it gets invoked.

Sources indicate that flight resolves chunks asynchronously. If an attacker constructs an object with a manipulated .then property and gets it into the chunk resolution pipeline, the runtime calls the attacker’s function during normal await behavior. The language semantics do the work.

Recent findings suggest that I initially focused on $F because forging Server Action references seemed like the obvious attack surface. After tracing the resolution path, $: property traversal looked much more interesting. I also spent a few hours examining chunk status transitions (pending, blocked, resolved, errored) to see if you could force a chunk into an unexpected state, though that approach didn’t yield any results.

Recent findings suggest that these two risks converge in Flight because the protocol doesn’t just deserialize data. It deserializes behavior. The $ prefix system dictates which execution path the parser takes: $F creates a callable server endpoint, $L sets up lazy code loading, $B triggers a blob handler, $@ exposes internal framework state. The parser’s control flow is driven entirely by what’s in the stream.

If an attacker can influence the stream’s content, they control which functions the parser calls, which objects it constructs, and which internal state it exposes.

This is the CVE that proved the theory. CVE-2025-55182, nicknamed React2Shell, is a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in the Flight deserialization layer. One HTTP request, no login required, full shell access.

I want to walk through the entire gadget chain because understanding it reveals how much power the Flight protocol hands to an attacker who can control the stream.

The vulnerability sits in getOutlinedModel, a function responsible for resolving deep property paths from the $: reference system. The instance used in the exploit chain lives in the server-side reply handling code (ReactFlightReplyServer.js). When the parser encounters a reference like $1:user:name, it splits on the colons and walks the path segment by segment. Here’s the vulnerable loop:.

Recent findings suggest that two lines. No hasOwnProperty check. No validation that the property exists on the object itself rather than somewhere up the prototype chain. Just parentObject[reference[key]] and move on.

It has been revealed that so an attacker supplies $1:__proto__:constructor:constructor, and the loop traverses from a plain JSON object up through Object.prototype to the Object constructor to the Function constructor. Function in JavaScript behaves like eval(). Function("arbitrary code")() executes.

Sources indicate that no allowlist on property names. No check for __proto__. I searched reviveModel and the chunk initialization path for any filtering. Nothing.

Getting from “I can reach the Function constructor” to “I have RCE” requires chaining several Flight protocol features together. The Resecurity write-up covers the full chain in detail; here’s the high-level sequence:.

Each step uses a legitimate Flight protocol feature in a way the designers didn’t anticipate. There’s no single “broken” feature. The vulnerability emerges from how these features compose when an attacker controls the input.

The numbers on this one are stark:.

It has been revealed that exploitation was immediate. Sysdig published research linking EtherRAT deployments to North Korean state-sponsored actors who weaponized the vulnerability within hours of disclosure. EtherRAT is a file-less implant that uses the Ethereum blockchain for command-and-control communication — a technique researchers call “EtherHiding” — making takedown nearly impossible because you can’t seize a blockchain.

According to recent reports, separately, Palo Alto’s Unit 42 documented a backdoor called KSwapDoor that masquerades as [kswapd1] on infected Linux systems, blending into process lists alongside the legitimate kswapd0 kernel swap daemon; their analysis confirms KSwapDoor uses RC4 encryption to protect its internal strings and configuration data, while C2 communications run over AES-256-CFB with Diffie-Hellman key exchange across a P2P mesh network. The speed and sophistication of these campaigns — state-sponsored actors deploying novel implants through a single unauthenticated HTTP request — underscores why a CVSS 10.0 in a deserialization layer demands immediate patching, not triage.

In a recent development, the React team’s patch is clean and targeted. The core change caches the genuine hasOwnProperty method at module load time:.

Then every property check in the deserialization path uses .call() to invoke the cached reference:.

According to recent reports, even if an attacker shadows hasOwnProperty on a malicious object, the check uses the original prototype method. The prototype chain traversal that powered the gadget chain is blocked. This fix shipped in React 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1.

The fix is correct. But reading through the patches, I noticed the React team hardened ownership checks while leaving the property traversal model intact. The $: prefix still walks colon-separated paths; it just validates each step now. I think exposing arbitrary property traversal through a network protocol was a design mistake, and the patch treats the symptom. If future bugs emerge, they’ll likely come from this same area.

Industry observers note that the framework patch closes the known gadget chain, but it doesn’t change the fundamental dynamic: the Flight protocol still reconstructs behavior — executable references, module imports, RPC endpoints, async state — from a stream of text. That reconstruction happens before your application code runs, before your validation logic fires, before your auth middleware even sees the request. Relying solely on the framework to protect your Server Components means trusting that every edge case in a complex deserialization parser has been found and fixed. The defenses that follow are the practical steps you can take to limit the blast radius on your own.

Sources indicate that some of these close real attack paths. Others mostly make you feel safer than you are. I’ve ranked these from most-to-least impactful based on what I’ve seen in the vulnerability research. If you only have time for one change, start at the top.

This is the single most impactful thing you can do at the application level. The Flight deserializer processes raw, unvalidated network input before your code takes control. Strict schema validation is your primary defense against whatever the protocol reconstructs.

Recent findings suggest that put a schema validation call at the very top of every Server Action, before any business logic runs — and I mean before anything, including logging. If you log an argument before validating it, and that argument triggers the stringification bug from CVE-2025-55183, you’ve leaked source code before your validation even had a chance to run.

Zod and Valibot both work well for this. Validate types, shapes, string lengths, numeric bounds, and enumerated values. Reject anything that doesn’t match. Use .safeParse(), not .parse() — the throwing variant can surface internal error details in the response if you’re not careful with your error boundaries.

One vital nuance: If your Server Action accepts a plain object argument (not FormData), validate the whole argument — don’t destructure first and validate fields individually. Destructuring before validation means you’re already accessing properties on the unvalidated input, which is exactly the kind of operation the Flight deserializer can exploit.

In a recent development, if your Server Action doesn’t start with a schema parse, it’s a vulnerability waiting to happen. I’d argue this should be a lint rule — and if you’re running eslint-plugin-react, consider writing a custom rule that flags any "use server" export without a validation call in its first statement.

The server-only package is straightforward and effective.

Import server-only at the top of any file that contains database credentials, raw API calls, internal business logic, or anything else that should never cross the server-client boundary. If a Client Component tries to import that file (directly or transitively), the build fails with a clear error.

According to recent reports, the failure mode to watch for is barrel files. If you re-export a server-only function through an index.ts that also exports client-safe utilities, any Client Component importing from that barrel will pull in the server-only module transitively and break the build — or worse, if the barrel doesn’t include the server-only import itself, it may silently let server code through. Keep server-only modules in separate files with their own import paths.

Industry observers note that it also won’t protect you from data leaking through return values. If a Server Component calls getUser() and passes the full user object (including passwordHash or internalRole) as props to a Client Component, that data rides the Flight stream to the browser. The server-only guard prevents the code from crossing the boundary, not the data the code returns. You must explicitly filter your return shapes.

Sources indicate that after CVE-2026-27978, relying solely on Next.js’s built-in Origin vs. Host header check isn’t enough. The Origin: null bypass showed that framework-level CSRF protection has edge cases.

For state-changing Server Actions (anything that writes data, deletes records, or modifies permissions), layer your own protections on top of the framework’s defaults.

Explicit CSRF tokens.For high-value operations (password changes, role assignments, payment actions), generate a per-session CSRF token on the server, embed it in a hidden form field or custom header, and validate it in the Server Action before proceeding.

Sources indicate that the allowedOrigins gotcha.Never, under any circumstances, add 'null' to experimental.serverActions.allowedOrigins in your Next.js config (even if the officially advisory is more nuanced, saying “unless intentionally required and additionally protected”). That string literal matches Origin: null — the exact header that sandboxed iframes send — and it reopens the CVE-2026-27978 bypass. If you’re seeing CSRF failures from legitimate requests, the fix is to configure your reverse proxy to set the correct Origin and Host headers, not to weaken the validation.

Recent findings suggest that I covered this in detail in the React2Shell section. The fix is correct, and it completely neutralizes the known gadget chain. It shipped fast, which I respect.

The action item here is to verify you’re actually running a patched version. The RCE fix landed in React 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1. Check your lockfile:.

If you see 19.0.0, 19.1.0â€“19.1.1, or 19.2.0, you’re vulnerable to the RCE. Enhancement immediately. And don’t stop there: the DoS fixes (CVE-2025-55184, CVE-2025-67779, CVE-2026-23864) require 19.0.4+, 19.1.5+, or 19.2.4+. If you updated after React2Shell and then stopped paying attention, you may still be running a version vulnerable to the DoS variants.

It’s a reactive patch, not a structural redesign.

Note: More on that in Where This Goes Next.

React’s taintObjectReference and taintUniqueValue functions register objects or strings with the runtime. If tainted data tries to pass through the Flight serializer, it throws an error. The idea is to prevent sensitive data — user records, API keys, tokens — from accidentally leaking into the client.

Here’s how it looks in practice:.

If a Server Component passes the tainted user object as props to a Client Component, React throws it at serialization time with your custom error message. That’s genuinely useful as a development-time guardrail.

The catch — and it’s a significant one — is that taint tracks object references, not data content. Any derivation breaks the tracking:.

It has been revealed that taintUniqueValue works on specific strings (like API keys), but it’s also reference-based. If the same key value appears in a different variable, the taint doesn’t follow.

Think of taint as a development guardrail, not a security boundary. It catches honest mistakes: a developer accidentally passing a full user object to the client. It won’t stop an attacker who can influence what gets serialized, and it won’t survive routine data transformations that your own code performs. It’s a useful defense-in-depth layer, but shouldn’t be your primary boundary.

In a recent development, web Application Firewalls can add a detection layer for known attack patterns. They can inspect POST requests carrying the Next-Action header, block payloads containing constructor:constructor or __proto__ chains, and flag error responses containing E{"digest" patterns that indicate the server is leaking internal error details.

If you’re running a WAF, here are specific patterns worth adding:.

But attackers know about WAF inspection buffers, and they’re usually around 128KB. Prepend 130KB of padding before the malicious payload, and the WAF inspects the padding, finds nothing, and lets the request through. Chunked Transfer-Encoding tricks accomplish the same thing.

Sources indicate that the failure mode is treating WAF coverage as a security boundary rather than a noise-reduction layer. WAFs catch automated scanners and low-effort attacks, and that has real value. But a motivated attacker will bypass them with padding or encoding tricks. The defenses that actually stop sophisticated attacks are the ones earlier in this list: validating input before it reaches your business logic, keeping sensitive code off the wire, and staying on patched versions.

According to recent reports, react2Shell wasn’t the end of it. The security audits that followed the December 2025 disclosure shook out a series of related vulnerabilities in the same deserialization surface. None of them are as severe as the original RCE, but they’re worth tracking because some of them required multiple rounds of patching.

Industry observers note that the DoS pair (CVE-2025-55184 and CVE-2025-67779) is a textbook example of why deserialization parsers are hard to patch correctly. The first fix shipped, researchers found edge cases it missed, and a second round was needed. CVE-2026-23864 added a third DoS vector through unbounded memory allocation rather than CPU exhaustion. (See the defenses section above for specific version checks.).

Recent findings suggest that CVE-2025-55183 is the sneaky one. It’s a source code exposure bug that triggers when a Server Function calls JSON.stringify (or any implicit stringification) on one of its arguments. Developers do this constantly for logging, debugging, or error reporting.

The attacker sends a crafted argument that, when stringified, causes the deserialization parser to reflect the function’s own source code back in the response. Business logic, database queries, and any hardcoded secrets sitting in Server Action files become readable by anyone who can send an HTTP request.

Industry observers note that CVE-2026-27978 is a different class of bug entirely. It’s a CSRF bypass in Next.js’s Server Action handling. Next.js validates that the Origin header matches the Host header to prevent cross-site request forgery. But when a request comes from a sandboxed , the browser sends Origin: null.

The CVEs above have patches. But some of the risk is structural, baked into how Flight is designed to work.

Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) On The Flight Stream

If an attacker can sit between server and client (CDN compromise, cache poisoning, rogue proxy), modifying the Flight stream in transit looks feasible. The format is plain text with a predictable structure.

Assuming stream control, an attacker could alter $I (Import) rows to redirect component loading to a different module in the webpack chunk map. They could inject $F (Server Reference) tags to embed hidden RPC triggers in the rendered UI. They could modify D (Data) rows to change component props, and if the target component uses dangerouslySetInnerHTML, that’s a direct XSS vector.

Flight escapes $ prefixes in user-supplied strings to prevent data from being interpreted as protocol instructions. But that only applies to data flowing through the serializer. A MITM attacker writes raw protocol directly into the stream. The escaping doesn’t help.

Server Action IDs are obfuscated hashes generated at build time. They look random. But server-reference-manifest.json maps every action ID to its source implementation. A public manifest hands an attacker a complete API map. This exposure usually stems from misconfigured hosting, an exposed .next directory, or path traversal.

Known action IDs expose Server Actions to standard IDOR and parameter tampering attacks. An attacker can forge direct requests with manipulated arguments. Developers often trust these inputs blindly because they originate from React’s internal machinery. The architectural consequences of that misplaced trust will be the focus of my next piece.

When a Server Action captures variables from its surrounding scope (closures), Next.js encrypts them before sending to the client. The key is in NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY, AES with a base64-encoded key (16, 24, or 32 bytes). decryptActionBoundArgs handles decryption on each invocation.

By default, this key regenerates every build. But multi-server setups often use a static key. If an attacker gets file read access (path traversal, SSRF), they extract the key, decrypt the closure state, modify it (changing a userId, a role, a query parameter), and re-encrypt. The server accepts the forged closure as legitimate.

Supply Chain Activation via Module IDs

I haven’t demonstrated this end-to-end, but the theory is straightforward.

Flight references client components by module ID, something like ["360","static/chunks/app/page-7f3480.js"]. The bundler assigns these IDs at build time based on the module graph. A compromised npm package sitting in node_modules as a transitive dependency gets bundled into a chunk but never loaded because no component references it. Inert.

But if an attacker injects $I import references into the Flight stream (via MITM, cache poisoning, or server-side injection), the parser should load that dormant module. There may be chunk-level validation I’m not seeing. But if the module ID is valid and present in the manifest, I don’t see what stops it. The attack doesn’t require the package to be imported anywhere in your code. It just needs to exist in the bundle output.

React Flight isn’t the first framework to invent a custom serialization format for server-client communication and then discover it’s an attack surface. And it won’t be the last.

Google Web Toolkit (GWT) used a custom RPC protocol to sync Java objects between browser and server. BishopFox demonstrated that attackers could manipulate the wire format to achieve arbitrary deserialization; GWT eventually disabled binary serialization entirely. It took years.

Java Server Faces (JSF) and ASP.NET both serialized ViewState to the client as a hidden form field. When cryptographic signing was weak or missing, attackers tampered with the serialized state and achieved remote code execution. Microsoft and Oracle patched it repeatedly. The underlying pattern kept resurfacing.

The pattern is always the same: a framework invents a custom wire format to move rich, stateful, sometimes executable data between server and client. The designers assume the server is the sole producer of that data and the client is a trusted consumer. Then someone demonstrates that the wire format can be manipulated in transit, or that the server can be tricked into deserializing attacker-controlled input. React Flight is the latest entry in this pattern. It is not an anomaly.

The React Flight protocol solves a genuinely hard problem: streaming interactive component trees from server to client in a way that enables progressive hydration, async data loading, and server-driven code splitting. It works. I don’t want to lose sight of that.

But it works by serializing executable references, async state, module pointers, and RPC endpoints over a streaming text protocol, and then trusting the structure of that stream on both ends. The React team has patched the known gadgets. The hasOwnProperty fix is correct. The DoS fixes are in place. The source code exposure bug is closed.

I think exposing arbitrary property traversal and executable Thenable reconstruction through a network-facing protocol was a design mistake. $:, $@, and $B are powerful internal primitives that were reachable through a parser that didn’t validate ownership of the properties it traversed. One check was missing, and the result was CVSS 10.0.

As more frameworks adopt server-driven UI patterns, the industry is going to need stronger primitives than “the server is trusted”: cryptographic validation of serialized payloads, signed component trees, and content integrity checks on the Flight stream itself.

Hoping the parser handles every edge case hasn’t worked historically, and I don’t see why it would start working now.

The code is in react-client/src/ReactFlightClient.js. If you ship Server Components, read it. Know what your framework is trusting on your behalf.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we posted two reviews of fresh Apple products this week in the Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K, and there was one common theme. Apple’s Siri AI still isn’t good enough.

Sources indicate that in fact, I’d argue that there’s still such a large gap between Siri and other AI assistants like Gemini, ChatGPT, Alexa+ and Muse that people could start to defect to other brands if Apple doesn’t get its act together. And soon.

For example, my colleague Mike Prospero compared the newly introduced HomeView against Amazon’s Echo Show 8 with Alexa+, and he found that Apple’s assistant isn’t nearly as capable. Mike could easily order a pizza through Uber Eats with Amazon’s device while Apple’s Siri just offered to make a call. Siri is not the AI agent you’ve been looking for.

Meanwhile, Engadget pointed out that Siri AI gets dumber the moment your iPhone is not within range. It defaults to generic world-knowledge answers. And Joanna Stern noted in her review that Siri stumbled on multi-step household tasks and at one point refused to open her front door despite recognizing her face.

It also didn’t help that the HomeView Siri started “talking” to other phone-based Siris in the house.

To be clear, Siri AI has improved versus previous versions, but it’s still quite limited as an everyday assistant compared to Google Gemini, Alexa+, ChatGPT, and Muse. And I’d argue that the longer Siri continues to lag, the more Apple is leaving the door open for competitors to overtake Apple.

According to recent reports, apple Intelligence, such as it is, also graces the latest Apple TV 4K, a streaming device that costs a whopping $299. Apple is justifying the premium partly by touting the fact that Siri is inside, which is supposed to help you find things to watch.

It has been revealed that but things didn’t go very well in our testing. When Mike asked Siri to find scary movies for kids, Siri first responded “I’m not finding anything for that.” Then on the second attempt asking for scary movies good for kids the recommendations were nightmare fuel like “Poltergeist,” “Alien,” and “Seven.”.

Meanwhile, the Google TV Streamer and Fire TV returned recommendations like “Coraline,” “Goosebumps 2,” “Hocus Pocus,” and “The Addams Family.”.

Industry observers note that asking “What’s that movie with Audrey Hepburn that takes place in Rome” resulted in a bunch of Christmas movies, none with Hepburn. Though, Siri AI performed better with Tom Hanks action flicks.

In a recent development, apple’s assistant has gotten better on the iPhone, especially with personal context. For example, I asked Siri AI to find the message from my daughter asking about earrings as a gift.

You can also perform multiple actions at once using your voice. I recently had it look up restaurants around Bryant Park that are rated 4 stars or higher but under $50 for lunch and then craft an outgoing message that includes the address for each and top dish. It worked seamlessly.

However, Siri AI is still missing two big things versus other assistants: live voice chat with video and powerful agentic features.

It’s not a good sign that I’ve now mapped Gemini Live to the Action button on my iPhone 17 Pro Max. That’s because I use Google’s voice assistant in combination with live video all of the time to ask questions and troubleshoot things around the house.

In a recent development, for example, I was able to fix a cantilever umbrella because Gemini could see what I was talking about and offer advice in real time. With Siri AI, you can share what’s on your screen but not a live video feed.

It’s getting to the point where I wish I could say “Hey, Gemini” to my iPhone.

Sources indicate that agentic AI is still in a nascent stage, but this is yet another area where Siri is still behind. In fact, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman recently reported that new CEO John Ternus has explicitly asked for the Siri AI team to speed things up here.

Right now you just can’t do things like book an Uber with Siri or perform complex tasks that Siri can work on in the background.

Assuming AI continues to be a driving force in consumer electronics, Apple could fall further behind in mind share and eventually lose market share.

Recent findings suggest that just this week I tried Google’s upcoming Intelligent Eyewear glasses, which start at $395 and essentially put Gemini on your face. You can use these specs, made by Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, to do everything from take calls and listen to music to get turn-by-turn directions and even real-time translation.

And because Gemini is truly live through the onboard camera, it can “see” what you see to answer questions or give advice on the fly. And, yes, they work with the iPhone.

Apple is reportedly working on its own Apple glasses, as well as an AI pendant and AirPods with cameras — all powered by Siri.

But I don’t think any of these new categories will take off for Apple unless Siri is up to snuff. Hey, Siri... the clock is ticking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enhancement: The ground stop has been lifted, and domestic flights resumed late Friday.

It has been revealed that for only the third time in U.S. history, flights across the United States have been ordered to stay on the ground. And as travelers found themselves stranded at airports, sitting in airport bars, and wondering when they might finally take off, the internet did what it does best and started posting.

It has been revealed that on Friday, Nov. 13, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for departing flights following widespread air traffic control communications problems. The agency cited extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns, ordering aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice. Flights already in the air were permitted to land, while inbound international flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis.

The scale of the disruption is difficult to overstate. The last time the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, when a computer system failure temporarily halted departing flights. Before that, it happened in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Recent findings suggest that it's the kind of historical comparison that can make an already unsettling situation feel even more alarming, particularly when thousands of travelers are left waiting for answers. The FAA's original communication was also extremely vague, citing only "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety.".

And on social media, people had plenty of questions.

For travelers caught in the middle of the disruption, the news wasn't just another breaking headline. It meant unexpected delays, uncertain departure times, and an increasingly familiar feeling of being at the mercy of systems entirely outside their control.

Some turned to social media to document the experience in real time, sharing updates from airport terminals.

Others were struck by the sheer rarity of the moment. A nationwide ground stop is not an everyday occurrence, and the fact that the previous two were associated with 9/11 and a major FAA systems failure only added to the unease.

Of course, this being the internet, it didn't take long for people to find humor in the situation, either. Even an unprecedented disruption to air travel isn't immune to a few jokes, particularly when it happens on Friday the 13th following a major Microsoft outage.

And then, there's this response from Stephen King:.

But beyond the immediate frustration and online commentary, the ground stop raises more serious questions about the aging technology underpinning America's aviation system. The FAA has been working to modernize its air traffic control infrastructure, and Friday's communications problems offer another reminder of how much depends on systems most travelers rarely think about until something goes wrong.

It has been revealed that the ground stop also comes at a particularly interesting moment for the FAA. Just days earlier, the agency announced that it was expanding its fresh AI-supported air traffic management system, known as SMART, to all 22 regional air traffic control centers nationwide. Shortly before that, the FAA announced it will finally phase out floppy disks by 2028.

The $875 million system is designed to analyze everything from weather patterns and flight routes to traffic congestion and controller staffing, helping aviation officials anticipate disruptions before they happen. According to the FAA, the technology is intended to reduce delays and make air travel more efficient, though human specialists remain responsible for reviewing its recommendations.

The timing has attracted attention online, particularly as questions swirl around what caused Friday's communications problems.

For now, travelers are left refreshing their flight statuses, waiting for updates, and sharing their experiences online. And while the jokes might offer a momentary distraction, there's nothing particularly funny about realizing just how quickly an entire country's air travel system can grind to a halt.

According to recent reports, oleksii Hrzhehorzhevskyi is a Senior Character Producer at MacPaw, specializing in character design, animation, and visual storytelling. He right now leads the … More about Oleksii ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at MacPaw who not only believe that making great products requires seeing the world in a different light, but also strive to innovate and create incredible software ecosystem for users’ Macs. Thank you!

According to recent reports, the phrase “artificial intelligence” has many excited, especially those in tech. But for those of us in creative fields like digital art and design, AI can be more concerning than it is exciting.

AI-generated art, videos, and images have flooded the internet, raising questions about whether more companies will turn to tools like OpenAI’s Dall-E, Midjourney, Leonardo.ai, and more, rather than employing human artists. What’s more, the fact that these AI models are trained on real artists’ work without their consent leaves many feeling as if they have no choice but to accept AI into their work and lives.

In a digital world increasingly dominated by faceless AI chatbots, agents, and features, it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the technology. AI will certainly play a huge role in reshaping many industries, including design. We can’t deny this. But at the same time, humanization, empathy, and having a person at the wheel have never been more crucial.

Rather than viewing AI as something that replaces human creativity, we at MacPaw saw an opportunity to explore how we could make AI feel more personal and accessible — all the while keeping humans at the center of the experience. That led us to rethink how AI assistants are created.

In a recent development, traditional AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT typically take the form of a conversational textbox or webpage on screen, as this is how consumers have interacted with their devices. It’s comfortable and familiar. While extremely useful for a variety of tasks, interacting with these AI assistants can feel transactional and technical.

Recent findings suggest that using the same textbox format across all AI assistants does provide consistency. But we wanted to create a latest, more personal and differentiated experience for users. But what format would be best? Even if we change how an AI tool looks, it still needs to be useful and intuitive to use.

Recent findings suggest that as humans, it’s easier to understand and connect with things that resemble us. This is why we often find ourselves drawn to things like animals and characters: they have traits that we recognize within ourselves. Understanding this, we saw an opportunity to combine these values: utility and personality.

Sources indicate that enter Eney: a new proactive AI assistant. MacPaw didn’t want Eney to simply be another AI tool for customers, but rather one that proactively assists within a user’s workflow. The vision was to help users connect with Eney more easily than with other AI tools, so we decided to create a character users could interact with. We wanted Eney to be expressive, friendly, and to emote as humans do. But we needed to strike an important balance: making Eney cheerful without it being overly goofy or childish.

Industry observers note that this is where human animation and intervention played a critical role. While challenging, it was crucial because an overloaded character UI could turn customers off and make navigating Eney difficult. To avoid this, the design team chose to create a select set of emotions and gestures for Eney to express, ensuring that its expressions conveyed useful information. For example, when working on a task, Eney’s figure resembles a loading icon. To do this, we worked to reduce Eney’s on-screen movement to make sure it wasn’t distracting or excessive.

After exploring a few different shapes and styles for Eney, we settled on a circular figure, as it felt the most approachable. It was simple and helped create the feeling of a calm, floating digital companion, rather than another rigid interface element on a user’s desktop. Eney’s minimal face design also plays an vital role in connecting with the user. Its eyes are the main emotional connector — a key feature in showing emotions without being cartoonish.

The color choice for Eney was also vital. Many AI assistants and companies use blue in their products, as it’s typically associated with intelligence. Blue is a great color, but we wanted Eney to stand out. We still wanted the color to be warm and inviting while slightly more visually stimulating, which led us to choose the color pink. Among dozens of other AI products that choose a more blue aesthetic, Eney was designed to catch a user’s eye and stand out in their mind (and on their screen).

Recent findings suggest that all in all, we wanted to create a character that was present but not attention-seeking; a warm and supportive digital helper that enhances a user’s workflow rather than distracts from it. Eney’s character gives personality to otherwise invisible processes.

While those who aren’t design professionals may assume there wasn’t much significance behind Eney’s character creation, this couldn’t be further from the truth. Like many other products, all these elements — style, design, emotion, size, name, and more — were intentionally chosen, not by machines but by humans.

Industry observers note that even though AI has streamlined many design processes, namely enabling faster design, there are still many things it can’t do well. Even when designing Eney, while technology supported the process, human designers controlled every step and decision.

It has been revealed that as designers, it’s more important than ever to have good judgment, artistic direction, integrity, and emotional sensitivity when working in the field. Technology like AI can help us work faster, but it can’t replace the values that inspire and shape our work.

What’s more, while anyone can easily generate something by typing a prompt into an AI image tool, there’s a true beauty and talent when intentionally crafting something through manual design.

Sources indicate that as designers, we shouldn’t stray away from the latest tools. Rather, we should learn them and see how they could potentially help us within our creative workflows. Personally, I like to use AI tools such as Perplexity and ChatGPT for research purposes in the early stages. However, we need to remember that they’re just that: tools. At the end of the day, technology like AI cannot, and should not, replace human artistry. It should help us express our visions, not replace us entirely.

If there’s one thing to take away from this piece, it’s that curiosity helps build taste over time, and taste becomes more valuable, not less, in the AI era.

In a recent development, the Moon is getting a little bit bigger each night as we work through the lunar phases. We're still in the Waxing Crescent phase, which means more of the Moon is becoming illuminated each evening as it makes its way towards the First Quarter.

It has been revealed that as of Saturday, Nov. 14, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Crescent phase, with 22% of its surface visible.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have any visual aids, you can see see some features on the Moon's surface tonight, specifically the Mare Crisium and the Mare Fecunditatis. With binoculars or a telescope, you'll also see the Endymion Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

The Moon takes approximately 29.5 days to complete one full cycle. As it orbits Earth, the amount of sunlight reflecting off its surface that we can see changes, creating the different phases. This takes us from the Upcoming Moon to the Full Moon and back again, before the cycle begins once more, according to NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

In a recent development, first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Industry observers note that waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

Industry observers note that these forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with people able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

#393. Tech Report: A rare glimpse inside the high-risk, high-reward Hormuz trade

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1633 w)

Tech Report: A rare glimpse inside the high-risk, high-reward Hormuz trade

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lloydslist

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The witness statement of Mercuria freight trader Renaud Hauspy in the case of Mercuria v Baltic Exchange, now at trial in London, sheds fresh light on the business of getting crude through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • In a recent development, BRINGING crude through the Strait of Hormuz is a highly secretive affair.
  • With Iran still attacking tankers eight months after the crisis began, providing details on Hormuz transit mechanics and naming names is not something you’d do outside of a court proceeding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The witness statement of Mercuria freight trader Renaud Hauspy in the case of Mercuria v Baltic Exchange, now at trial in London, sheds fresh light on the business of getting crude through the Strait of Hormuz.

In a recent development, BRINGING crude through the Strait of Hormuz is a highly secretive affair. The transaction terms are very private, the players are exceptionally press-shy, the security risks are extreme, and the financial rewards are enormous.

With Iran still attacking tankers eight months after the crisis began, providing details on Hormuz transit mechanics and naming names is not something you’d do outside of a court proceeding.

As it happens, there’s a proceeding now underway.

According to recent reports, the Mercuria v Baltic Exchange trial is ongoing in London, with Mercuria seeking to invalidate the Baltic Exchange’s assessments for the TD3C Middle East Gulf-China index from March 1-July 3. Witness statements have just been made public.

The witness statement of Renaud Hauspy, a Switzerland-based crude freight trader at Mercuria, provides a rare inside glimpse of the Hormuz crisis charter market — or lack thereof.

Hauspy’s account (supported by email and chat message documentation) begins in early March, just after the missiles began flying, and extends through the US-Iran “peace” Memorandum of Understanding period in June and July.

Mercuria turns to Sinokor in the early days.

Recent findings suggest that mercuria has a fleet of around 200 vessels, he wrote, with around 60 in the crude segment, including very large crude carriers, suezmaxes and aframaxes. All its VLCCs are chartered in.

The organization did not have any VLCCs or suezmaxes inside the strait when the war broke out, but did have VLCCs outside the strait that had been fully fixed with commitments to load in the Middle East Gulf after hostilities began.

These fixtures were either renegotiated to load outside of Hormuz, such as in Fujairah, or were cancelled. “I believe our customers, including TotalEnergies, CNOOC, Unipec and IOC, all agreed that it was impossible to load inside the Arabian Gulf,” stated Hauspy.

Mercuria also had oil cargo inside Hormuz that needed to be moved on a contracted schedule that was agreed to before the crisis began.

Industry observers note that it couldn’t use the VLCCs it chartered from owners including Olympic Shipping and Maran Tankers. The owners “were not comfortable with ships transiting the strait”, he stated.

So Mercuria turned to Sinokor, which has since grown into the key non-state-backed player in the strait.

In early March, Larry Johnson, Mercuria’s global head of marine business, reached out directly to Sinokor’s chartering manager, KB Lee, Hauspy testified.

Sinokor had tankers inside Hormuz when the conflict began. To get its crude out, Mercuria fixed Sinokor’s Singapore Loyalty (IMO: 9322293) on March 11 and Habrut (IMO: 9500730) on March 13.

Sources indicate that the prices on the fixtures were redacted in the court filing; Hauspy said, “They were extremely high. We agreed primarily because we had little choice.”.

Importantly, the charter terms included a special demurrage structure taking into account the risk of not being able to transit the strait, a structure that would become a model for future charter negotiations.

Mercuria agreed to pay a daily demurrage rate as the cargo holder that declined as time passed, “meaning that if the ship was trapped inside the Arabian Gulf for a long time, the fixture essentially became cheap floating storage for Mercuria”, Hauspy recounted.

“This structure was designed to incentivise the shipowner to cross the strait as soon as it was possible to do so, given that the demurrage recovery would continuously decrease.”.

Industry observers note that singapore Loyalty was promptly loaded but then waited “for at least a month” before it transferred its cargo to another VLCC, Fujairah Energy (IMO: 9723071), off Dubai on May 24-25. Fujairah Energy then successfully transited the strait.

Industry observers note that hauspy remarked Fujairah Energy was thought to be “better able to cross the strait”, although he did not explain why. He added that Sinokor originally opposed the switch but “ultimately agreed to perform the operation” after he called Lee.

It has been revealed that by contrast, Habrut transited the strait in April without incident or any warning from the Iranians. “It was a bit of a surprise,” stated Hauspy.

It has been revealed that “I believe she was ultimately owned or operated by a partially or fully Omani-state-owned tech giant. My belief is that because of this ownership, the Omani government assisted somehow with the ship’s transit through the strait, but I don’t know for sure.”.

According to data from Lloyd’s List Intelligence, the beneficial owner of Habrut is the government of Oman.

Hauspy said that one of the early Mercuria fixtures of Sinokor tonnage was reported by McQuilling at Worldscale 1,020, and that he called the broker to dispute that it was a “market” rate, because the fixtures were off prompt dates (not 15-30 days forward as usual), and had a storage-deal aspect due to the special demurrage terms.

‘Impossible’ to fix VLCCs inside Hormuz.

With the Mercuria crude cargoes exiting the strait, Hauspy focused on finding newly introduced business inside the strait and making money on the crisis.

“It was apparent to me that the profit from such a fixture would potentially be significant” and “significantly greater than we might make from alternative employment”, he explained.

However, owners would not allow VLCCs chartered to Mercuria to enter the strait without a special clause. “That became known as a ‘Strait of Hormuz Clause’ or ‘SOH Clause’, and became a feature of my negotiations involving ships loading inside the Arabian Gulf,” said Hauspy.

Sources indicate that that clause permitted a ship to wait until it was deemed safe for the vessel and crew to transit Hormuz. Either the owner or the master could refuse the voyage.

Industry observers note that for some customers, this wouldn’t work. “Unipec had very strict requirements, essentially requiring a warranty that the ship could transit the strait as scheduled. This was simply not possible,” stated Hauspy.

For other customers, there was potential to negotiate. In return for accepting an SOH clause, customers required “some sort of compensation structure to incentivise that transit as soon as possible”.

The decreasing demurrage fee concept previously used by Sinokor and Mercuria was discussed for newly introduced potential fixtures, with some tweaks. One idea was to pay a portion of the demurrage to the owner chartering the ship to Mercuria, and for terms allowing the charterparty to be cancelled after a certain number of waiting days.

Hauspy tried hard, making almost daily unsolicited offers for inside-Hormuz business, but to no avail. In the court filing, he listed 24 attempts between April 22 and June 15 to fix five VLCCs chartered by Mercuria: Maran Leo (IMO: 9602473), Maran Arete (IMO: 9776547), Maran Thetis (IMO: 9421427), Sophia (IMO: 9776559) and Olympic Luck (IMO: 9424211).

“I cast the net wide with these offers,” he remarked. There were some negotiations, a few ships placed on subjects, but no fixtures that didn’t fail.

“I was not able to fix any of Mercuria’s VLCCs to load exclusively inside the Arabian Gulf, no matter the rate offered,” mentioned Hauspy. “It was impossible.”.

The rise of the Adnoc shuttle trade.

The dynamics described by Mercuria’s freight trader highlight two key hurdles amid the crisis: the high safety risk to ships and crew on one hand, and the high commercial risk of “who pays if we get stuck waiting?” on the other.

The shuttle tanker system pioneered by Adnoc solved both problems.

Owners wouldn’t have to take Hormuz risk — they could load by ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman — cargo interests wouldn’t risk having to pay massive demurrage costs on cargo stuck inside the strait, and charterers wouldn’t have to risk loss of hire if tonnage was waylaid in the AG.

Hauspy stated he first become aware of the Adnoc shuttle service in mid-April. “The benefit of this for the customer is that their ship did not have to risk crossing the strait. Adnoc would take on that risk.”.

Mercuria took advantage of the Adnoc shuttle service and fixed “a number” of VLCCs loading off Oman.

Hauspy did not directly deal with Adnoc headquarters, but with Richard Lewis, chief commercial officer of Navig8 (Adnoc bought Navig8 for $1bn-plus in 2025). Lewis and Navig8 “effectively acted as the middleman between Adnoc and Mercuria”, he noted.

It has been revealed that hauspy described the first shuttle fixture done by Mercuria in late April. “I remember negotiating this fixture with Richard directly. We had agreed that he would provide us with the Barakah (IMO: 9902615), which would load inside the Arabian Gulf and perform an STS operation in Fujairah.”.

Brief respite during ‘peace’ MOU period.

The market changed yet again with the US-Iran peace MOU in mid-June. “I noticed more willingness from shipowners to explore options to load inside the Arabian Gulf following this agreement,” mentioned Hauspy.

Mercuria was able to fix some of its fleet, although none of its VLCCs, and was able to charter in VLCC tonnage on a spot basis loading inside the AG. Hauspy said he believed these fixtures included SOH Clauses.

Mercuria was offered US military support during this period. He testified that he held a Teams call in mid-July with Chimi Zacot and Andrew Weiner of the US Department of Energy.

“They were exploring ways to move ships through the strait with some military assistance,” Hauspy said, adding that Mercuria subsequently secured a US escort for a voyage of Sinokor’s Monaco Loyalty (IMO: 9312511).

Then the peace MOU fixture window closed.

“Only a few weeks after the MOU was signed, attacks on ships in the strait resumed, and my experience was that confidence in the market deteriorated again,” noted Hauspy.

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a fresh AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse ….

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Sources indicate that reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary owners – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […].

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most key takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”.

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”.

“The enshittification continues.”.

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”.

Sources indicate that “This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”.

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”.

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”.

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”.

It has been revealed that I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.
