#387. The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1888 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach. He loves speaking at conferences like Smashing Conf and is a founding member of the Adobe Design … More about Andy ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way. Not always in those exact words, obviously. It usually comes out as something more reasonable: we didn’t get enough engineering time, product had already decided the solution, the roadmap was too packed, leadership only cared about this quarter’s numbers, research got cut, the experiment was never run properly, the design debt was known about, but nobody wanted to spend a sprint fixing it.

Much of this is true. Most designers have worked inside that awkward middle space between product and engineering. Product frames the problem, or at least thinks it does. Engineering decides what is feasible, or at least what is affordable. Design is expected to make the thing clearer, simpler, more coherent, more usable, and occasionally more desirable, while also being careful not to disrupt the blueprint too much.

That position has always been uncomfortable.

Industry observers note that they can spot the broken onboarding flow, the confusing upgrade path, the empty state that makes owners feel stupid, the feature that looks reasonable in a product review but makes no sense in real use. Seeing the problem is one thing. Getting it fixed is another.

So design often becomes an argument. You make the case. You annotate the flow. You bring the research clip. You point to the support tickets. You show the Figma prototype. You explain why the “small edge case” is actually the first-run experience for half your fresh people. Then everyone nods, agrees it matters, and moves on to whatever had already made it onto the roadmap.

Sources indicate that this is one reason AI is more interesting for design than the usual “will it replace designers?” debate suggests. The real change is not that designers can make more screens. Nobody needs more screens. The interesting change is that designers may need less permission.

A good designer can now move from “we should fix this” to “I fixed this, and pushed it live.” They can prototype the alternative onboarding flow, write and test clearer product copy, build a rough working version of the interaction, clean up small pieces of design debt without waiting three months for a roadmap slot, and make the better thing visible enough that it becomes harder to ignore.

That changes the politics of the work. Design has often relied on persuasion because designers lacked direct means of production. AI weakens that dependency. Not everywhere, and not for everything. Complex products still have architecture, infrastructure, data models, permissions, security, compliance, legacy systems, and all the other unglamorous reasons software is hard. But the boundary is moving.

Recent findings suggest that in this version of the future, designers become less permission-dependent: less reliant on product to bless the problem, less reliant on engineering to make every small improvement real, less trapped in the role of internal critic, taste-provider, or Figma operator. More able to make, test, repair, and ship.

Recent findings suggest that the best designers start to look less like traditional product designers and more like hybrid product leaders. They still care about interaction, hierarchy, language, flow, brand and craft, but they also understand the commercial shape of the problem. They can make trade-offs. They can prototype in code, or close enough to code. They can use AI to explore options swiftly, then use judgment to throw most of them away. They can sit with a founder or PM and move from a vague product concern to something tangible by the end of the day.

In a recent development, there may be fewer of these people, but they will be harder to ignore. The current design-org model was partly built around scarcity: scarce engineering time, slow production, expensive prototypes, handoffs between specialists, heavy coordination across teams. If AI reduces some of that scarcity, it probably reduces the need for some of the roles that grew around it. The optimistic case is not that every designer keeps their job and gets a productivity boost. That feels like wishful thinking. The more believable version is that the total number of designers goes down, but the designers who remain have more direct influence over the product.

That is not a bad outcome for the strongest designers. It may even be the thing many of them have wanted for years.

Autonomy has teeth. If AI gives designers more room to act, it also removes some of the cover. The same constraints that held good designers back have also protected weaker ones from being tested too directly.

It has been revealed that for years, it has been easy to say: I had a better idea, but we never got the engineering time. Sometimes that was exactly what happened. Sometimes the better idea was never really more than a critique. It had not been made concrete. It had not been tested. It had not dealt with the awkward trade-offs. It sounded strong because it lived safely in opposition to the shipped thing.

It has been revealed that if you can prototype the recommendation, the recommendation has to get better. If you can make the alternative flow, the flow has to survive contact with details. If you can test the product copy, you have to care what happens when owners read it. If you can fix the small piece of design debt, you have to decide whether it was really worth fixing.

Some designers are not as strategic as they think they are. They have learned the language of strategy without the discomfort of owning outcomes. They can talk about user needs, business goals, systems thinking, and product quality, but struggle when asked to make a call. They want influence, but not the exposure that comes with it.

The profession has spent a long time arguing that design deserves more power. Fine. But more power means fewer excuses. It means the work is judged less by the elegance of the argument and more by the quality of the thing you made, tested, or changed. That is a better standard, but it will not be kind to everyone.

Recent findings suggest that there is a second bear case, and it is probably the one large design teams should worry about most. Product and engineering already have more institutional power than design in most companies. They own the roadmap, the technical architecture, the sprint machinery, the metrics, and usually the language leadership understands. Design often has to translate its concerns into someone else’s terms before they count.

AI may not rebalance that power. It may hand product and engineering enough design capability to make design easier to bypass. A PM who can generate a decent flow, decent copy, and a decent prototype may not feel the same need to involve design early. An engineer who can use AI to produce a reasonable interface may decide the design system covers enough of the decision-making. A founder who can get to a polished demo in an afternoon may confuse polish with product thinking.

The problem is not that these people will suddenly become great designers. The problem is that many companies do not know the difference between great design and plausible design. Plausible design is dangerous. It looks coherent in a product review. It uses the right components. The spacing is fine. The copy is not embarrassing. The flow mostly works. Nobody in the meeting feels strongly enough to object. So it ships.

If a company already thinks design is mostly screens, prototypes, and polish, AI gives it a cheaper way to get those things.

According to recent reports, in that world, design does not gain more agency. It gets narrowed. The remaining designers manage the design system, police component usage, review flows that have already been decided, tidy the interface, maintain brand consistency, and get pulled into high-stakes launches, executive demos, and the occasional messy cross-platform problem. Useful work, but a smaller surface area. Less shaping the product, more maintaining the furniture.

According to recent reports, this is why the “AI will automate the boring 20%” argument feels too comforting. In some companies, perhaps that is what happens. But in large tech organisations, where design teams grew around coordination, production and process, the cut could be much deeper. Not 20%. Maybe 50%. Maybe more. Especially in places where leadership never really understood why the design team had grown so large in the first place.

In a recent development, the painful part is that both futures can be true at the same time. AI can make the best designers more capable and many average designers less necessary. It can give design more agency while reducing design headcount. It can help a small number of designers move closer to product leadership while pushing others into governance and clean-up work. It can free designers from waiting for permission, then reveal that some were more comfortable waiting than acting.

The designers who do well will not be the ones who merely use AI to produce more options. Options are cheap now. They will be the ones who know which option is worth pursuing, why it matters, how to test it, what to cut, where the product is lying to itself, and when “good enough” is quietly damaging the business.

Recent findings suggest that they will have taste, but taste will not be enough. They will need product judgment, technical curiosity, commercial awareness and the nerve to make decisions before every variable is settled. They will need to be comfortable moving between a customer conversation, a prototype, a pricing concern, a brand question, and a messy implementation detail without insisting that all of those belong to someone else.

I’m not completely sure where we end up. I hope it is closer to the bull case: fewer permission structures, more making, more agency, better designers finally able to show what they can do without being held back by the machinery around them.

I fear it may be closer to the bear case: product and engineering absorb much of the work, companies decide plausible design is good enough, and design loses status, headcount, and strategic ground.

In reality, it will probably be some uncomfortable mix of the two. Some designers will use AI to gain more agency. Some companies will use it to need fewer designers. Some teams will produce better work because the distance between judgment and execution gets shorter. Others will ship more plausible mediocrity because nobody in the room can tell the difference.

For years, designers have said they could create more value if they were less constrained by the organisation around them. AI is about to test that claim. Some will finally get to prove it. Some will find out the constraints were doing them a favour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple rolled out the upcoming MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the tech giant remarked that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”.

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the new system living up to Apple’s claims ….

It has been revealed that the real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple mentioned that the latest model has a completely newly introduced cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the latest PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

According to recent reports, cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone ….

It has been revealed that as we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The manufacturer’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

Industry observers note that I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the tech giant.

Industry observers note that I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an concern with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you were very latest to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

5 AI agents you can actually use on Android in 2026 (and who should use them)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The AI industry has evolved significantly over the last few years.
  • Agentic AI could transform how we do many tasks, from planning and tracking finances to scheduling our lives and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

The AI industry has evolved significantly over the last few years. While chatbots remain one of the most common entry points into the world of AI, agentic systems are also gaining momentum. Early on, most agents had pretty limited capabilities, but that’s slowly changing as agents emerge that not only assist you with minimal manual oversight, but also offer deeper control over apps, platforms, and even Android itself.

Agentic AI could transform how we do many tasks, from planning and tracking finances to scheduling our lives and more. Right now, there are multiple different types of agentic AI systems out there. Let’s take a look at just five of the most interesting platforms out there, designed as semi-autonomous assistants useful to a wide range of folks, from everyday people to power users and professionals.

Claude Duet runs on its own virtual machine, not your physical phone’s hardware. That means it keeps working even if you turn off your device. The entire experience is much more hands-off than an AI chatbot. The AI runs mostly semi-autonomously in the background, only prompting the user when it needs confirmation before sending messages, signing documents, or making other sensitive moves.

In a recent development, duet is easily the most polished experience out there so far, at least as far as the app is concerned. You’ll find the stand-alone Duet app is not only extremely easy to navigate, but it also makes it easy to quickly follow up on ongoing tasks via a dedicated “tasks” tab. It’s capable of continuously monitoring connected cloud services with a variety of supported options like Gmail, Slack, Salesforce, and HubSpot. It can then use that data to help alert you about notable reminders, create daily briefings, and suggest possible tasks.

According to recent reports, you can even use Duet to track payments, flight info, draft emails, create social media campaign drafts, track invoices, and other tasks that an ordinary personal assistant might be trusted with. The catch is that you’ll find some sites and services simply don’t support Duet yet. For example, Walmart works well with Duet as it has embraced AI agents with its Walmart Agent Gateway. In contrast, Amazon has made it clear they aren’t interested in doing the same.

What you won’t find is deep Android-level integration. While it can interact with apps like WhatsApp, Slack, and many email and messaging apps, there are some real limits. While it can input destinations into apps like Google Maps or log data into Health Connect, you won’t be able to influence on-device system controls or anything like that.

It has been revealed that naturally, I’d recommend it most for entrepreneurs, small business owners, executives, and other management roles. It’s arguably less suited for power users or those who want to use it for larger corporate roles.

Industry observers note that google’s agentic platform can be a little confusing, at least unless you’ve been following along carefully. There are actually a few different agentic capabilities, though both are part of the broader Gemini Intelligence framework. First, let’s talk about Gemini Spark.

This part of the experience is probably the closest thing to options like Claude Duet. Spark is an always-on cloud system that lets you offload specific tasks to the AI agent. Maybe you want it to round up every email sent in the last 24 hours so Google can prioritize them for you. Perhaps you want it to plan a trip or research a subject for a school assignment. Spark also offers deep integration around core Google tools like Gmail, Calendar, Google Docs, and Google Drive. There’s even a growing list of third-party services like GitHub, Dropbox, and Canva.

Industry observers note that the second part of this experience goes a bit deeper. While Duet can automatically gather information to create things like daily briefings, Gemini Proactive Assistance takes things up a level. With deep Android integration, you’ll find it can automatically read app alerts, notifications, emails, Pixel screenshots, and more. It uses this information to anticipate needs. For example, you might be walking into a concert hall, and the app notices the context and automatically pulls up your digital ticket. It can also learn from your routines and perform certain tasks automatically, such as sending a weekly work recap to your manager or team.

While Google might take several different approaches to its agentic capabilities, Gemini Intelligence brings it all together into a cohesive experience.

According to recent reports, while some of the Gemini Spark features might be more geared towards the same individuals as Duet, there are a lot more features here for everyday users who are looking to bring a bit of automation into their lives. For Android users especially, Gemini Intelligence opens up a lot of doors thanks to its heavy-handed integration.

Meta Muse is a powerful agentic system that runs entirely on its own virtual machine and is powered by the Muse Spark model. Muse makes a strong first impression, mostly because it doesn’t feel like work. While some of these options were a bit harder to set up, Muse greets you with a cheerful yet somewhat creepy mascot who walks you through the app’s features and helps you get started. There’s even a way to change the avatar’s appearance later.

As with other options above, you can assign it specific tasks and even let it complete purchases, though it stresses that a human gets the final say before any money is spent. Maybe you’re hunting for a deal on a new computer and are looking to save money. You could ask Muse to search stores for open-box or refurbished models and track sale prices for new-in-box units. It would then search the web, complete the research, and present it back to you.

Industry observers note that of course, handing that much access to Meta isn’t something everyone will be comfortable with. Meta notes conversations and VM data aren’t shared with its ad systems, though Muse’s own browsing can influence ads indirectly, and agent interactions can be used for training unless you opt out in the settings.

Similar to Gemini, Muse is clearly aimed at everyday users rather than specifically targeting folks like power users or developers. The friendly onboarding and mascot make it one of the more approachable agentic tools out there, especially for people who’ve been put off by AI in the past. It’s also easy to get started. There’s a free tier that covers most of what people need, though there are also monthly subscriptions starting at $20 a month for those who need more usage. For now, Muse is available to US adults 18 and older on iOS, Android, and the web, with AI glasses support coming later.

Sources indicate that perplexity’s agentic tools come in two flavors, each aimed at a slightly different job. Comet is an AI-powered browser with a built-in assistant, while Perplexity Computer is a more ambitious cloud agent that can handle entire workflows on its own.

It has been revealed that comet is the easier one to wrap your head around. It works like a normal browser, but you can call up the assistant anytime to summarize pages, compare information across tabs, or even research and shop on your behalf. You can also watch what actions the assistant is taking and step in if needed. It’s available on Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows. While it has agentic capabilities, it’s really just scratching the surface.

Perplexity Computer takes things much further. Rather than relying on a single AI, it coordinates a whole lineup of different models, breaking a single prompt into parallel tasks running in the background. Maybe you need a research report with sources, a spreadsheet built from that data, and some code to tie it together. Computer can split the work up and handle each piece at the same time. This is also where Perplexity’s roots in search really shine, making it especially good at research, fact-checking, and pulling in real-time information.

Comet is free and a great fit for everyday people who mostly want help researching and browsing. Computer is a different story. It rolled out as part of the $200 per month Max strategy, with usage-based credits on top for heavier tasks. Since then, it’s come to a few other looks like the $17 a month Pro tier, but you’re only given a very limited amount of credits, and Computer can eat them up fast. Ultimately, Perplexity Computer is best suited to researchers, analysts, and power users.

In a recent development, first, don’t confuse this one with the programming-focused agent of the same name. Available directly from the Play Store, Droid Agent is a bit different from everything else on the list. While many of these options run entirely in the cloud, Droid Agent works at the local device level.

Like Google Intelligence, you’ll have the ability to directly control Android apps that normally wouldn’t be able to talk to each other. This includes moving data from a webpage or document into a specific app, or reading all the PDFs on your phone for expense tracking. Droid Agent is also great at scheduling routine tasks and much more. I’ll be honest, I played around with this one a little directly, but I didn’t feel comfortable giving it unlimited control over my device for long. There’s likely much more capability under the surface I didn’t get to.

Sources indicate that the bottom line, though, is that this is the app for those who want truly deep-level Android capabilities that you can’t even pull off easily with Gemini Intelligence. As for how it works? Basically, it uses wireless ADB to send commands. As you might guess, it requires a lot of setup to get started. It’s also pretty flexible, as it supports a wide range of models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and more.

In a recent development, droid Agent is free to use, beyond the costs of the AI model you bring to the table. Since it’s designed for deep Android control, it’s also very much a power user’s tool and not recommended for everyday users. Still, it might be worth a look if you like tinkering and are fascinated by agentic AI.

In a recent development, AI agents are definitely not slowing down or going away, and I personally think they are worth playing around with. For most users, I wouldn’t pick just one.

In a recent development, if you are highly invested in the Google ecosystem, Gemini Intelligence is a logical place to start. Likewise, Meta Muse is free to test and has decent pricing for those who need more from it.

Recent findings suggest that while we’re seeing the AI agent market take off, it’s important to remember that it’s still very early days. Regardless of which AI agent you use, I strongly recommend using restraint when first testing any of them out. Start by slowly connecting it to apps and services, or even using limited/dummy accounts until you are comfortable that the AI will work exactly how you intend it to.

Industry observers note that why is that? 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a new option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for customers to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a newly introduced Contacts hub that would bring together consumers’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were presently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a newly introduced green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the new Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp indicates who is at the moment online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can promptly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows users to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the upcoming Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

Industry observers note that the motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot notes it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Sources indicate that HUAWEI may have been nearly wiped out of international markets by sanctions imposed on it during the first tenure of US President Donald Trump, but it remains at the top of China’s leaderboard. Along with its innovations across slab phones, foldables, and laptops—including laptops with foldable screens —HUAWEI also offers a broad range of wearables, including ones that monitor blood pressure. So far, the lineup has only comprised smartwatches and fitness bands, but HUAWEI is now adding a health-centric utility in the form of a glucose monitor.

The HUAWEI Sence G1 is the firm’s first continuous glucose monitor (CGM). The device works alongside other HUAWEI products, allowing users to view glucose levels on their phones, a smartwatch, or a HUAWEI fitness band. Besides monitoring a user’s glucose levels, the CGM will also alert them in case of any unusual spikes or dips.

While HUAWEI revealed its entry into the segment in a Weibo post, it refrained from sharing details such as the monitor’s price, availability, or how long the sensor lasts before it must be replaced. Based on the image, we can see the CGM is about the size of a quarter-dollar coin and is ideally worn on the upper arm. Previous leaks cited by the Chinese outlet IT Home suggest that the CGM offers a lag time of 5 to 15 minutes and a MARD of less than 10%.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, in a separate post, HUAWEI’s VP Bruce Lee notes that the product has long been in development. In fact, it is one of the products that it has taken the longest to master. Lee mentions that the first time they tried it was three years ago, i.e., in December 2023, while teams working on it have been wearing it for much longer.

Industry observers note that beyond the development efforts, the long product launch cycle may have been due to the required medical certifications. #370. How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3040 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

In a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

Recent findings suggest that the reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

In this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

Before we start deleting things, let’s quickly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

Industry observers note that baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:.

That 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

You can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page highlights a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

It’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your consumers, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

Industry observers note that so before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

It has been revealed that not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your users would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

2. What does the swap actually cost?

Sources indicate that dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

It has been revealed that libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

Keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

This is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:.

Let’s walk through some of them.

Recent findings suggest that timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

The numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

Industry observers note that you may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:.

humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:.

According to recent reports, one thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

In a recent development, if your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

The browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

The one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():.

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:.

It has been revealed that I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of people and have seen lots of success with it.

It has been revealed that none of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

Recent findings suggest that the libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

Recent findings suggest that A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

Sources indicate that calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

It has been revealed that that single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:.

If you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:.

Clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

The other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:.

Anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between , the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

In a recent development, lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

According to recent reports, lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:.

structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:.

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it indicates the framework telling you to wait.

Industry observers note that temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

It has been revealed that however, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari users don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

The official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

In a recent development, the verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for consumers on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

The clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to customers:.

Industry observers note that for a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

For each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

For each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

Recent findings suggest that for Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the latest code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:.

That way you ship less code to the people who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

Add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.).

It has been revealed that I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:.

None of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships latest features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Google has been giving its Android apps a fresh coat of paint, but Gmail’s settings have remained stubbornly old-fashioned. That’s beginning to change, as a redesigned settings experience we uncovered last month is finally reaching owners, complete with Google’s Material 3 Expressive styling.

Back in October, we discovered that Google was preparing a major cleanup of Gmail’s cluttered settings menu. We enabled the upcoming interface manually on an Android 15 device, but it lacked the system-level Material 3 Expressive styling introduced with Android 16. As a result, we could see the reorganized settings, but not the full visual makeover Google had planned.

Now, thanks to screenshots shared by Telegram user Neacared in AssembleDebug’s channel, we’re getting a much better look at the redesign as it begins rolling out.

The screenshots, captured on Gmail version 2026.11.02.1020540846.Release, reveal a colorful interface featuring rounded cards, expressive switches, and icons that make different settings easier to identify. Instead of scrolling through a seemingly endless collection of options, users get neatly organized sections for notifications, inbox customization, email preferences, writing assistance, and more.

Individual pages have received the same treatment. Settings for Smart Compose, Smart Reply, and Proofread now sit together under Writing assistance, while Chat and Meet have their own dedicated sections. The fresh interface also uses larger touch targets and more generous spacing throughout.

This isn’t happening in isolation. We’ve previously uncovered similar settings redesigns for the Google app, Gemini, and Google Messages. These changes point to a broader effort to make Google apps feel more consistent with Android’s modern design language while simplifying navigation.

As for availability, the refreshed Gmail settings are rolling out server-side, meaning installing the latest app version alone won’t necessarily unlock them. We haven’t established how widely the new interface is available yet, so don’t be surprised if your settings still look unchanged.

In a recent development, scarlet Witch might have one of the most interesting roles to play in “Avengers: Doomsday,” and I’m not just saying that because Wanda Maximoff is one of my favorite Marvel characters. After seemingly meeting her end in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” fans have been waiting to find out whether Elizabeth Olsen will return to the MCU. Now, with Doctor Doom seemingly taking an interest in Wanda and her extraordinary powers, there’s plenty of room for speculation about what Marvel has planned.

It has been revealed that but why would Doom need Scarlet Witch in the first place? Wanda is one of the most powerful magic users in the Marvel universe, with reality-altering abilities that could make her an incredibly valuable ally or a terrifying enemy. Her comic-book history also offers some intriguing possibilities, particularly when you look at storylines like “House of M” and “The Children’s Crusade.”.

Of course, Marvel hasn’t confirmed exactly how Wanda fits into “Avengers: Doomsday,” so we’ll have to wait and see how much of this speculation holds up. Still, there are several fascinating directions the studio could take her story. Here are five Scarlet Witch theories that could explain Doctor Doom’s interest in Wanda and what her potential MCU comeback might look like.

One popular theory is that “Avengers: Doomsday” could take inspiration from Marvel Comics’ “The Children’s Crusade.” In the comic, Wanda disappears after the events of “Avengers Disassembled” and “House of M.” Her sons, Billy and Tommy, eventually set out to find her with the Young Avengers. They discover that Wanda is living in Latveria with Doctor Doom, having lost her memories. Doom is secretly using her powerful magic for his own purposes. The young heroes eventually confront him and help Wanda escape, revealing that she has been manipulated rather than acting as a villain herself.

In a recent development, there are a few reasons this storyline could work in the MCU. At the end of “VisionQuest,” Vision, Billy and Tommy are together, leaving Wanda as the missing member of the family. One possibility is that Doom could erase Wanda’s memories or take advantage of her vulnerability to control her powers.

He might even use her desire to reunite with her family to keep her on his side. Of course, Marvel hasn't confirmed that it’s adapting this storyline, and we don’t yet know how much of the comic could make it into the movie. It’s also possible that Wanda’s reunion with her children will be saved for “Avengers: Secret Wars” instead.

Scarlet Witch could be connected to a mysterious group of masked characters known as the “Latverian Witches.” These figures have appeared in “Avengers: Doomsday” promotional material, including posters, convention displays and leaked concept art. One particular poster caught fans’ attention because one of the masked witches is red. This has led to speculation that Scarlet Witch could be part of the group, possibly working alongside Doctor Doom.

In a recent development, there have also been reports of a “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” page on Disney+ featuring promotional artwork showing Wanda and Doctor Strange in front of a Latverian mural. However, the details surrounding the witches are still unclear. Some reports describe three masked figures wearing different colored robes, while others point to artwork featuring four characters. There is no official confirmation that Wanda is one of them.

According to recent reports, this theory also fits with the idea that Doom is gathering powerful characters to help carry out his plans. In the post-credits scene attached to the “Avengers: Endgame” theatrical rerelease, Doom approaches Bruce Banner in an underground bunker and tells him, “I've come to collect you.” Banner then disappears alongside Doom, leaving behind a glowing green symbol. We know he’s also collected Scarlet Witch, meaning these “witches” might all hold a special power to help Doom complete his plans.

According to recent reports, it’s possible that Scarlet Witch could take the place of Molecule Man in Marvel’s “Secret Wars” storyline. In the comics, Doctor Doom uses enormous amounts of power to reshape reality and create Battleworld, a world made from the remains of destroyed universes. He then rules over it as God Emperor Doom.

Industry observers note that some fans think Marvel could use Wanda instead of introducing Molecule Man, especially since she’s already an established character with incredible reality-warping abilities. We’ve seen her create an entire town in “WandaVision” and travel between universes in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.” That makes her a believable target for Doom, particularly after his apparent promise that her power will be his.

But how would he use it? One possibility is that Doom steals Wanda’s chaos magic to build Battleworld and take control of the multiverse. This could also connect to the Darkhold prophecy mentioned in “Agatha All Along,” which claims that the Scarlet Witch is destined to destroy the world.

In a recent development, there’s another possibility, though. Rather than simply forcing Wanda to help him, Doom could offer her a deal. He might promise to create a new reality where she can live happily with Vision, Billy and Tommy in exchange for her help. That would give Wanda a personal reason to side with him, even if she doesn’t fully understand his looks. It could also set up a heartbreaking conflict when her family discovers what Doom has done.

One of the biggest theories following “VisionQuest” is that Doctor Doom could use Wanda to destroy Earth-10005, the universe home to the original Fox “X-Men” movies. “Avengers: Doomsday” is expected to bring together heroes from three different universes: the MCU’s Earth-616, the Fantastic Four’s Earth-828 and the X-Men’s Earth-10005. With Marvel planning to introduce its own version of the X-Men after this saga, some fans believe the Fox universe could be destroyed as part of the story.

This theory has an interesting connection to House of M, one of Scarlet Witch’s most famous comic-book storylines. In it, Wanda utters the iconic line “No more mutants,” causing mutants to lose their powers. Elizabeth Olsen has previously noted she would love to deliver the line in the MCU, but there’s been no opportunity yet. Having Wanda use her powers against the Fox “X-Men” universe could be Marvel’s way of bringing that moment to life.

In a recent development, it’s possible that the Sentinels shown in the “Doomsday” trailer might actually be designed to contain Wanda rather than hunt mutants. There’s also a less villainous possibility. Instead of Wanda destroying the mutants, she could turn against Doom and use her powers to stop him from wiping them out. This could lead to a twist on her famous comic-book line: “No, more mutants.” It might even set up the arrival of mutants in the rebooted MCU.

As we know in the “VisionQuest” finale, the post-credit scene revisits Wanda’s apparent death beneath Mount Wundagore in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” but this time we see what happened after the temple collapsed. Doctor Doom uses green magic to lift the rubble before telling Wanda, “Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine.” Moments later, her eyes open.

But how exactly did Doom bring her back? One popular fan theory notes Wanda never actually died. Instead, the red flash of magic seen as Wundagore collapsed could have been her Chaos Magic protecting her and placing her in some kind of healing coma. Doom may simply have found her and awakened her. Another possibility is that Doom rescued Wanda immediately after the collapse but kept her hidden for years. This would explain why nobody else managed to find her and why she was considered gone. Some fans even believe he could have used time travel to return to the moment Wundagore fell and save her.

Sources indicate that there’s also the possibility that Wanda really did die and Doom used magic to resurrect her. In fact, he could have stolen power from Franklin Richards, who demonstrated the ability to bring someone back to life in “The Fantastic Four: First Steps.” Whatever the explanation, Doom clearly has a reason for bringing Wanda back, and his warning that her power will be his suggests she’s central to his prepares, and could be the most powerful weapon against the Avengers.

Sources indicate that today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sources indicate that sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.

Recent findings suggest that but ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.

We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.

When front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

Sources indicate that when our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

It has been revealed that we didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

For instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

Industry observers note that the tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

According to recent reports, because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

To achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:.

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:.

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:.

It has been revealed that the result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

Sources indicate that because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Recent findings suggest that since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:.

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:.

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:.

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:.

In a recent development, another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

We handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:.

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

Industry observers note that lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:.

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

Sources indicate that because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

It’s an exciting time to be an Android emulation fan. Not only is the emulation scene moving quickly lately, but native recompilation projects are also speeding up, letting you bypass the emulator layer to run console titles “natively” on Android. Nintendo Switch 2 emulators have recently landed on various platforms, including Android, and projects like BananaNative have inspired other devs to port console titles like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake to Android within a week of release! Now, the upcoming Peanuts Native open-source project builds on BananaNative to convert several Nintendo Switch games into standalone Android games with live second-screen companion support for Android handhelds.

Revealed by Reddit user SuperbShop4757, who also created Eden Duo (a fork of the Eden Switch emulator focused on dual-screen Android handhelds like the AYN Thor), Peanuts Native is a fork of BananaNative. As such, it is a native translation layer and not an emulator.

Industry observers note that users supply their own legally dumped game files (NSP, XCI, or dump folders) alongside their console’s prod.keys file. The Peanuts Native app processes the game files directly on the device by rewriting the game’s ARM64 code to execute directly on the phone’s CPU, replaying graphics over Vulkan, and pre-translating shaders. The build process takes between five and 40 minutes on an AYN Thor, which is impressive given the technical complexity and overhead involved.

The standout feature of Peanuts Native is its dual-screen functionality tailored for handhelds like the AYN Thor. While the main game runs on the top display, the bottom screen renders touch-enabled companion overlays that support interactions and haptic feedback. Peanuts Native also uses the same companion package format as Eden Duo, so existing companions — which display live maps, inventories, quests, and party stats pulled directly from game memory — work out of the box here too.

Single-screen Android devices can still run the converted games without the secondary display features.

At launch, Peanuts Native supports these 12 Switch titles:.

To run Peanuts Native, consumers need a device running Android 13 or later with at least 12GB of RAM and a Snapdragon GPU supporting Vulkan 1.3, with custom Turnip drivers recommended.

As an early release, the developer notes that users should expect bugs and missing features like SD card support and mods, adding that Peanuts Native will coexist alongside Eden Duo rather than replace it.

Sources indicate that pip install gawain without an extra installs only the gawain command. It then needs a checker on PATH, or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.

Use gawain with care. ty is in beta, and its diagnostics may change between versions. If that is a problem for your project, use pyrefly, or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.

Recent findings suggest that gawain exits with 0 when nothing is reported, 1 when it reports an error, and 2 on a usage error or when the type checker cannot run. The type checker's warnings are printed but do not fail the check.

docs/rules.md has the full rules, the exemptions and the suppression syntax.

The default mode is obvious. A name may go without an annotation when its value has an obvious type and the name is never assigned again: a literal (count = 0), a container of literals (ids = [1, 2, 3]) or a constructor call (user = User("ada")). strict asks for an annotation on every assignment:.

New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling
