#297. Tech Report: Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2804 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac

Tech Report: Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that apple’s HomeView smart display is here.
  • I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen.
  • Recent findings suggest that homeView is an adorable little thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-newly introduced software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

Recent findings suggest that homeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

Sources indicate that homeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

Industry observers note that I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

Sources indicate that in terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-glitch. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

According to recent reports, sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In a recent development, in practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

It has been revealed that homeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could promptly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone people.

Industry observers note that you can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple indicates that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

Recent findings suggest that the faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

In a recent development, swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

Sources indicate that there is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:.

According to recent reports, I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

It has been revealed that I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

Recent findings suggest that I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

In a recent development, one of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

Recent findings suggest that this is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

It has been revealed that the feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

Recent findings suggest that homeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

Sources indicate that in practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

Industry observers note that in addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

In a recent development, homeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple indicates that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Industry observers note that many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

Industry observers note that there is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software patch coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

Recent findings suggest that homeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

Industry observers note that when you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

It has been revealed that at first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It has been revealed that it’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

It has been revealed that in fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

Google’s newly introduced Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.
  • Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.
  • Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

According to recent reports, google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

On the privacy front, there is a blinking white indicator light when you use the camera to take pictures or record clips that are saved to your library. If the light is covered or disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Android XR running a hardware check when charging.

It has been revealed that gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

According to recent reports, battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

In a recent development, warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#293. Industry News: A family tree of software job titles

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zwischenzugs

Industry News: A family tree of software job titles

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zwischenzugs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’.
  • So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.
  • It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from.

So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.

It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree.

There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom.

Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family:.

According to recent reports, A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold.

On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE).

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with:.

Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows.

In a recent development, A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common, not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug.

Drawing it out made a few patterns hard to miss.

In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women.

It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer.

According to recent reports, go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming.

The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it).

Sources indicate that by the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers.

Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008.

This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before, playing out in job titles.

The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears.

The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles.

Recent findings suggest that the newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it presently claims “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets.

‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation.

‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef.

The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations.

Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem.

Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.).

Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’.

The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting upcoming names.

In a recent development, when I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far.

Recent findings suggest that the dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo.

Which brings me back to the coders.

In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same noted about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part.

I’ll leave you to draw that arrow yourself.

Several Pixel users have taken to platforms like Reddit and the Google Support forum to report that their phones’ screensavers aren’t dimming while charging at night. Naturally, this is leaving users with unusually bright bedrooms.

Industry observers note that for reference, the feature, which can be accessed via Settings > Display & touch > Screen saver, lets you select a built-in screensaver that appears while your device is charging. It can be set to only show while charging, while upright and charging, or only while wirelessly charging. Considering that a lot of us charge our phones overnight, the accompanying low-light mode is a nifty addition that ensures screensavers adjust to the surrounding lighting conditions.

Industry observers note that the feature lets you use your Pixel as a bedside clock without its screen light filling up your entire bedroom, and that functionality is exactly what seems to be broken right now. And before you comment, yes, you can manually lower your phone’s brightness, but that makes low-light mode redundant.

Multiple reports about the issue describe similar problems, and almost all affected say that their screensaver’s low-light mode worked perfectly before the November upgrade.

More importantly, people report that manually lowering brightness doesn’t help as it slowly creeps right back up:.

At least one other user added that in addition to their clock screensavers being bright, they look functionally different too:.

Although others haven’t corroborated the change to the basic clock design, the repeated complaints about screensavers struggling to dim (and stay dim) suggest that something is indeed wrong with the feature.

Adding to the reports, in a different article about a Pixel Camera bug that the November update seemingly introduced, an Android Authority reader also added that the update had broken low light mode on their Clock screensaver:.

The revision also broke Low Light Mode on the Clock Screensaver.

On Pixel cameras are failing after November enhancement.

Based on the number of reports available, this doesn’t appear to be a widespread matter. However, it isn’t an isolated one either — and it’s clearly one that can disrupt a good night’s sleep. Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a significant upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole newly introduced set of powers with the new patch.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:.

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

It has been revealed that I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m presently viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

It has been revealed that in theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch. For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

#281. 5 best Christmas movies to watch on Netflix now — including festive favorites starring Kurt Russell, J.K. Simmons and Minka Kelly

5 best Christmas movies to watch on Netflix now — including festive favorites starring Kurt Russell, J.K. Simmons and Minka Kelly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christmas starts at the beginning of November for me, and I’m not ashamed to admit that my tree is already up.
  • Industry observers note that whether you’re after a feel-good family adventure, a heartwarming romantic story or something with a little more star power, there’s a festive flick worth adding to your queue.
  • So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and get comfortable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christmas starts at the beginning of November for me, and I’m not ashamed to admit that my tree is already up. That means we’re officially entering my favorite time of year, when there’s nothing better than getting cozy, switching on the TV and settling in with a festive movie. If you’re anything like me, it’s never too early to start working through your Christmas watchlist, and Netflix has plenty of options to get you in the holiday spirit.

Industry observers note that whether you’re after a feel-good family adventure, a heartwarming romantic story or something with a little more star power, there’s a festive flick worth adding to your queue. I've rounded up five of the best Christmas movies streaming on Netflix right now, including favorites starring Kurt Russell, J.K. Simmons and Minka Kelly.

So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and get comfortable. The countdown to Christmas is officially on.

“The Christmas Chronicles” is one of those festive films I find myself coming back to every year, and it's firmly part of my Christmas viewing tradition. Kurt Russell makes for a brilliantly unconventional Santa Claus, swapping the usual jolly grandfather image for something a little more street-smart, sarcastic and action-ready. Apparently, Russell even went as far as writing a 200-page backstory for the character, covering Santa’s history and his relationship with Mrs. Claus. It’s a fun twist on the familiar Christmas formula, and its popularity was strong enough to launch a sequel in 2020.

Recent findings suggest that siblings Kate (Darby Camp) and Teddy Pierce (Judah Lewis) come up with a proposal to catch Santa Claus (Kurt Russell) on camera on Christmas Eve. After spotting him arriving at their home, the pair sneak aboard his sleigh, but their unexpected appearance causes it to crash in Chicago. With Santa’s reindeer scattered, his magical hat missing and his sack of presents lost, the children agree to help him recover everything before morning. Their night takes them on a chaotic adventure involving police chases, unexpected encounters and a visit to the North Pole, as they race against the clock to make sure presents reach children around the world.

“Klaus” is easily one of the most beautiful animated Christmas films out there, with its hand-drawn visuals giving it the feel of a storybook brought to life. It’s also a pretty remarkable success story, considering traditional studios initially passed on the project because 2D animation was seen as commercially outdated. Thankfully, Netflix gave it a home, and it went on to win seven Annie Awards, a BAFTA and an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. I’d say it deserved every bit of that recognition. It’s a wonderfully heartfelt festive watch and one I always recommend adding to your Christmas movie lineup.

Industry observers note that spoiled postman-in-training Jesper (Jason Schwartzman) is sent to the remote, snow-covered town of Smeerensburg, where he must deliver 6,000 letters within a year or lose his family fortune. However, the miserable locals are locked in a bitter feud and have little interest in sending mail. Just as Jesper considers giving up, he meets Klaus (J.K. Simmons), a mysterious carpenter living alone in the woods with a cabin full of handmade toys. The pair strike a deal to deliver toys to the town’s children, but their growing popularity soon threatens to disrupt the locals’ long-standing rivalry.

Industry observers note that I have to admit, 2025 turned out to be a surprisingly strong year for Netflix’s original Christmas movies, and “My Secret Santa” was one of the ones I genuinely enjoyed. Alexandra Breckenridge is a big part of its appeal, particularly if you know her from “Virgin River,” and it’s easy to see why Netflix wanted her front and centre in its festive lineup. There’s plenty of silly physical comedy and amusing disguise antics to keep things light, alongside the cozy romance you’d expect from a seasonal Netflix movie. It’s not reinventing the Christmas rom-com, but I had a good time with it.

When single mom Taylor Jacobson (Alexandra Breckenridge) loses her job just before Christmas, she finds herself struggling to make ends meet while trying to afford snowboarding lessons for her daughter. Desperate for work, Taylor hatches an unusual blueprint with the help of her friends: disguise herself as an elderly man and land a seasonal job playing Santa Claus at the luxury Sun Peaks ski resort. Her transformation works, and she soon finds herself entertaining holiday guests while working alongside resort manager Matthew Layne (Ryan Eggold). However, keeping her real identity under wraps becomes increasingly difficult.

“The Best Christmas Pageant Ever” is a lovely festive surprise, particularly if you’re after something a little different from the usual sugary holiday movies. Based on Barbara Robinson’s beloved 1972 children’s novel, this 2024 adaptation brings plenty of cheeky humor to its small-town Christmas setting while still delivering plenty of seasonal warmth. It also proved to be a sleeper hit at the box office, and its impressive Rotten Tomatoes scores speak for themselves, with 92% from critics and 97% from audiences. That’s a pretty strong endorsement for a Christmas movie, and I’d say it's well worth giving a chance.

Six troublesome siblings known as the Herdmans have a reputation for causing chaos wherever they go. But when they turn up at church looking for free snacks, they unexpectedly land the leading roles in the town’s annual Christmas pageant. First-time director Grace Bradley (Judy Greer) is left scrambling to keep the production on track, while her daughter Beth (Molly Belle Wright) watches as the newcomers turn rehearsals upside down. With the townspeople convinced the performance is destined for disaster, the Herdmans’ unconventional approach to the Nativity story leads to an unexpectedly memorable Christmas production.

Recent findings suggest that “Champagne Problems” was another festive highlight from Netflix last year, swiftly finding an audience with more than 20 million views in its opening week and topping the streamer’s global film chart. Director Mark Steven Johnson has clearly found his niche with these feel-good romantic comedies, having previously worked with Netflix on “Love, Guaranteed” and “Love in the Villa.” This one has all the ingredients of a Hallmark-style holiday romance, complete with a charming European setting and plenty of seasonal escapism. I’m always happy to start watching these sorts of films in mid-November, and this is exactly the kind of cozy pick I’m talking about.

Recent findings suggest that ambitious American executive Sydney Price (Minka Kelly) travels to Paris just before Christmas with an important career opportunity on the table: securing the acquisition of Château Cassell, a renowned French champagne house. After arriving, she takes a night off from negotiations to explore the city and meets a charming stranger named Henri (Tom Wozniczka). The pair hit it off, but their budding romance takes an unexpected turn when Sydney discovers Henri is the son of the champagne company’s founder. With several other potential buyers competing for the deal, Sydney heads to the family vineyard, where she must navigate the increasingly complicated negotiations.

In a recent development, alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#279. Latest Update: Astronomers watched a planet vanish in space. Now they know why.

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (953 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable

Latest Update: Astronomers watched a planet vanish in space. Now they know why.

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For seven years, a NASA telescope watched a planet the size of Jupiter cross in front of its star again and again — until one day it didn't.
  • It has been revealed that the planet, TOI-2535 b, had been acting a little weird for a while.
  • Then, earlier this year, the planet just stopped showing up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For seven years, a NASA telescope watched a planet the size of Jupiter cross in front of its star again and again — until one day it didn't.

It has been revealed that the planet, TOI-2535 b, had been acting a little weird for a while. Each time it passed, which astronomers call a transit, it arrived as much as six hours early or late. The crossings also grew shorter and fainter.

Then, earlier this year, the planet just stopped showing up.

According to recent reports, astronomers knew an exoplanet could drift out of view like this, but they figured it would take decades or even centuries to happen. Imagine their surprise.

"The planet's orbit is tilting so swiftly that its transit disappeared while we were watching," mentioned Samuel Yee, a UCLA postdoctoral fellow and the study's corresponding author, in a statement.

The findings reveal the most extreme case yet of two worlds yanking on each other's orbits. The research also offers a rare clue to how giant planets could end up sidling so close to their stars. Scientists think most of these snuggly planets got there in some violent way. Perhaps a close encounter with another object, for example, knocked them onto a stretched-out orbit, and then their star reeled them in. But this pair likely took a gentler route and spiraled in slowly together, according to the new paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Sources indicate that planet TOI-2535 b sits about 1,000 light-years from Earth. It's what's known as a "hot Jupiter," a gas giant that orbits so close to its star that it finishes a lap in about eight days. By contrast, Mercury, our solar system's closest world to the sun, needs 88 days to make a revolution.

According to recent reports, to be clear, NASA's TESS, short for Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, never saw the planet directly. It infers the presence of a planet by catching the tiny decrease in starlight when one passes in front of its star. One day, TESS could no longer track those fluctuations.

But planets don't normally just disappear into thin space. Astronomers knew something else was going on.

According to recent reports, those fading crossings told the team that the planet's path was sliding from the middle of the star toward its edge until it was no longer traceable. The planet still circles its star, but from Earth it now passes above or below it.

UCLA astrophysicist and co-author Erik Petigura compares it to eclipses.

It has been revealed that "If the moon's orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth's orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month," he said. "But because the moon's orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon's orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.".

That raised a bigger question. What tipped TOI-2535 b's orbit?

Timing (or the lack of it) gave it away. A planet on its own crosses its star on a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b's early and late arrivals told the team that something unseen was tugging on it.

In a recent development, the researchers combined those timing clues with measurements of how the star wobbles as its planets pull on it. Everything pointed to a second planet, likely at least as massive as Saturn, circling nearby and also on a tilted orbit.

Nobody has seen that world, and for the same reason TOI-2535 b has gone AWOL. Its tilted path carries it above or below the star from our space telescope's vantage point, so the mystery planet never blocks any starlight that TESS can detect. But astronomers know it's there because of how hard it pulls on TOI-2535 b.

The two planets continue to pull on each other, so their orbits wobble slowly like spinning tops. The researchers expect TOI-2535 b to swing back into view in 30 to 50 years. But its hidden neighbor may show up sooner.

The pair also tells a story about the past. Astronomers have found hundreds of hot Jupiters, but these planets rarely have a massive neighbor close enough to tug on them. A violent fling couldn't have left two giant planets this close together, according to the research, so this pair likely took the scenic route.

It has been revealed that but a gentler journey should have left the two orbits lying flat. Something had to have later tipped them, though the team doesn't yet know what. This star system may reveal a rare way of forming planets.

The discovery took patience. TESS's first four years of data wouldn't have been enough to reliably catch the change. As the telescope keeps watching, the researchers expect to find more planets slipping in and out of sight.

"We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular," Yee noted, "but that's not true.".
